t: Normal CPU temp at idle, and the GPU's, from 150 hours of mine
d: Idle, my Ryzen 7 5700X3D sat at about 48°C and my RTX 3080 Ti at about 48°C too, over about 150 hours of minutes. What a normal CPU and GPU temp at idle is, why it jumps around, and when a warm idle is worth fixing.
l: PC problems Temperatures normal cpu temp idle normal gpu temp idle average cpu temp idle average gpu temp idle normal cpu and gpu temps idle ideal cpu temp idle cpu temp idle 50c high cpu temp at idle normal cpu idle temp ryzen 7 5800x
b: RigSight has about 150 hours of minutes where my PC sat nearly idle, with the CPU and GPU both under 10% busy while I was at the desk. In those minutes my Ryzen 7 5700X3D averaged 48°C, and 9 in 10 of them stayed under 53°C. My RTX 3080 Ti averaged 48°C too, with most minutes between 45 and 50°C. That's a normal CPU temp at idle and a normal GPU one, and it's warmer than many people expect. Normal CPU temp at idle For most desktop CPUs, somewhere around 35 to 55°C at idle is normal. Where yours sits depends on a few things. The CPU. Many AMD Ryzen chips idle in the 40s or 50s because they boost to high clocks for a moment even at light load. Intel chips often idle a little cooler. The cooler. A big air cooler or a liquid cooler holds idle lower than the small cooler that came in the box. The room. A room 5° warmer makes the idle about 5° warmer. The fans. Quiet fan curves let the CPU sit warmer at idle on purpose. My 5700X3D's idle minutes spread from the low 40s up to about 60°C. One in 10 was under 43°C, and only 1 in 100 reached 60. Normal GPU temp at idle Roughly 30 to 50°C. Many current cards stop their fans when cool and start them once the GPU passes a set point, often around 50 to 60°C. A card like that idles warmer, in the high 40s or low 50s, because nothing is moving air until it needs to. That's why my GPU's idle is so steady at 45 to 50°C. Its fans sit still below about 52°C. GPU fan not spinning has more on that. For the GPU under load, see normal GPU temperature while gaming . Two screens, a high refresh rate or video playing can keep a GPU's memory clock up at idle, which adds a few degrees. Why idle temperatures jump Open a browser, and the CPU jumps 10 or 20° within a second, then falls back. Background tasks do the same thing on their own, like Windows Update, antivirus scans, indexing and app updaters. The CPU's temperature follows its boost almost instantly, so a tool that refreshes every second shows a jumpy line. What counts is where it settles. Normal CPU temperature while gaming covers the jumps under load. When a warm idle is worth fixing The CPU sits above about 60°C, or the GPU above about 60°C, with nothing running. The idle temperature has climbed over weeks or months at the same room temperature. Fans run loud at idle to hold the temperature. If so, check Task Manager for an app keeping the CPU busy first. Then clean dust from the filters, the CPU cooler and the GPU, check that the case fans pull air in at the front and push it out at the back, and set Windows to the Balanced power plan. If it still idles hot on an older PC, new thermal paste on the CPU often helps. How RigSight caught it RigSight records the CPU and GPU temperature every minute along with how busy each was, so it can pick out the minutes when the PC was resting. That's where the numbers above come from. Since 1.12.0, the Temperatures page uses them in its Over the months card, which shows how far each part climbs above its resting temperature under the same load, week by week or month by month. Measuring from rest is what makes slow changes visible. As the card puts it, a warmer room lifts load and rest together, so the gap shows the cooling itself, and a slow climb can come from dust or aging thermal paste. When the CPU or GPU runs hotter at the same load than it used to, Home's PC health card says so. CPU temperature needs RigSight to run with admin rights. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to note your idle temperatures today, with nothing running. That number is your own normal, and it's the one to compare against in a few months. What is a normal CPU temp at idle? Roughly 35 to 55°C for most desktop CPUs. Ryzen CPUs often idle a little higher than Intel ones, in the 40s or 50s, because they boost briefly even at light load. My Ryzen 7 5700X3D idles at about 48°C, and 9 in 10 idle minutes stay under 53°C. What is a normal GPU temp at idle? Roughly 30 to 50°C. Many modern cards stop their fans while cool, so they idle warmer, often in the high 40s or low 50s, and the fans start once the card warms past a set point. My RTX 3080 Ti idles at about 48°C with its fans mostly stopped. Is 50°C idle bad for a CPU? No. 50°C at idle is normal for many CPUs, especially Ryzen chips and small cases. It's worth a look if the idle temperature climbs over weeks, or if it sits above about 60°C with nothing running. Why does my CPU temperature jump at idle? Opening an app, a background task starting or Windows checking for updates makes the CPU boost for a moment, and its temperature follows within a second. Jumps of 10 to 20° that fall back quickly are normal. What matters is where it settles.

t: Can my PC run GTA 6? What's known about the PC version
d: GTA 6 comes out on 19 November on PS5 and Xbox, and Rockstar hasn't announced a PC version or PC requirements. What's known, why the spec lists you see are guesses, and how your heaviest game today tells you more about your PC than any of them.
l: PC problems FPS and games can my pc run gta 6 will my pc run gta 6 gta 6 pc requirements gta 6 pc release date gta 6 pc specs gta 6 pc can my pc handle gta 6 gta 6 pc requirements 1440p gta 6 pc port
b: GTA 6 comes out on 19 November on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. As of 18 November, Rockstar hasn't announced a PC version, a PC date or PC requirements. So the honest answer to "can my PC run GTA 6" is that nobody knows yet, including the sites with spec tables. What you can know is how your PC handles today's heaviest open-world games. Mine has 36 hours of Phantom Blade Zero on record, and that tells me more than any guessed list. What's known about GTA 6 on PC Rockstar's site lists PS5 and Xbox Series X|S for the 19 November launch, and no PC version. GamesBeat reported, from four anonymous sources, that the PC version is planned for early 2027. Rockstar hasn't confirmed it. Take-Two has said news about a PC version will come from Rockstar. Rockstar's last two big games came to PC later. GTA V took about 19 months after consoles, and Red Dead Redemption 2 about a year. Why GTA 6 PC requirements lists are guesses Every list you see is built from something else, GTA V's newer PC edition, the consoles' hardware, or other new games. The lists disagree with each other, and some sites call them leaks without saying where from. Rockstar published minimum and recommended specs for its earlier PC versions, and until it does for GTA 6, there's nothing real to check your PC against. Can my PC run GTA 6? Check it with today's heaviest game Play your heaviest open-world game for an hour, with an overlay or a tool that records, and look at four things. The frame rate and the 1% low. A 1% low far below the average means stutters you'll feel. 1% low FPS explains it. GPU usage. Near 100% means the GPU sets the pace, and lower settings or upscaling give more frames. Normal GPU usage while gaming has more. Graphics memory. A card already near full in today's games has the least room. How to check VRAM usage shows how. Committed memory in Task Manager. Near its limit, 16 GB is tight. Normal RAM usage while gaming covers it. If your PC is comfortable in a big new open-world game today, it starts from a good place. If it's already at its limit, that's worth knowing before any big new game, and the real requirements will show how far off it is. Should you upgrade for GTA 6 now? Not for GTA 6 alone. Nobody knows yet what it needs on PC, and the PC version may be months away, with new parts and prices by then. If your PC runs out of something in the games you play today, that's a reason to upgrade now. What to upgrade in my PC first shows how to find which part. How RigSight caught it RigSight records every play's frame rate from RivaTuner, next to how busy the GPU and CPU were, the graphics memory the game used and how full Windows' memory got. On the Games page, each game's Can it run better? card says how often the GPU was at full load, 95% busy or more, and what sets the pace when it isn't. Since 1.13.0, a game's page also has a Memory card beside Heat and power. Here's Phantom Blade Zero on my RTX 3080 Ti and Ryzen 7 5700X3D, at my settings. 68 FPS on average, with a 1% low of 50. The GPU at full load in 87% of the minutes. It's the limit. The CPU at 47% on average, never near full. About 7 GB of graphics memory for the game itself, of the card's 12. Windows' committed memory at 94% on average, back when the PC had 16 GB. Crimson Desert looked much the same, at about 71 FPS with the GPU at full load 89% of the time. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to play your heaviest game this week and note its frame rate, GPU usage and graphics memory. When Rockstar posts the real PC requirements, you'll know where your PC stands in a minute. Can my PC run GTA 6? Nobody can say for sure yet, because Rockstar hasn't announced a PC version or its requirements. What you can check now is how your PC runs today's heaviest open-world games. If it's comfortable in those, it starts from a good place. When is GTA 6 coming to PC? Rockstar hasn't said. GTA 6 launches on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S on 19 November 2026. GamesBeat reported, from anonymous sources, a PC release planned for early 2027, which Rockstar hasn't confirmed. GTA V came to PC about 19 months after consoles, and Red Dead Redemption 2 about a year after. What are the GTA 6 PC requirements? There are no official ones yet. Lists online are estimates, often based on GTA V's newer PC edition or the consoles, and they disagree with each other. Rockstar will publish the real ones when it announces the PC version. Should I upgrade my PC for GTA 6 now? Not for GTA 6 alone, since nobody knows what it needs on PC yet. Upgrade for the games you play today, based on what your PC runs out of in them. Prices and requirements will both be clearer once the PC version is announced.

t: Normal RAM usage while gaming, and how much games really use
d: When my PC had 16 GB, Phantom Blade Zero used about 4 GB of memory itself, while the whole PC sat at nearly 14 GB. What normal RAM usage while gaming looks like, how much games use, and when it's too much.
l: PC problems Storage and memory normal ram usage while gaming how much ram do games use how much ram do games actually use is 80 ram usage normal while gaming what percentage of ram usage is normal while gaming average ram usage while gaming how much ram should be used while gaming is 16gb ram enough for gaming
b: Until 14 November my PC had 16 GB of memory. While I played Phantom Blade Zero, the game itself used about 4 GB on average and 6.8 GB at its highest. The whole PC meanwhile sat at 13.8 GB on average and reached 15.6 GB. So the game was well under half of what Task Manager showed. The rest was Windows and the apps I keep open. That gap is the first thing to understand about normal RAM usage while gaming. How much RAM do games use? Here's each game's own memory on my PC, and the whole PC's at the same time. Slay the Spire 2 used about 1 GB, with the PC at 9.5 GB. Risk of Rain 2 used about 2 GB, up to 4.9, with the PC at 11 GB. Dota 2 used about 2.9 GB, with the PC at 12.9 GB. Phantom Blade Zero used about 4.1 GB, up to 6.8, with the PC at 13.8 GB. Crimson Desert used about 4.6 GB, up to 5.8, with the PC at 14.5 GB. With no game running, my PC sits around 9 GB. Big open-world and new games can use 8 GB or more of their own, and some recommend 32 GB on their store pages. Normal RAM usage while gaming, in percent 60 to 90% is common, and on a 16 GB PC with a browser open, 80 to 90% is ordinary. High usage alone isn't a problem. Windows keeps recently used files in spare memory to load them faster, and gives that memory back the moment a game needs it. It becomes a problem when there's nothing left to give back. Then Windows moves data to the page file on the drive, which is far slower, and you feel it. Stutters or long hitches, especially when you turn into a new area. Alt-tabbing out takes seconds, and the game is slow to come back. A Windows warning that the PC is low on memory, or a game closing on its own. How to check RAM usage while gaming Open Task Manager with Ctrl + Shift + Esc and go to Performance > Memory . In use is the PC's total. Committed shows two numbers, what apps have asked for and the limit. When the first gets close to the second, Windows is nearly out of memory. On the Processes tab, sort by Memory to see the game's own share and what else is holding memory. How to lower RAM usage while gaming Close browsers and apps you don't need while you play. Browsers with many tabs or video are often the biggest after the game. Turn off apps that start with Windows under Settings > Apps > Startup . Restart the PC before a long session, which clears apps that grew over the day. Leave the page file on, managed by Windows. Turning it off makes running out of memory worse, not better. Lower texture quality if the game also fills the GPU's memory, since some spills into the PC's memory. If you're always near full, more memory is the real fix. Going from 16 to 32 GB is the usual step for gaming now. How RigSight caught it RigSight records memory every minute twice, once for the whole PC and once for each app. That's what splits the 13.8 GB into the game's own 4 GB and everything else. The Memory page lists each app's memory next to its usual, so an app holding more than it normally does stands out. Since 1.13.0 it also says when RAM was 85% full or more today, and which apps held the most then. It also watches Windows' committed memory, which is what apps have asked for, against the limit of memory plus the page file. During Phantom Blade Zero mine averaged 94% of that limit. When stutters bunch up, five or more within 15 minutes, while committed memory is at 90% or more, RigSight names that as what was going on, "while Windows was nearly out of memory". Since 1.7.0 it can also tell you when an app keeps growing in memory for hours, under Apps that keep growing in memory in Settings, off at first. RigSight is free and open source. On 14 November I went to 32 GB. Since then committed memory has averaged about 45% and never gone above 62%, against 94% on average in Phantom Blade Zero before. What that did to my games is in what to upgrade in my PC first . Your next step is to check Committed in Task Manager during your heaviest game. If it stays well below its limit, your memory is fine, however high In use looks. If it gets close and the game stutters, close apps first. For what's holding memory on the desktop, see what is using my RAM . More on memory What is using my RAM , finding the apps that hold it on the desktop. How to check VRAM usage , the GPU's own memory. What to upgrade in my PC first , with my move from 16 to 32 GB. What is normal RAM usage while gaming? Often 60 to 90% of your memory, so 80% is normal on a 16 GB PC with a browser open. Windows and games use memory that would otherwise sit empty. It's only a problem if you get stutters, long pauses when switching apps, or a warning that the PC is low on memory. How much RAM do games actually use? The game itself usually uses 2 to 8 GB. On my PC, Slay the Spire 2 used about 1 GB, Risk of Rain 2 about 2 GB, and Phantom Blade Zero about 4 GB on average and up to 6.8 GB. The rest of what Task Manager shows is Windows and your other apps. Is 16 GB of RAM enough for gaming? For most games, yes, but with little to spare if you keep a browser and other apps open. On my 16 GB PC, a big game plus my usual apps took the PC to 14 to 15.7 GB, close to full. After I moved to 32 GB, Windows' committed memory never went above 62%. How do I lower RAM usage while gaming? Close browsers and apps you don't need, especially ones with many tabs or video, turn off apps that start with Windows, and restart the PC before a long session. Leave the page file on, set to be managed by Windows.

t: A year in review from your own PC, not only Steam
d: Steam Replay arrives in mid-December and covers your Steam games. RigSight's year Rewind is made from your own PC's history once the year ends, with every game, the hottest moments and what went wrong. What goes in it, and what my October looked like.
l: Building RigSight
b: Every December, Steam Replay shows people their year on Steam. Last year it arrived on 16 December. It's fun, and it's also only part of the picture. It counts games on Steam, played while connected, up to about the middle of December. Games from other launchers, the last two weeks of the year and everything else the PC did aren't in it. RigSight already records all of that, minute by minute, on your own PC. So since 0.31.0 it has turned that history into Rewinds, a short look back you can watch and share as a picture. One of them covers the whole year. When a year Rewind is made RigSight makes a Rewind for a month, 3 months, 6 months and a year, once that period has ended. The year one comes after 31 December, when the PC was used on at least 84 days of the year. A PC that was barely on wouldn't have much of a year to show. History has to be kept for at least a year too, which it is unless you've set it shorter in Settings. It's made on your PC, from what your PC recorded, and it stays there. Since 1.11.0 every Rewind covers everything, and Settings > Rewind lists them to watch or share again. Share makes a picture in the shape you pick, for a story, a post or a wide screen. Nothing leaves the PC unless you share that picture yourself. What goes in it How long your PC was on, on how many days, and your biggest day. Month by month, the hours and the game or app you used most in each. When in the day you play, how many different games, your most played and your longest sitting without a break. The hottest your CPU, GPU and the GPU's hot spot got, with the day and what was running. What changed, the apps installed, updated or removed, and new graphics drivers. What went wrong, from app and game crashes to blue screens and sudden shut-offs, with the worst day. Or that nothing did. How much you downloaded and uploaded, and which apps used the most. Games count from every launcher RigSight finds them in, not only Steam, because its Games library reads them all. What my October looked like My own year will be a short one, since RigSight started recording on this PC on 23 September. So here's my October Rewind instead. My PC was on for about 385 hours, on 29 of the month's 31 days, and my biggest day was 5 October. About 106 of those hours were in 18 games. Risk of Rain 2 was my most played, at about 33 hours over 22 plays. My longest sitting was Phantom Blade Zero, 3 hours and 34 minutes without a break on 30 October. The GPU's hottest moment was 73°C, in No Man's Sky on 7 October. That month I installed 15 apps, updated 45 and moved to graphics driver 621.01. A few of those I'd have guessed. The 385 hours I wouldn't have. Why it's built like this The Rewind started as a lot more than this. It had switches for which kinds are made, which topics go in and what's left out, and a full-screen showing when one was ready. In 1.11.0 I cut it down to watching and sharing, so each one covers everything and there's nothing to set up. It's the same history the rest of RigSight already shows, put in an order that's fun to scroll through once a month or once a year. My 2026 has about 52 days of use so far, and needs 84 by the end of December. If it gets there, mine will be made in January, after the year it covers has ended.

t: How to test a new PC or GPU you got for Christmas
d: A new GPU or PC is easiest to check in its first week, while it can still go back, and its first two weeks become the normal you compare against for years. How to test a new GPU or PC, what to look at on a used one, and what RigSight records from day one.
l: PC problems Temperatures how to test a new gpu new pc after installing new gpu what to do how to stress test a new gpu how to test if new gpu is working new pc checklist what to do after building a new pc how to check used gpu before buying games to test a new gpu new gpu what to do
b: On 14 November I put 32 GB of memory in my PC, up from 16. RigSight's Timeline lists that day as "Memory changed to 32 GB", and from then on, everything it records is the PC with the new part. That's worth knowing if a new GPU or a whole new PC turns up this Christmas. Its first week is when you can still send it back, and its first two weeks become the normal you'll compare it against for years. Here's how to test a new GPU or PC while both still matter. On the first day Plug the monitor into the GPU, not into the motherboard. It's the most common reason a new card seems to do nothing. Install the latest driver from NVIDIA, AMD or Intel. If you switched brands, uninstall the old driver first. Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc , open Performance and click the GPU. Check its full name and memory match what you bought. Set your monitor's refresh rate under Settings > System > Display > Advanced display . Windows often starts a new screen or card at 60 Hz. For new memory, check Task Manager's Memory page shows the full amount, and turn on XMP or EXPO in the BIOS if you want its rated speed. How to test a new GPU A real game is the best test, because it's what the card is for. Turn on an overlay that shows FPS and the GPU's temperature. How to show FPS on PC covers each one. Play your most demanding game at high settings for 30 minutes or more. Watch for crashes, a black screen that comes back, or artifacts, like flickering shapes, checkerboards or wrong colours. Check the GPU is near full load. In a demanding game it should sit at 95% or more. Normal GPU usage while gaming explains when lower is fine. For a repeatable number, run a benchmark like 3DMark Time Spy or Unigine Superposition and compare your score with others for the same card. FurMark loads a card harder than any game. It's a test of the extreme, not something a new card needs to pass. What temperatures to expect Look at three readings, not one. The GPU core, the hot spot, which is the warmest point on the chip, and the memory. Rough ranges while gaming are 60 to 80°C for the core, a hot spot about 10 to 20° above it, and 70 to 90°C for the memory, higher on GDDR6X cards. These guides have the detail. Normal GPU temperature while gaming GPU hot spot temperature VRAM temperature while gaming Testing a used GPU or PC Check GPU-Z shows the model you were sold. It reads the card itself, not what the box says. Under load, the hot spot far above the core, like 30° or more, can mean old thermal paste or a cooler that sits badly. Every fan should spin under load. Listen for rattles and grinding. For drives, check hours on and life left in CrystalDiskInfo, or on RigSight's Storage page. SSD health check explains the readings. The first week Use it normally and watch for problems. A game crashing now and then can be the game. The same game crashing again and again, a black screen that recovers, or the PC shutting off on its own is worth reporting while the return window is open. Keep the box and receipt until you're sure. How RigSight caught it RigSight reads the PC's parts and records when one changes, as "Graphics card added", "Drive added", "CPU changed to" or "Memory changed to" on the Timeline page. Once there's history on both sides, the change's Before and after shows any game that ran better or worse since, marked as the new hardware. On a brand new PC there's no before, so the history starts that day. The first weeks matter most for later. On the Temperatures page, Over the months takes the first two weeks of history as each part's usual and shows how far it has moved since, at the same load. On a new PC, those are the new parts' own first weeks. Until there's enough history it says so, "Too soon to say", with what it still needs. My own GPU averaged 68.0°C while gaming in its first two weeks of history, at about 290 W, and 69.6°C in the last two at about 280 W. At rest it was 47.6°C then and 47.7°C now. That's a part holding steady, and I can only say so because the first two weeks were recorded. For a used drive, Storage shows the hours it has been on and the life left it reports, which tells you how much use it had before you. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to play your heaviest game on the first day with an overlay on, and write down the GPU's temperature and frame rate. That's your new part's normal, and the number you'll want in a year. How to test a new GPU and see it's working? Open Task Manager, go to Performance and check the GPU shows its full name and memory. Then play your heaviest game or run a benchmark like 3DMark or Unigine Superposition for 20 to 30 minutes. No crashes, no artifacts like flickering shapes, and temperatures within the card's limits mean it's working. How do I stress test a new GPU? Play your most demanding game at high settings for 30 minutes or more, or loop a benchmark like 3DMark Time Spy or Unigine Superposition. Watch the core, hot spot and memory temperatures. FurMark loads a card harder than any game, so it's an extreme test, not a needed one. What should I do after installing a new GPU? Plug the monitor into the GPU, not the motherboard. Install the latest driver from NVIDIA, AMD or Intel. Set your monitor's refresh rate in Windows display settings. Then test it in a game, and keep the box until you're sure it's fine. How do I check a used GPU before buying? See it running a game or benchmark for at least 15 minutes. Check that GPU-Z shows the model you were sold, that the fans all spin under load, and that the hot spot and memory temperatures aren't far above the core. Look for artifacts and listen for fan rattle.

t: What to upgrade in my PC first? My RAM upgrade, before and after
d: I went from 16 to 32 GB of memory on 14 November. Windows' committed memory dropped from 94% in my heaviest game to never above 62%, but Dota 2 ran about the same. How to find what to upgrade in your PC first, from what it already does.
l: PC problems FPS and games what to upgrade in my pc first upgrade ram pc upgrade should i upgrade cpu or gpu first is it worth upgrading from 16gb to 32gb ram is 16gb ram enough for gaming what to upgrade on my pc for better fps do i need to upgrade cpu when upgrading gpu is black friday a good time to buy pc parts what to upgrade in my pc
b: On 14 November I took my PC from 16 to 32 GB of memory. In the two weeks before, Windows' committed memory, what apps have asked for against the limit of memory plus the page file, reached 90% or more in 2,106 minutes, and averaged 94% while I played Phantom Blade Zero. Since the upgrade it has averaged about 45% and never gone above 62%. But in Dota 2, the one game I played on both sides, the frame rate went from 203 to 208 FPS. Barely a change. That's the whole question of what to upgrade in my PC first, in two numbers. An upgrade helps where the PC was running out, and only there. What to upgrade in my PC first, from my own history The GPU, an RTX 3080 Ti, was at full load 87% of the time in Phantom Blade Zero, and 89% in Crimson Desert. In those games, it was the limit. The CPU, a Ryzen 7 5700X3D, averaged 13 to 47% across my games and never reached 90% in any minute. Nothing pointed at it. Memory was the one that ran out. 16 GB with my usual apps open left Windows' committed memory near its limit for hours. The after side so far is a few days and mostly other games. Phantom Blade Zero, the game that pushed memory to 99%, I haven't played since, so it's too soon to say what the upgrade did there. Dota 2 never got near the limit, at 85% at most, which is why more memory changed little in it. Its 1% low went from 102 to 105 FPS, and it didn't stutter less. Should I upgrade my CPU or GPU first? Play the games you care about with GPU usage on screen, from an overlay or Task Manager. GPU at 95% or more most of the time. A faster GPU gives more frames. This is the usual answer for gaming PCs. GPU well below that, with no frame limit or V-Sync, and the frame rate lower than you want. The CPU or the game sets the pace. A new GPU would wait like the old one. Normal CPU usage while gaming explains why a CPU can be the limit at 30%. Both fine, but stutters or slow alt-tabs. Look at memory next. Is it worth upgrading from 16GB to 32GB RAM? Open Task Manager's Memory page while you play your heaviest game, with the apps you usually keep open. Committed shows two numbers. When the first gets close to the second, Windows is nearly out of memory and starts leaning on the page file, which is far slower. Then 32 GB helps, as it did on my PC. When it stays well below, more memory won't change your frame rate. Normal RAM usage while gaming has more. Buy memory that matches what's in the PC, same type and speed, or replace all of it as a matched kit. Check the motherboard's supported list, and turn on XMP or EXPO in the BIOS afterwards. Before you buy on Black Friday Decide the part from your own games first, then look at deals. A discount on the wrong part is still the wrong part. Check the price history in a price tracker. Some Black Friday prices are the usual price with a new label. Check it fits. For a GPU, the case's length and the power supply's wattage and cables. For memory, the type and the slots. Note how your PC runs now, so you can tell what the upgrade changed. How RigSight caught it RigSight records the CPU, GPU and memory every minute while you play, so the answer is already in your history before you shop. Three readings point at the part to upgrade. GPU load. On the Games page, each game's Can it run better? card says how often the GPU was at full load, 95% busy or more. Most of the time means the GPU is the limit. When the GPU rarely or never reaches full load and there's no frame limit, the same card says something else sets the pace, most likely the CPU. Committed memory. When stutters bunch up while it's at 90% or more, RigSight names that as "while Windows was nearly out of memory". Since 1.13.0, the Memory page also says when RAM was 85% full or more today, and which apps held the most then. The Timeline lists the upgrade itself, mine as "Memory changed to 32 GB", so you can compare before and after. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to play your two most played games with GPU usage and memory on screen this week. Whatever runs out first is what to upgrade, and once it's in, how to test a new GPU or PC covers the first week. What to upgrade in my PC first, the CPU or the GPU? Check GPU usage in the games you play most. At 95% or more, the GPU is the limit, so a better GPU helps first. Well below that with no frame cap, the CPU or the game sets the pace, and a GPU upgrade gives little. Most gaming PCs gain the most from the GPU. Is it worth upgrading from 16GB to 32GB RAM? If Windows' committed memory gets close to its limit while you game, yes. On my PC it averaged 94% in my heaviest game before the upgrade and never went above 62% after. In games that weren't near the limit, like Dota 2, the frame rate barely changed. Is 16GB RAM enough for gaming? For many games, yes, but with little room if you keep a browser and other apps open. Big new games can push a 16 GB PC close to full. Check Committed in Task Manager while you play your heaviest game. Is Black Friday a good time to buy PC parts? Often, for parts that are already a generation old, like memory, SSDs and last year's GPUs. t: Normal CPU usage while gaming, and when 100% isn't
d: My Ryzen 7 5700X3D averaged between 13% and 47% busy across six games and never reached 90% in any minute of play. What normal CPU usage while gaming looks like, why 100% is different from GPU usage, and how to fix it.
l: PC problems FPS and games normal cpu usage while gaming average cpu usage while gaming is 100 cpu usage normal while gaming cpu 100 while gaming cpu usage 100 while gaming normal cpu utilization while gaming normal gpu and cpu usage while gaming cpu at 100 while gaming fix
b: Across six games since 18 October, my Ryzen 7 5700X3D averaged between 13% and 47% busy. In about 88 hours of play it never reached 90% in a single minute. The highest minute was 87%, in Phantom Blade Zero. That's what normal CPU usage while gaming looks like on a current 8-core processor, and it isn't like the GPU, which in the same game sat near 100% most of the time. Normal CPU usage while gaming Here's what each game did on my 8-core, 16-thread 5700X3D. Phantom Blade Zero averaged 47%, with its busiest minute at 87%. REMATCH averaged 45%. Dota 2 averaged 34%. Crimson Desert averaged 28%, with the GPU at full load nearly the whole time. Risk of Rain 2 averaged 24%. Slay the Spire 2 averaged 13%. With nothing much running, the same CPU sits around 7%. A CPU with fewer cores reads higher in the same game, because the same work is spread over less. A 4-core CPU at 70 or 80% in a modern game isn't unusual. Is 100% CPU usage normal while gaming? Not usually, and this is where the CPU and GPU differ. A GPU at 99% is doing its job. Most games can't spread their work evenly over every core, so a CPU at 100% for minutes at a time usually means something extra is going on. A background app is busy, like a browser, a launcher downloading or installing, an antivirus scan or cloud sync. The CPU has few cores for the game, so the game alone fills it. The game is building shaders, often the first time you play after a game or driver update. That passes. Something is stuck, like a process using a full core in a loop. A CPU at 100% leaves nothing for the moments a game needs a little more, so it often comes with stutters. Low CPU usage can still hold the frame rate back Total CPU usage is the average of every core. Many games do most of their work on one main thread. If that thread fills one core, the game waits for it, even while the total reads 25%. My Risk of Rain 2 sessions are a good example to look at, with the CPU 24% busy and the GPU only 55% busy at about 151 FPS. Something other than the GPU set that pace, the CPU or a frame limit. To check, open Task Manager's Performance tab, click CPU , right-click the graph and choose Change graph to > Logical processors . One or two cores near the top while the rest idle is what a main thread looks like. How to fix high CPU usage while gaming Open Task Manager with Ctrl + Shift + Esc while the game runs, sort Processes by CPU , and close anything busy that isn't the game. Pause launcher downloads, cloud sync and browser video while you play. Give it a second session after a game or driver update, in case it was building shaders. Use the Balanced power plan, or Best performance under Settings > System > Power & battery , and play laptops on the charger. Update the game, the chipset driver from AMD or Intel, and Windows. Lower the settings that lean on the CPU, such as crowd or unit density, view distance, physics and shadows' draw distance. Check the CPU's temperature. A CPU that gets too hot slows itself. Normal CPU temperature while gaming has the numbers. How RigSight caught it RigSight records the CPU's usage every minute, for the whole PC and for each app, next to the frame rate and the game in front. That's how I can see not only how busy the CPU was, but whether the game or something else made it busy. When stutters bunch up, five or more within 15 minutes, and you open the play frame by frame, RigSight checks what else was going on. If another app used 20% of the CPU or more there, and at least twice what it used in the rest of the play, it names that app as busy in the background. On the Games page, a game whose GPU rarely or never reached full load gets the line that something else sets the pace, most likely the CPU. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to watch CPU and GPU usage together in a game that feels slow. A GPU near 100% means the CPU is fine. A GPU well below that, with no frame limit, means the CPU or the game sets the pace, so start with the list above. Normal GPU usage while gaming covers the GPU side. Is 100% CPU usage normal while gaming? Not on most PCs. Games rarely use every core fully, so a CPU pinned at 100% usually means a background app is busy, the CPU has few cores for that game, or something is wrong like a stuck process. Short spikes while a game loads or builds shaders are fine. What is normal CPU usage while gaming? It depends on the game and the CPU. On my 8-core Ryzen 7 5700X3D it ranged from 13% in Slay the Spire 2 to 47% in Phantom Blade Zero. A 4-core CPU in the same games would read much higher. Why is my CPU usage low but the CPU is still the bottleneck? Total CPU usage averages every core. A game whose main thread fills one or two cores can be held back while the total reads 25 or 30%. Look at the per-core graphs in Task Manager, or at GPU usage. A GPU well below 95% with no frame limit points at the CPU. How do I fix 100% CPU usage while gaming? Close background apps, especially browsers, launchers that download, and cloud sync. Check Task Manager for anything busy that isn't the game. Update the game and the chipset driver, use the Balanced power plan, and lower settings that lean on the CPU, like crowd density, view distance and physics.

t: Normal GPU usage while gaming, and why 99% is a good sign
d: On my PC, Phantom Blade Zero kept the GPU 95% busy or more 87% of the time, and Risk of Rain 2 only 1% of the time. What normal GPU usage while gaming looks like, why near 100% is fine, and what low usage tells you.
l: PC problems FPS and games normal gpu usage while gaming is 100 gpu usage normal while gaming is 99 gpu usage normal while gaming average gpu usage while gaming gpu 100 usage while gaming is high gpu usage normal while gaming normal gpu and cpu usage while gaming gpu usage 100
b: Two of my games show how wide normal GPU usage while gaming can be. In Phantom Blade Zero, my RTX 3080 Ti was at full load, 95% busy or more, in 87% of the minutes I played, at about 68 FPS. In Risk of Rain 2 on the same PC, it was at full load in 1% of the minutes and averaged 55% busy, at about 151 FPS. Neither one is a problem. They just tell you different things about what holds the frame rate back. Normal GPU usage while gaming Here is what each of my games did, all on one RTX 3080 Ti with a Ryzen 7 5700X3D. Crimson Desert averaged 97% GPU usage, at full load 89% of the time. Phantom Blade Zero averaged 95%, at full load 87% of the time. REMATCH averaged 87%, at full load 24% of the time. Dota 2 averaged 64%, at full load 1% of the time. Risk of Rain 2 averaged 55%, at full load 1% of the time. Slay the Spire 2 averaged 41% and never reached full load, at almost 400 FPS. The heavy, good-looking games kept the GPU near 100%. The lighter ones ran at high frame rates with the GPU half busy. Both are normal. Is 100% GPU usage normal while gaming? Yes, and in a demanding game it's what you want. A GPU at 95 to 99% is drawing frames as fast as it can, so nothing else is holding it back. It's built to run like that for hours. Watch the temperature, not the usage. Normal GPU temperature while gaming has the limits. Two cases where near 100% is worth a look. High usage on the desktop or in a light game with a low frame rate. Check Task Manager's Processes tab sorted by GPU for something else using it, like a browser with video or a background app. A game in a menu running at hundreds of FPS. Some games don't cap their menus, which keeps the GPU busy and hot for nothing. A frame limit fixes it. Why GPU usage is lower in some games A frame limit or V-Sync. The GPU finishes each frame early and waits, so usage drops while the frame rate stays flat. The CPU. If the processor can't prepare frames fast enough, the GPU waits for it. Games with many units or players lean on the CPU, and total CPU usage can look low while one or two cores are full. A light game. A card made for heavy games has room to spare in a small one. Low usage only matters when the frame rate is lower than you want. Then GPU not at 100% usage but low FPS walks through finding what the GPU waits for. How to check GPU usage while gaming Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager, open Performance and click your GPU. The graph marked 3D is what games use. For the game itself, the Processes tab has a GPU column you can sort by. To see it while you play, use an overlay that shows GPU usage, like Xbox Game Bar's Performance widget, the NVIDIA app or RivaTuner. How to show FPS on PC covers each. How RigSight caught it RigSight records the GPU's usage every minute, next to the frame rate from RivaTuner and the game in front. On the Games page, each game's Can it run better? card turns that into one line. When the GPU was at full load most of the time, it says so and that lower settings would give more frames. When it was at full load only some of the time, it says the GPU is the limit in busy scenes. When it rarely or never was, it says something else sets the pace, most likely the CPU. If the game holds a flat frame rate, the card names what holds it there, the game's own frame limit or V-Sync, from the game's saved settings when RigSight can read them. You can also put GPU usage in the overlay, the taskbar or a widget to watch it live. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to check GPU usage and the frame rate together in your heaviest game. Near 100% means the GPU is the limit, so lower settings or upscaling give more frames. Well below that, with a frame rate you're unhappy with, means look at the CPU or a frame cap next. Is 100% GPU usage normal while gaming? Yes. In a demanding game with no frame limit, the GPU should be close to 100% busy, because it draws frames as fast as it can. Usage shown as 97 to 99% is the same thing. It's safe as long as the temperature stays within the card's limits. Is 99% GPU usage bad? No. It means the GPU is what limits your frame rate, which is how a gaming PC is meant to run. To get more frames, lower the graphics settings or use upscaling like DLSS or FSR. What is normal GPU usage while gaming? There isn't one number. On my PC it ranged from 41% in Slay the Spire 2 to 97% in Crimson Desert. Light games, frame caps and games that lean on the CPU all keep it lower. Why is my GPU usage low while gaming? Usually a frame limit or V-Sync is holding the frame rate, the CPU can't prepare frames fast enough, or the game is light. If your frame rate is fine, low usage isn't a problem. If it isn't, see GPU not at 100% usage but low FPS.

t: VRAM temperature while gaming, and what's normal for GPU memory
d: My RTX 3080 Ti's memory averaged 78°C over about 100 hours of heavy gaming and never went above 84°C. What VRAM temperature is normal, where it gets too hot, how to check it, and how to bring it down.
l: PC problems Temperatures vram temperature gpu memory temperature gpu memory temperature while gaming vram temperature range vram temperature max gpu memory temperature normal vram temperature 3080 gpu memory junction temperature vram temperature monitor
b: Since 23 September, RigSight has recorded my RTX 3080 Ti's memory temperature every minute. In about 100 hours of heavy gaming, with the GPU 80% busy or more, the memory averaged about 78°C. The highest it reached was 84°C, on 30 September in a game that kept the GPU 99% busy. That card uses GDDR6X, the memory known for running hot, so I expected worse. Here's what VRAM temperature is normal while gaming, where it gets too hot, and how to check yours. What VRAM temperature is normal VRAM is the GPU's own memory, the chips around the GPU on the card. They get warm because games keep them busy, and they sit under the same cooler as the GPU, often with less of it touching them. That's why memory usually reads warmer than the core. Somewhere around 70 to 90°C while gaming is common for many cards. GDDR6X cards, like the RTX 3080, 3080 Ti, 3090 and 3090 Ti, run hotter. Reviewers measured an RTX 3080 Founders Edition at about 102°C in a heavy game at 4K, and 3090 owners report the 90s and 100°C. Idle memory is usually in the 40s to 50s. The number depends on the card's cooler, the case's airflow and the room, so two owners of the same card can see 15° apart. VRAM temperature max, and when it's too hot For GDDR6X, Tom's Hardware reported that RTX 3080 and 3090 cards only slow their memory at about 110°C. The memory's rated range is often quoted up to 95°C, a little higher in some readings of Micron's sheets, and the sensor reads the hottest spot inside the chip, so the two numbers aren't measured the same way. A practical line is this. In the 80s and low 90s, nothing to do. Staying above 100°C for long sessions is worth fixing, even before anything slows down, because heat over years is what wears parts. Near 110°C the card is protecting itself. How to check GPU memory temperature Task Manager shows the GPU's temperature, not its memory's. For memory you need a tool that reads the card's own sensor. Install HWiNFO or GPU-Z, both free. In HWiNFO, open Sensors and find your GPU. Look for GPU Memory Junction Temperature . In GPU-Z, open the Sensors tab and look for Memory Temperature . Play your heaviest game for at least 20 minutes, then read the maximum, not the current value. Not every card reports it. Many older and smaller cards have no memory sensor, so the line is missing. How to lower VRAM temperature Improve the case's airflow first. Make sure front fans pull air in and the back and top fans push it out, and clean dust off filters and the GPU's fins. Raise the GPU's fan curve in MSI Afterburner or your card maker's tool. Memory often follows the fans more than the core does. Cap the frame rate a little below your monitor's refresh rate. Fewer frames means less work for the memory. Lower the memory clock if you overclocked it. On an older card, new thermal pads on the memory can drop it a lot. This means opening the card, which can affect its warranty, so check that first or ask the maker. How RigSight caught it RigSight records three GPU temperatures each minute, the core, the hot spot and the memory, and keeps the highest of each minute so a short peak doesn't get averaged away. On the Temperatures page, GPU memory has its own line next to the others. You can also put it in the taskbar, the overlay, a widget or a dashboard from its row on All sensors. Seeing it next to the core is what makes the number useful. In those heavy minutes my GPU core averaged 69°C and the memory 78°C, so the memory ran about 9° above the core. With the GPU nearly idle, the core sat around 48°C and the memory around 53°C. In the heavy minutes, the memory's highest stayed between 68 and 84°C, and none reached 85. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to check your memory's highest reading after a long game. If it's in the 80s or low 90s, leave it alone. If it stays above 100°C, start with airflow and the fan curve. For the GPU chip itself, see normal GPU temperature while gaming and GPU hot spot temperature . What is a normal VRAM temperature while gaming? Often somewhere between 70 and 90°C. Memory usually runs warmer than the GPU core next to it. GDDR6X cards like the RTX 3080 and 3090 can read in the 90s and close to 100°C in heavy games and still work as designed. My RTX 3080 Ti averaged 78°C. What is the max VRAM temperature? It depends on the memory. GDDR6X is commonly reported to slow itself at about 110°C, and Micron's rated range for it is often quoted up to 95°C or a little more. Treat readings that stay above 100°C as too hot, even if nothing slows down yet. How do I check GPU memory temperature? Task Manager doesn't show it. Free tools like HWiNFO and GPU-Z show it on cards that report it, often as Memory Junction Temperature or Memory Temperature. RigSight records it every minute as GPU memory, so you can look back at a whole session. Is GPU memory temperature the same as hot spot? No. The hot spot is the warmest point on the GPU chip itself. Memory temperature is the memory chips around it. Both run above the core temperature, and each has its own limit.

t: How to show FPS on PC with an overlay, and fix RivaTuner
d: My PC already has four FPS overlays, from Windows, Steam, NVIDIA and RivaTuner. How to show FPS on PC with each of them, which to pick, what to do when the RivaTuner overlay is not showing, and how RigSight keeps the numbers after the game.
l: PC problems FPS and games how to show fps on pc how to show fps overlay fps overlay windows 11 fps counter windows 11 how to see fps in games how to show fps on steam fps overlay nvidia fps overlay amd fps overlay hotkey rivatuner overlay not showing
b: My PC already has four ways to show FPS on screen. Xbox Game Bar came with Windows, Steam has its own counter, the NVIDIA app has one, and RivaTuner is installed too. Since 18 October, RigSight has also kept about 88 hours of my games' frame rates, read from RivaTuner. That's about 38 hours of Risk of Rain 2 at 151 FPS on average and about 36 hours of Phantom Blade Zero at 68. Here's how to show FPS on PC with each overlay, which one to pick, and what to do when the RivaTuner overlay is not showing. How to show FPS on PC with Xbox Game Bar Game Bar is the FPS counter built into Windows 10 and 11, and it works in most games. Start your game and press Win + G. Open the Performance widget from the Widget menu if it isn't already on screen. The first time, the FPS tab may show Request access . Click it, approve the Windows prompt, and restart your PC. FPS stays empty until you do. Drag the widget to a corner and click the Pin icon so it stays when Game Bar closes. If Game Bar doesn't open, check that Settings > Gaming > Xbox Game Bar is on. If FPS shows N/A, go to Settings > Apps > Installed apps , find Xbox Game Bar, open Advanced options and press Repair , then Reset if that doesn't help. How to show FPS on Steam For games you run through Steam, this is the simplest one. In Steam, open Steam > Settings > In Game . Find Performance Monitor , which older Steam versions call In-game FPS counter , and pick the corner you want. Choose how much it shows. The lowest level is the frame rate alone. Higher levels add CPU, GPU and memory readings. The Steam overlay only works in games started from Steam, which includes other games you add with Add a Non-Steam Game . NVIDIA FPS overlay The NVIDIA app has a statistics overlay for GeForce cards. Press Alt + Z in game, or open the NVIDIA app, to bring up the overlay. Open Statistics and choose what to show, or pick Custom to choose each reading. Press Alt + R to show or hide the numbers while you play. The overlay itself must be on in the NVIDIA app under Settings > Features . Recent versions add CPU temperature and clock speed next to the GPU readings. Instant Replay and recording are separate features. They keep the video encoder working in the background, so turn them off if you only want the counter. AMD FPS overlay Open AMD Software and go to Performance > Metrics . Pick the readings, the position, the size and the colour of the overlay. Press Ctrl + Shift + O in game to show or hide it. If the shortcut does nothing, check in AMD Software's settings that the overlay and its hotkeys are turned on. You can change the shortcut there too. RivaTuner and MSI Afterburner RivaTuner Statistics Server is the overlay most PC builders use. It draws inside the game itself, so it works in exclusive fullscreen games where a normal window can't appear. MSI Afterburner feeds it hardware readings. Install MSI Afterburner, which comes with RivaTuner, or RivaTuner on its own. In Afterburner, open Settings > Monitoring . Click Framerate in the list and tick Show in On-Screen Display . Do the same for GPU temperature, GPU usage and anything else you want. Make sure RivaTuner is running in the tray, then start the game. What to check when the RivaTuner overlay is not showing Work through these in order. Restart the game after each change. Start RivaTuner before the game. It only attaches to games that start after it, so a game already open won't show the overlay until you restart it. In RivaTuner, check that Show On-Screen Display is on, for the global profile and for the game's own profile if it has one. Check Application detection level . If it says None , the game is ignored. Set it to Low , and try Medium if Low doesn't work. If you made a profile for the game, make sure it points at the game's real program file. Some games run from a different program than their launcher. Close other overlays for a test, such as Steam, Discord, Xbox Game Bar, the NVIDIA app and Overwolf. Overwolf's own help suggests detection level Low with Stealth mode and Custom Direct3D support off when they clash. Update RivaTuner. New graphics APIs and new games often need a newer version. Some anti-cheat systems block overlays in some games. If one game never shows it while others do, that is the likely reason. Which FPS overlay should you use? For a quick look in any game, Xbox Game Bar is already on your PC. For Steam games only, Steam's counter is the least work. For readings matched to your GPU, use the NVIDIA app or AMD Software. For exclusive fullscreen games and the most control over what shows, use RivaTuner. To keep the numbers after the game, use something that records them, like RigSight with RivaTuner. Show one at a time. Two or three overlays drawing over the same game is a common cause of crashes, missing overlays and lost frames. How RigSight caught it A counter in the corner tells you the frame rate right now, and it's gone when you close the game. RigSight reads every frame from RivaTuner Statistics Server while you play and keeps it. On the Games page, every play has its average FPS and its 1% low, so the numbers above come from what RigSight kept, not from catching them in the corner. For the moment itself, RigSight has its own overlay on its Overlay page. You pick the readings, like frame rate, frame time and 1% low for the game, and temperature, load, clock speed and power for the CPU and GPU. Press Alt + Shift + O to show or hide it, or click the shortcut on the Overlay page to pick another. Since version 1.8.0, an Only over games switch keeps it hidden over the desktop and other apps, and it comes back as soon as a game is in front. In windowed and borderless games, RigSight draws the overlay as its own see-through window. In exclusive fullscreen, where no window can appear on top, it hands the same overlay to RivaTuner, and both look the same. When RivaTuner draws it, the overlay doesn't turn off G-Sync. Since 1.8.0 you can also put FPS in the taskbar, where it shows a dash while no game is running. The taskbar readings, the widgets and the overlay can each be turned off and on from the tray menu. Widgets have an FPS tile and a Last game tile with its average frame rate, and they sit on the desktop under your windows. The frame rate always comes from RivaTuner, so it has to be running before the game starts, and the Games page has Install RivaTuner and Start RivaTuner buttons. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to pick one overlay, set it up once, and turn the rest off. If the number you see looks wrong, FPS drops in games is the place to go next. How to show FPS on PC without extra software? Use Xbox Game Bar, which comes with Windows 10 and 11. Press Win + G in the game, open the Performance widget and pin it. The first time, the FPS tab may ask for access, and it stays empty until you allow it and restart the PC. How do I show the FPS overlay in Steam? Open Steam, go to Steam > Settings > In Game and turn on the Performance Monitor, which replaced the old In-game FPS counter in 2025. Pick a corner and how much detail to show. It works in Steam games and in other games you add to Steam and start from it. Why is the RivaTuner overlay not showing? Most often RivaTuner wasn't running before the game started, Show On-Screen Display is off, or the game's profile has Application detection level set to None. Another overlay or anti-cheat can also block it. Start RivaTuner first, check those settings, and restart the game. Does the GeForce overlay affect FPS? Showing the statistics overlay costs very little. Recording features such as Instant Replay keep the video encoder busy in the background and can cost some frames, more so on slower PCs. Turn off what you don't use. How do I show an FPS overlay on AMD? Open AMD Software, go to Performance > Metrics, choose what to show and turn the overlay on. Ctrl + Shift + O shows or hides it in game by default, and you can change the shortcut in the hotkey settings.

t: Why opening RigSight from the tray waited up to a second
d: Every time you opened RigSight from the tray, a notification or a widget, it waited 290 ms to over a second before the window even started. The tests never saw it, because they started the window another way. How 1.11.0 cut it to tens of milliseconds.
l: Building RigSight
b: RigSight is two programs. A small background part runs all the time, records your PC and owns the tray icon. The window you look at is a separate app that opens when you want it. When you click the tray icon, a notification or a widget, the background part starts the window. On 12 November I started working on speed. I measured page switches, first visits and how long the window takes to open, all with the end-to-end tests that drive the real app. Everything looked fine. Then I timed the one thing the tests didn't do, which was a click on the tray icon. Why there was a hop at all The background part runs as administrator, because reading some sensors, like the CPU's temperature, needs it. Anything a program starts gets that program's rights, so if it started the window itself, the window would run as administrator too, and so would anything you opened from it, like a link or a folder. The window should run with your normal rights, like any app you open yourself. So RigSight asked Explorer to start it instead. It ran explorer.exe with the window's program as the argument. That starts a new copy of Explorer, which hands the job to the Explorer already running your desktop and quits. The desktop's Explorer runs with normal rights, so the window does too. How long the hop took Started directly, the window's program begins in about 15 ms. Through the extra Explorer, I measured 280 to 650 ms on my PC, and from an administrator program, which is what the background part is, 290 to 1,150 ms. That's before the window even starts loading. Every open waited that long. The tray icon, a click on a notification or a widget, a widget shortcut, and starting RivaTuner for the overlay all went through the same hop. And none of my speed tests saw it, because they start the window's program directly to time it. The slowest step happened only in real use. Asking the desktop's Explorer directly Raymond Chen at Microsoft wrote about this exact problem in 2013, on his blog The Old New Thing. An administrator program can ask the desktop's own Explorer to open something, the same way a double-click on the desktop does. It finds the desktop among Explorer's windows, asks it for the object Explorer uses to run things, and tells that to open the program. Explorer runs it, with normal rights, and no new copy of Explorer has to start. Asked that way, it took 11 to 18 ms in my tests, the first ask included. I checked from an administrator PowerShell that what it started ran with normal rights. If the desktop's Explorer can't be asked, because another shell is running or Explorer crashed, RigSight falls back to the old way and writes why in its log. What it does on my PC now 1.11.0 went out on 13 November. RigSight's log now writes how long each open took. On my PC today, the window started 43, 23 and 92 ms after the click. Before, the same click waited between a quarter of a second and over a second first. The same release counts Storage's space you could free faster, by recounting only the folders that changed since the last count. On my folders that went from about 3.8 seconds of CPU time to under 0.1 when nothing had changed. The window also compiles about a third fewer methods while opening, because the messages between the two programs are now read with generated code. The lesson I took is about where I measure. The tests timed everything they could reach, and the slowest part sat just outside them. Now the log times the real click, so the next time something like this creeps in, it shows up where I'll see it.

t: What my own chats with RigSight AI got wrong
d: For two weeks I asked RigSight AI about my own PC like anyone would, then read every answer. It assumed a 144 Hz screen, suggested the same fix three times, and blamed a September crash on a November update. What I changed after each.
l: The AI journey
b: The pretend PCs I built in October are good at one thing, checking answers to problems I already know. They can't tell me what it's like to use the helper on a real PC, with real questions asked the way people ask them. So from late October I used RigSight AI on my own PC like anyone would. I asked about my crashes, my games and my temperatures, asked follow-ups, pasted errors into it, and then read every answer as if someone else had written it. Most answers were fine. The ones that weren't went wrong in ways I hadn't expected. It assumed what it didn't look up On 29 October an answer told me my screen runs at 144 Hz. No look-up had said that. The model filled in a common number, and it read as fact. The rule I added is short. Never state something about the PC's setup that no look-up gave. The same day it called the next day "two days after". It had worked the gap out loosely instead of counting the dates. Now it counts how far apart two dates are, and says "the same day" only when it is. It almost never searched The helper can search the web on the paid plans. Its first instructions said to search only for what my records couldn't answer. That sounded careful, and in practice it meant it almost never searched. A crash in Control got "play with OBS closed". When I asked it to guide me step by step, I got the diagnosis again instead of steps. On 30 October I changed it to search for crashes, known fixes and when I push back. For a crash in an app I might not recognise, it does one search on the file name with the error code and the module, and says what the app is. I replayed both conversations against the real model, twice before the change and twice after. After it, both searched and named the app. The same replay caught a smaller thing. I asked about an app's memory, then asked again later, and the second answer called the first one wrong because the number was higher. Nothing was wrong. The app had grown, from 732 to 839 MB. A reading that changes between two look-ups is now said as a change, not a mistake. It got the order of things wrong On 6 November I read back ten of my chats from that week. In one, an app that had crashed on and off since September was tied to an update from 2 November. The update came weeks after the crashes started, so it couldn't have caused them. In another, on an install two minutes old, the answer called the PC healthy, with almost no history to say so. A search that found nothing about the app I'd asked about still got its own paragraph, about other programs. The fixes were rules about reading. Read the whole crash finding, including since when. Check there is history before calling a PC fine. Leave out a search that found nothing. On 12 November I added that a change has to come before the first problem it's used to explain. It said the same thing three times The longest chat was on 12 November, about blue screens. Over several follow-ups it suggested running System File Checker three times. The questions offered under each answer came back the same twice. When I asked "what do I do now?", I got one step. And it said my drives' health was unchecked, though it had already looked it up in that chat. Follow-ups now get the steps earlier answers gave, so it builds on them instead of starting over. "What do I do?" gets a numbered plan. Asked again, it gives something new and concrete, never "as I said". And if RigSight records something, the helper looks it up instead of sending you to check it yourself. Two of the fixes from that chat were in the app, not the instructions, and both shipped in 1.11.0. The questions offered under an answer now skip ones the chat already asked or offered. And the same chat cleared heat as a cause because the CPU was at 85°C while only 9% busy, reading low load as proof it wasn't overheating. A crash no longer says the CPU wasn't overheating when it sat well above its usual while doing little. What reading my own chats taught me Almost none of these were about knowing PCs. The model knows what a blue screen is and how to read a crash. What it got wrong was the ordinary care a person takes in a conversation. Don't assume, count the dates, don't repeat yourself, and check the order of events. Each of those had to be written down as a rule before it held. It's also why I keep testing on my own PC first. The pretend PCs check that the right answer comes out. My own chats check that the answer is one I'd want to read.

t: SSD health check on Windows 11, and why mine says Healthy at 70%
d: The SSD Windows runs on in my PC says Healthy and has used 30% of its rated life. How to do an SSD health check on Windows 11, why Healthy and life left are two different readings, and what RigSight tells you when either one changes.
l: PC problems Storage and memory ssd health check windows 11 how to check ssd health how to check ssd health windows 11 check ssd health windows 11 powershell ssd health check software ssd health check is my ssd dying signs my ssd is dying ssd health check windows 10
b: My PC has three drives, and every health check I run calls all of them Healthy. But the Kingston SSD that Windows runs on reports 69% of its rated life left today, after 12,387 hours on. The newer Samsung SSD my games sit on reports 97%. Both are Healthy, and they're in very different places. That's the thing to know before an SSD health check on Windows 11. It gives you two readings, and they answer different questions. Healthy and life left are different readings The health status is the drive's own pass or fail. It turns to Warning or Bad when something the drive tracks crosses the line its maker set, like errors it couldn't fix or spare memory running out. Life left is wear. SSDs wear a little with every write, and makers rate how much they can take. 70% left means the drive estimates it has used about 30% of that. It's an estimate, and drives often keep working past 0%. Most home PCs write far less than the rating, so this number usually falls slowly. My Windows drive took nearly 12,000 hours on to use its 30%, so at that pace it has years of use left. A drive can be Healthy at 70%, and a drive can fail at 98% without warning, from a controller fault for example. A health check makes a surprise less likely. Only a backup protects your files. How to do an SSD health check on Windows 11 in Settings Windows has a drive health page built in, but Microsoft says it only covers NVMe SSDs, which most of the small stick drives in an M.2 slot are. My Kingston is a SATA SSD, so this page has nothing to say about the drive Windows itself runs on. SATA SSDs, M.2 SATA drives and hard drives need PowerShell or software instead. Open Settings with Windows+I . Go to System > Storage . Under Storage management , open Advanced storage settings > Disks & volumes . Pick your SSD and select Properties . Read the Drive health section. It shows estimated remaining life, available spare, which is the extra memory the drive keeps to replace worn cells, and the temperature. If the drive reports a problem, Windows shows a warning such as "Reliability is degraded" and asks you to back up. Windows 10 has the same page under Settings > System > Storage > Manage disks and volumes . Check SSD health in Windows 11 with PowerShell PowerShell reads any drive, SATA or NVMe. The old wmic diskdrive get status no longer works, because Microsoft has removed WMIC from current Windows 11. Right click the Start button and choose Terminal (Admin) . For the health status, run this. Get-PhysicalDisk | Select-Object FriendlyName, MediaType, HealthStatus, OperationalStatus For wear and errors, run this one. It needs the admin window. Get-PhysicalDisk | Get-StorageReliabilityCounter | Select-Object DeviceId, Wear, Temperature, PowerOnHours, ReadErrorsUncorrected, WriteErrorsUncorrected HealthStatus should say Healthy , as all three of mine did today. Warning or Unhealthy means back up now. Wear counts up, so it's the opposite of life left. A new drive reads 0, and Microsoft describes 100 as the point where the rated wear is reached. Some drives leave it empty. The uncorrected error counts should be 0. Free SSD health check software CrystalDiskInfo is free, small and reads almost any drive. Each drive gets a box marked Good , Caution or Bad , with a percentage for SSDs, and below it the full SMART table, the hours on and the total data written. Most SSD makers also have a free tool for their own drives, such as Samsung Magician, Sandisk Dashboard for WD and Sandisk drives, Crucial Storage Executive and Kingston SSD Manager. They show health in the maker's own terms and can update the drive's firmware, which sometimes fixes bugs. Back up before a firmware update, and only update with the maker's own tool. Signs your SSD is dying The health status says Warning, Caution, Bad or Unhealthy. Reallocated, pending or uncorrectable sectors that keep growing. A few that never change aren't an emergency. A count that climbs is the clearest sign. Available spare under the drive's threshold, which Windows reports as a warning. Files that won't open or copy, and the PC freezing for seconds when it reads the drive. Low life left with none of these means the drive has used most of its rated writes. Keep a backup and plan a replacement, but it isn't failing yet. What to do if your SSD isn't healthy Back up what matters now, to another drive or a cloud service. Check the maker's tool for a firmware update. Check the warranty. Many SSD warranties cover a set number of years or a written total, whichever comes first. Plan to replace the drive, and check it every week until you do. If the drive is just full, that's a different problem, and what is taking up space on your C drive helps with that. How RigSight caught it RigSight's Storage page lists every drive with its health, the life left an SSD reports, its temperature and how much was written in the last 7 days. A drive that needs a look sits on top. Open one and it answers "Is this drive okay?" in plain words, with its hours on, how it compares with weeks or months ago, and every reading it gives in plain words. The health is one word, Healthy, Early warning or Failing. That word takes the worse of two things. One is SMART, the drive's own health check. The other is life left, because SMART can still say Good on an SSD that has used nearly all of its rated writes. An SSD at 10% life left or less shows Early warning, with "The drive reports almost all of its rated life used. Keep a backup of what's on it." Bad sectors give "Bad sectors are an early warning. Keep a backup, and watch whether the count grows." Only SMART reporting a failure makes a drive Failing. RigSight also tells you when a drive changes, so you don't have to remember to look. Since 1.7.0, a failure comes as an urgent notification, "Your Samsung SSD 980 1TB reports a failure", telling you to back up now. Early warning signs, new or more bad sectors, and 10% life left or less each come once, and the bad sectors one gives the count and what it was before. Since 1.12.0, an SSD that reaches half or a quarter of its life left gets a notification with how fast it has been wearing, and a drive that reaches its own warning temperature gets one too. Each has its own switch in Settings, Drive health , Drive life milestones , Drive temperature and Drive almost full . On my PC, RigSight's log shows it checking all three drives several times an hour, and they're still Good. My Kingston went from 70% in October to 69% now, about 500 hours on later. RigSight hasn't sent a single drive notification, which is how it should be. Drive health needs RigSight to run with admin rights, and RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to run the first PowerShell command or the Settings check today, and write down each SSD's life left. Checking again in a few months tells you how fast it wears, which one reading never can. How do I do an SSD health check on Windows 11? Open Settings > System > Storage > Advanced storage settings > Disks & volumes, pick the SSD and select Properties. Drive health shows estimated remaining life, available spare and temperature, for NVMe SSDs only. For SATA SSDs, run Get-PhysicalDisk in PowerShell or use CrystalDiskInfo. What is a good SSD health percentage? Anything well above 10% is fine for daily use. The number is the drive's own estimate of its rated write life left, and a home PC that mostly games and browses usually uses it up slowly. When it gets low, keep a good backup and plan a replacement. A drive at 0% doesn't stop working that day. What are the signs my SSD is dying? A health status of Warning or Bad, a growing count of reallocated, pending or uncorrectable sectors, files that won't open or copy, and the PC freezing on disk access. A low life left on its own means the drive has used most of its rated writes, which is a reason to keep a backup, not proof it's failing. What is the best free SSD health check software? CrystalDiskInfo is the best known free SSD health checker and reads SMART data from almost any drive. Your SSD maker's own tool, like Samsung Magician, Sandisk Dashboard, Crucial Storage Executive or Kingston SSD Manager, also shows health and can update the drive's firmware. Can I still check SSD health with wmic or chkdsk? Not with wmic on current Windows 11, because Microsoft has removed it. Use Get-PhysicalDisk in PowerShell instead. Chkdsk checks the file system, the way files are organised, and doesn't read the SSD's wear or SMART data.

t: Rebuilding RigSight's widgets as boxes of tiles
d: RigSight 1.9.0 turned every widget into a box you fill with tiles, your readings next to a clock, notes, a to-do list or the weather. Getting there meant centring clocks by their ink and making a picture on the desktop take clicks and typing.
l: Building RigSight
b: Until 1.9.0, a RigSight widget was one layout with a handful of readings in it. You picked a line of readings, a grid of them, a few rings or a graph, and each widget did that one thing. On 9 November I started rebuilding them. I wanted widgets good enough to use instead of Windows' own, and I wanted you to decide what goes in one and how it looks. The main rule was no limits. If someone wants an odd widget that doesn't even fit on their screen, that's their call. Desktop widgets as boxes of tiles So a widget became a box you fill with tiles. The box is a grid of small cells, 40 by 32 pixels at size M, and a tile covers as many cells as you give it. There are 16 kinds of tile. Six are about your PC. One shows any reading as a number, a ring or a graph, and the others show a line of readings, a temperature graph, FPS, your day so far and the app you're using. The other ten are everyday things. There's a clock, the date, a calendar, notes, a to-do list, a timer, what's playing, the weather, shortcuts and photos. A widget can hold as many tiles as you like and be any size. Tiles never overlap. Drop one on another and the other moves out of the way, and RigSight never rearranges them by itself. If a widget gets wider than your main screen, the editor tells you and lets you carry on. The editor is a whole page now, with the widget shown as it will look and ready sizes for each tile. Where widgets sit changed too. Until 1.9.0 they stayed on top of your windows. Now every widget sits on the desktop, under your windows, and a shortcut you set brings them all in front. Clocks that only looked centred In my mock-up of the new widgets, none of the clocks looked centred in their tiles. So I took pictures of each one and measured the gap between the drawn digits and each edge of the tile. A 1 pixel border, counted inside the box, pushed everything a pixel up and to the left. The clocks made only of text sat 2 pixels low, and the flip clock's digits sat 1.5 pixels low. After the fixes, every clock in the mock-up measured within 1 pixel. 2 px How low the clocks made only of text sat in my mock-up, because their line of text was centred instead of their digits. A line of text keeps room above and below its letters, so the middle of the line isn't the middle of the digits. In the app, RigSight centres a clock by its ink, the pixels it draws. It draws the text once on its own, finds where those pixels start and stop, and moves the whole clock until that box sits in the middle of the tile. A test draws every clock style and the date, finds the ink on the picture, and fails if the gap on one side is more than 1 pixel bigger than on the other, or 2 pixels at 150% scale. Clicks and typing on a picture The RigSight window you open doesn't draw the widgets. The recorder does, the part of RigSight that runs all day. Each widget is a picture in a see-through window, and that window never takes focus, so the app you're typing in keeps the keyboard. That was fine while widgets only showed readings. The new tiles need clicks and typing, and a picture has no buttons in it. So each time the recorder draws a widget, it also notes where it drew each thing you can click, like a to-do's box or a timer's Start. A click on one of those places does that thing. A press anywhere else still drags the widget. Typing was harder, because a window that never takes focus can't be typed into. My first try showed a real text box over the note when you clicked it. It didn't look like the widget, and a new to-do item went behind it. Now a click on a note or a to-do list opens a window you can't see, holding a text box that takes the keys. The widget draws what you type itself, in its own font and colours, with its own caret. Nothing takes the keyboard until you click, and Esc or a click anywhere else gives it back. The one tile that goes online Every other tile works without the internet. Weather can't, so it's the only tile that goes online. The forecast comes from MET Norway, the Norwegian Meteorological Institute. RigSight sends only the place's position, rounded to about a kilometre, and asks for a place's forecast at most every half hour. When you look a place up in the editor, the name you typed goes to OpenStreetMap's Nominatim to find it. The tile's settings credit both, and the privacy page says what each one sees. Remove the tile or turn its widget off, and RigSight stops asking. Two bugs on my own desktop The first was a widget that kept going back. Drag it on the desktop, change something in the editor, and it jumped back to where it had been. Drag it on the Widgets page's map of your screens, and the widget on the desktop didn't move at all.
