The editor saved its whole copy of the widget at every change, including where it sat when you opened it. I fixed that first, but the map still did nothing. So I followed one move the whole way, from the map to the widget's window on the desktop. The recorder moves that window when you drag a widget on the desktop, so it keeps its own record of where each widget sits. When the app sent its settings over, the recorder kept its own spot for every widget and threw the map's move away. Now the app sends the recorder a move of its own, and the recorder moves the window. I checked it on a running copy, and a test now drags a widget on the map and checks that the move reaches the recorder. The second was worse. On the morning of the release, with a test build on my own PC, all 13 of my widgets disappeared at once. The recorder's log showed the app removing them, and the Remove button explained why. Before the fix After a Remove, the page picked the next widget, with its own Remove button right under the pointer. A double click, or one more click to be sure, took that widget too. In 1.9.0 The page picks nothing after a Remove. It says which widget went, with Undo where Remove was, for a few seconds. The editor's Remove has the same Undo now. A test presses Remove six times in a row and checks that only one widget goes. After those two, I went through all of it again in five parts before the release, one each for the settings, the windows on the desktop, the drawing, the Widgets page and editor, and privacy and security. About fifty smaller fixes came out of it. One was a Photos tile set to a folder on another PC that couldn't be reached. It froze the widgets for about 21 seconds every minute, because Windows waits that long before saying the folder isn't there. RigSight reads a folder like that in the background now, and the widgets keep drawing.

t: My PC reported 146 GB of VRAM. Here's what happened
d: Writing these guides from my own history, I found a game using 146 GB of a 12 GB GPU and a 16 GB PC using 20.8 GB of RAM. Neither was real. Where each came from, and what 1.10.0 changed.
l: Building RigSight
b: Most of the guides on this blog open with my own PC's history. To write one, I query what RigSight recorded, then check every number before it goes in. Twice in the last two weeks, a number failed that check because it couldn't be true. 146 GB on a 12 GB card On 7 November I was writing how to check VRAM usage , and I wanted how much graphics memory each of my games used. Since 0.31.2, RigSight records the game in front's own GPU memory each minute, next to the whole card's. Phantom Blade Zero came back at up to 7.2 GB, which fits a 12 GB RTX 3080 Ti. Crimson Desert came back at about 146 GB. The whole card was at 7.3 GB in those same minutes, on 28 and 30 October. The game's own figure comes from Windows, the same per-app number Task Manager shows as Dedicated GPU memory. Windows doesn't hold that number to the card's size. It can count memory the game refers to without it all being on the card. For most games it stays sensible. For this one, on those days, it didn't. The Games page was showing it as is. So were the export and the AI's look-ups, since they all read the same play figures. In 1.10.0, a play where the game's own figure goes above the whole card even once isn't trusted for that play. It shows the card's figure instead, said as the whole GPU and all apps, the same way it does when Windows doesn't report a game's own use at all. The change is in how plays are read, not in what's stored, so plays from before the fix are covered too. 20.8 GB of RAM on a 16 GB PC On 10 November I was writing what is using my RAM . My PC has 16 GB, and RigSight's own list of my parts says so. Its history said the highest RAM in use was 20.8 GB. The 142 minutes above 16 GB were all on 23 September, the first day RigSight ever recorded on this PC. The hardware library RigSight reads sensors through names the RAM group and the virtual memory group the same way, both "Memory". Virtual memory is RAM plus the page file, so it can go well past 16. A build from that first day sometimes read the wrong group. I fixed that the same day, before 0.4.0, but those minutes stayed in my history for seven weeks. On 11 November I blanked the 213 minutes of RAM readings from that first day, after a backup. Nothing else in those minutes changed. 1.10.0 then fixed the cause of the confusion for everyone. Virtual memory's readings now have names of their own, Virtual Memory, Virtual Memory Used and Virtual Memory Available, so the taskbar, the overlay, the widget pickers and All sensors no longer show two readings called Memory. Names you gave readings yourself keep working. Today the highest RAM in my history is 15.7 GB, on a 16 GB PC. That's the number the normal RAM usage while gaming guide uses. Why the guides are worth checking this hard Both readings sat in my own history for weeks, and I look at RigSight every day. A number on a page gets a glance. A number I'm about to publish gets questioned, because someone else will read it and maybe act on it. Writing from my own data has turned out to be one of the better tests RigSight has. It's also why the guides say what they don't know. When a reading looks wrong and I can't explain it, it stays out of the post until I can.

t: What is taking up space on my C drive in Windows 11
d: My C drive grew from 198 to 271 GB in seven weeks, 68 GB of it in one day, and my Steam games aren't even on it. How to see what is taking up space on your C drive in Windows 11, what you can safely clear, and what to leave alone.
l: PC problems Storage and memory what is taking up space on my c drive windows 11 what is taking up so much space on my c drive see what is taking up space on my c drive what is taking up space on my c drive windows 10 what is taking up space on my hard drive windows 11
b: On 23 September my C drive had 198 GB used. Seven weeks later it had 271 GB, out of 446. On 30 October alone it grew by 68 GB. That morning Steam downloaded a 58 GB game update, which looks like the obvious answer. It isn't, because every Steam game I have lives on my E drive. Something else filled C, and I'd never have known the day without a record. Here is how to see what is taking up space on your C drive in Windows 11, what you can safely clear, and what to leave alone. What is taking up space on my C drive in Windows 11? Check Settings first Open Start > Settings > System > Storage . Wait a few seconds while Windows adds up each category for the C drive. Click Show more categories to see all of them, biggest first. Click any category to see what is inside. Apps lists installed apps by size, Temporary files lists what can be removed, and Other lists the biggest folders Windows couldn't sort. This answers most cases straight away. A huge Apps figure usually means games. A huge Other figure is often a game library or an app's data folder. A big System & reserved figure is Windows itself plus a few large files covered further down. Clear what Windows already suggests In Settings > System > Storage , open Cleanup recommendations . Look through Temporary files , Large or unused files , Files synced to the cloud and Unused apps . Tick only what you are sure about and press Clean up in each section. Check the Downloads folder before you tick it. Windows lists it with temporary files, but it often holds installers and documents you meant to keep. Turn on Storage Sense Storage Sense clears temporary files and old Recycle Bin items for you. Turn it on in Settings > System > Storage > Storage Sense . By default it runs when the drive is low on space, and you can set it to run every day, week or month. It leaves your Downloads folder alone unless you tell it otherwise, and it only looks after the C drive. Microsoft says it can't run until you have been signed in and online for more than 10 minutes, so don't expect it to work the moment you switch it on. Remove old update files with Disk Cleanup Press Start, type Disk Cleanup and open it. Choose the C drive and press OK . Press Clean up system files and choose C again. Tick Windows Update Cleanup , Temporary files and anything else you recognise, then press OK and Delete Files . If you upgraded Windows in the last ten days, a previous Windows installation shows here too, often many GB. Deleting it is fine once the new version works, but you lose the option to go back. The big system files, and which are safe to shrink hiberfil.sys This hidden file in the root of C holds your memory while the PC hibernates. Microsoft says it is roughly the size of your RAM, so 16 or 32 GB on a gaming PC. If you never use hibernate, open Command Prompt as administrator and run powercfg.exe /hibernate off . The file goes away. You also lose Fast Startup and hybrid sleep, so a cold boot can take a little longer. Run the same command with on to bring it back. Don't delete the file by hand. pagefile.sys The page file is where Windows puts memory that doesn't fit in RAM. It can be several GB. Leave it on and let Windows manage its size. Turning it off can make apps close when memory runs out. Restore points System Restore keeps snapshots of Windows that can grow large. Press Start, type Create a restore point , pick the C drive and press Configure to see how much they use and to lower the limit. Keep some space for them, as they are your way back after a bad driver or update. WinSxS The WinSxS folder inside Windows looks huge in Explorer, partly because many of its files are the same files you see elsewhere in Windows, counted twice. Microsoft warns that deleting files from it can stop your PC from booting or updating. Shrink it only with Windows' own tools, such as Disk Cleanup's Windows Update Cleanup. Windows also trims it by itself over time. Games, caches and your own files On a gaming PC, games are usually the biggest thing on C. Each launcher has its own place to see sizes and uninstall. In Steam, open Settings > Storage . It shows each game's size per drive, and you can tick a game and press Move to put it on another drive without downloading it again. Uninstall games you have finished through their launcher, so their save data and leftovers are handled properly. Graphics drivers keep a shader cache that can reach several GB. Games and Windows rebuild it on their own, so clearing it is safe, but the next launch of each game may take longer while it builds again. Disk Cleanup has a DirectX Shader Cache option for this. For your own files, OneDrive's Files On-Demand keeps files online and frees the local copy until you open one. Videos, old phone backups and the Downloads folder are the usual surprises, and typing size:gigantic into Explorer's search box while C is open finds files over 4 GB on the whole drive. Start with Settings > System > Storage and Cleanup recommendations, then Disk Cleanup's system files. If C is still tight after that, move a game library to another drive. If the drive also feels slow or throws errors, run an SSD health check . How RigSight caught it Windows shows what fills a drive today. RigSight also keeps track of how it got there. Its Storage page lists the drives inside your PC, fullest first, with USB and network drives below them, and shows how much each has grown over the last few days, such as +3.7 GB in 8 days. A drive that fills fast stands out before it is full. With admin rights, each drive also shows its health in plain words. Below the drives, Space you could free lists what RigSight found. That can include temporary files, the Windows temp folder, downloads you haven't touched in 90 days, the Windows Update cache, NVIDIA, AMD and DirectX shader caches, crash dumps, a previous Windows installation and the Recycle Bin. Nothing is deleted for you. Each line opens its folder or a list to review, and only the Recycle Bin has an Empty button. Scan a drive and RigSight shows its folders as a list and a map side by side, coloured by kind of file, and you can open any folder down to its files or switch to the largest files. A scan also finds big files you haven't changed in a year. Each drive keeps its last scan after a restart, so you can come back to it. On the Games page every game shows its size and the drive it sits on, and you can uninstall it through its own launcher. The Timeline notes when a drive's used space jumped or dropped within a day, and by how much. That's how I found the 30 October jump, and why I knew not to blame Steam. RigSight records each drive's used space every day. Steam's own download log, which RigSight reads, says what Steam fetched, and Steam's library list says which drive each game sits on. The rest of the 68 GB is what a scan of C is for. RigSight is free and open source. Why is my C drive full for no reason? Windows updates, temporary files, browser and shader caches, restore points and your Downloads folder grow on their own. Games often install to C by default and get large updates. Settings > System > Storage shows which of these is biggest on your PC. What is taking up so much space on my C drive under Other or System? System & reserved holds Windows itself, the page file, the hibernation file and restore points. Other holds folders Windows can't sort into a category, often game folders or app data. Click it to see the biggest folders. Shrink these with the Windows settings below, never by deleting files from the Windows folder. Is it safe to delete the WinSxS folder? No. Microsoft warns that deleting files from WinSxS can leave your PC unable to boot or update. Let Windows shrink it with Disk Cleanup's Windows Update Cleanup instead. Can I delete hiberfil.sys and pagefile.sys? Don't delete either by hand. hiberfil.sys is about as big as your RAM and goes away if you turn hibernation off, which also turns off Fast Startup. Leave pagefile.sys for Windows to manage.

t: How to get desktop widgets on Windows 11, with CPU temperature
d: Windows 11 keeps its widgets on a board beside the taskbar. How to get desktop widgets on Windows 11 that stay where you put them, with a clock, notes, the weather and your CPU and GPU temperature, and the other options people use.
l: PC problems Tools desktop widgets windows 11 windows 11 widgets on desktop desktop widgets windows 11 free desktop widgets windows 11 clock does windows have widgets windows 11 widgets alternative cpu temperature widget windows 11 gpu temperature widget windows 11 pc monitor widget windows 11 rainmeter alternative windows 11 clock widget windows 11 desktop weather widget windows 11 desktop sticky notes desktop windows 11 to do list widget windows 11
b: Windows 11 has widgets, but they open on the Widgets board, a panel that slides in from the taskbar. Close it and they're gone again. If you want desktop widgets on Windows 11 that stay where you put them, like a clock, a note or your CPU temperature, you need an app that draws them. I wanted that on my own PC, and I wanted widgets good enough to use instead of Windows' own, so in RigSight 1.9.0 I rebuilt its widgets from tiles. Here's what Windows gives you, how RigSight does it, and the other options people use. Where Windows 11's own widgets live Most of the time, Windows 11 shows the weather on the taskbar. Select it, press Windows key + W, or swipe in from the side of the screen, and the Widgets board opens. On the board you can add, remove, resize and arrange widgets, and the Widgets page in the Microsoft Store has more for apps that support them. To take the button off the taskbar, right-click the taskbar, open Taskbar settings and turn off Widgets under Taskbar items . The board still opens with Windows key + W. Microsoft's page describes widgets only on that board. It says nothing about putting one on the desktop itself. So for Windows 11 widgets on the desktop, or a Windows 11 widgets alternative that stays in view, you need another app. Desktop widgets on Windows 11 with RigSight In RigSight, a widget is a box you fill with tiles. You can put as many tiles in one as you like, in any arrangement, and the widget sits on the desktop under your windows. The part of RigSight that records all day draws them, so they stay when you close the RigSight window. RigSight is free and open source. There are 16 kinds of tile. Ten are everyday things. A clock, in five styles. Digits, hands, flip cards, the time in words, or the day in big letters with the time under it. The date, and a calendar of this month with today marked. Notes you type straight onto the desktop. Turn on Sticky note and the note gets yellow paper and handwriting. A to-do list you tick off and add to on the widget itself. A timer, a stopwatch, or a countdown to a day. A timer tells you when it's up. Media, which shows what's playing on the PC with play, pause and skip. The weather for a place you pick. Shortcuts to up to 12 apps, folders and links, each opened with one click. Photos from a folder, one after another, from every 10 seconds to every hour. The other six are about your PC. Most tiles come in ready sizes, Small , Medium and Large , and any size in between. A CPU temperature widget for Windows 11 The Any reading tile shows one reading or sensor. CPU temperature, GPU temperature, a load, memory, a fan or anything else RigSight reads. It can be a number, a big number, a ring, a level, blocks, or a line, filled or bar graph of the last five minutes. For CPU and GPU temperature there's one more look that puts the load and power next to the temperature. Rings, levels and blocks need a temperature or a percentage, so they don't show for every reading. The rest of the PC tiles are these. Temperature graph draws CPU and GPU temperatures over the last five minutes. Line of readings puts several readings in one slim line, made for the top of the screen. FPS shows your game's frame rate, frame time and 1% low. It needs RivaTuner Statistics Server. Today shows screen time so far today, your most used app and today's peaks. Now playing shows the app or game you're using, for how long, and its peak temperatures. CPU temperature needs RigSight running with admin rights. How to put widgets on your desktop with RigSight Install RigSight from rigsight.app , open it and go to Widgets . Click Add widget and pick a ready-made widget or a single tile. It appears at the top right of your main screen. To start from nothing, click Create widget instead, which opens an empty widget in the editor. In the editor, click Add tile and pick a kind. The editor fills the page and shows the widget as it will look. Drag tiles to arrange them. Tiles never overlap. Drop one on another and the other moves out of the way. Click a tile to change just that tile, like a clock's style, a reading's look or the size. For the weather, type a town or city and click Find . Use Place to put the widget in a corner of any screen, or drag it on the desktop. Because the widgets sit under your windows, you can set a Shortcut to bring them in front . Press it, glance at them, and Esc or a click anywhere else sends them back. There's also a shortcut to turn them all off and on. Lock in place makes a widget click-through, so a click lands on whatever is under it. Weather is the only tile that goes online. Its forecast comes from MET Norway, and RigSight sends only the place's position, rounded to about a kilometre. When you look a place up in the editor, the name you typed goes to OpenStreetMap's Nominatim to find it. The privacy page says what each one sees. Every other tile works without the internet. Other ways to get widgets on Windows 11 Rainmeter is free and open source under the GNU GPL v2, and has been since 2001. It shows skins on your desktop, such as hardware usage meters and audio visualizers, and runs on Windows 7 through Windows 11. It suits people who enjoy building their desktop's look skin by skin. Microsoft Sticky Notes is Microsoft's own app for quick notes. Sign in with a Microsoft account and your notes sync to your other devices, to the web, and to OneNote on phones. If your notes need to follow you to your phone, it's the one to use. The Widgets board is still there for news and the widgets apps add to it. You can keep using it next to RigSight's widgets. Your next step is to decide what you look at most during the day. If it's the time and a few notes, one widget with a clock and a sticky note covers it. If you keep wondering how hot your PC is while you play, add a CPU and GPU temperature ring next to them, and you won't have to open anything to check. Does Windows have widgets? Yes. Windows 11 has a Widgets board that opens from the weather on the taskbar, with Windows key + W, or by swiping in from the side of the screen. You can add, remove, resize and arrange widgets on the board, but Microsoft's page describes them only there, not on the desktop. How do I put widgets on my desktop in Windows 11? Use an app that draws them on the desktop. In RigSight, open Widgets and click Add widget for a ready-made one, or Create widget to build your own from tiles. Place puts it in a corner of any screen, or you can drag it where you like. Is there a CPU temperature widget for Windows 11? Yes. RigSight's Any reading tile shows CPU or GPU temperature as a number, a ring, a level or a graph, and its Temperature graph tile shows both over the last five minutes. CPU temperature needs RigSight running with admin rights. Are there free desktop widgets for Windows 11? Yes. RigSight is free and open source under the MIT licence, and Rainmeter is free and open source under the GNU GPL v2. Windows' own Widgets board is free too, but it stays on its board. What is a good Rainmeter alternative for Windows 11? If you want widgets without writing or installing skins, RigSight builds them in an editor from tiles, with PC readings next to a clock, notes and the weather. Rainmeter is the better fit if you like designing every part of a skin yourself.

t: What is using my RAM? How to find it on Windows 11
d: The biggest memory user on my PC isn't a game, it's a local AI model at up to 7.8 GB. How to find what is using your RAM on Windows 11, what the numbers in Task Manager mean, and how RigSight spots an app that keeps growing.
l: PC problems Storage and memory what is using my ram windows 11 high memory usage windows 11 nothing running what is using all my ram high memory usage windows 11 not showing in task manager high memory usage windows 11 chrome high memory usage windows 11 idle high memory usage windows 11 after update
b: When I sorted RigSight's history by memory, the biggest user on my PC wasn't a game. It was Llama Server, a local AI model I run, at up to 7.8 GB. The heaviest game came next, Phantom Blade Zero at up to 6.9 GB, then Apex Legends at 6.6 GB. Task Manager would only have shown me whichever was open at that moment. Here is how to find out what is using your RAM on Windows 11, which numbers are normal, and what to do when one app keeps taking more. What is using my RAM on Windows 11? Check Task Manager Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager. Pick Processes on the left. Click the Memory column header. The apps holding the most memory move to the top. Click the arrow next to an app to see the separate processes inside it. Browsers, Discord, Steam and many other apps run as several processes, so one name can hide twenty of them. The list is split into apps, background processes and Windows processes. Lines called Service Host are parts of Windows, grouped by the service they run. If one app is clearly holding the most, you have your answer. Close it, or close the tabs or projects inside it you don't need. If nothing in the list looks big but the total is still high, read on. Why the total is higher than the list adds up to The Processes list only counts memory that apps hold. Windows also uses RAM for itself, for drivers and as a cache. To see all of it, open Performance in Task Manager and pick Memory . The figures under the graph mean the following. In use is memory that apps and Windows hold right now. The number next to it in brackets is the compressed part. Compressed memory is memory apps aren't touching at the moment, squeezed by Windows so more fits in RAM. It is faster than writing it out to the drive, and it is normal to see a few hundred MB or more. Cached is files and programs Windows keeps in RAM in case you open them again. Windows hands this memory to any app that asks for it, so a big cache is a good thing. Available is what apps can still get, which is free memory plus the cache that can be given back. Committed is memory promised to apps, counted against your RAM and the page file together. When it gets close to the limit, Windows warns that the PC is low on memory. Non-paged pool is memory the Windows kernel and drivers use. It should stay fairly steady. Hardware reserved is set aside before Windows starts, for example for integrated graphics. The figure to watch is Available. Plenty available means you have room, even if In use looks high. Get a clearer split with Resource Monitor Press Start, type resmon and open Resource Monitor. Pick the Memory tab. Click the Private (KB) column to sort by it. Private memory belongs to that process alone, so it is the best single figure for which app is holding your RAM. The bar at the bottom splits all memory into Hardware Reserved, In Use, Modified, Standby and Free. Standby is the same cache Task Manager calls Cached. Modified is memory waiting to be written to the drive before it can be reused, and it is usually small. High memory usage on Windows 11 with nothing running When you haven't opened anything and memory is still high, it is usually one of these. Apps that start with Windows Game launchers, chat apps, RGB and peripheral software, cloud sync and updaters all load at sign-in and sit in the tray. Open Task Manager, pick Startup apps , right-click anything you don't need right away and choose Disable . It still works when you open it yourself. A browser that never closed Chrome and Edge can keep running in the background after you close the last window, so extensions and apps can keep working. Turn that off in the browser's settings if you don't want it. In Chrome it is under Settings > System , in Edge under Settings > System and performance . The cache after a game After a big game, Cached can stay high for a while. That is Windows keeping files ready, not memory being lost. You don't need a RAM cleaner app to clear it. Those tools empty the cache, and Windows fills it again. Work after an update After a large Windows update, Windows often reindexes files and does other background work for a while. Restart and give it a few hours before you chase it. A memory leak If one app grows hour after hour while you do nothing more in it, it is leaking. Restart that app to get the memory back, then update it. If it keeps happening, the app's own support page or forum usually knows about it. High memory usage not showing in Task Manager If Performance > Memory says most of your RAM is in use but the Processes list adds up to far less, look at the Non-paged pool figure. If it keeps climbing over hours and reaches several GB, a driver is probably leaking memory. Drivers you installed or updated recently are the first suspects. Update or reinstall them, and restart. To see exactly where memory has gone, Microsoft's free Sysinternals tool RAMMap splits all of it by use, including driver memory, the cache and each process. It needs to run as administrator. Browser tabs and Chrome's high memory usage Each tab and extension in Chrome or Edge is its own process, which is why a browser so often tops the list. Two settings help. In Chrome, open Settings > Performance and turn on Memory Saver . Tabs you haven't used for a while are put to rest and reload when you go back to them. In Edge, open Settings > System and performance and turn on sleeping tabs, which does the same. To find the one heavy tab, press Shift + Esc inside Chrome or Edge. The browser's own task manager lists every tab and extension with its memory. When high memory use is a real problem High In use on its own is fine. It is a problem when Available is close to zero, the drive light stays busy while apps stutter, or Windows tells you the PC is low on memory. Then the fix is to run less at once, find the leaking app, or add RAM. Windows 11 needs at least 4 GB to run, and games and browsers with many tabs need a lot more than that. Leave the page file on and let Windows manage its size. Without it, apps can close without warning when memory runs out. For how much memory games use and what's normal while you play, see normal RAM usage while gaming . Start with Task Manager's Memory column and the Available figure. If nothing stands out, check Startup apps and your browser's settings. If something keeps growing, restart it and update it, and if the Non-paged pool is the one growing, update your drivers next. How RigSight caught it Task Manager shows what is using memory right now. It doesn't tell you whether an app always uses that much, or only started today. RigSight keeps a record of each app's memory all day, so it can. The Memory page shows how full your RAM is, with today's lowest and highest, and splits it into apps, compressed and free. Below that, every running app is listed with what it holds now beside its usual, which is its average over the days before today. An app well above its usual is marked, such as "Twice its usual", and a Worth a look card points it out. When nothing is above its usual, the page shows the apps holding the most instead. Today's biggest memory users lists each app's peak and average, and a card shows when memory was fullest today and which apps held the most around then. Since version 1.7.0, RigSight can also tell you about a leak while it happens. Turn on Apps that keep growing in memory in Settings, and when an app's memory has risen every hour for three hours, ending at 2 GB or more and at least twice where it started, you get a notification such as "Google Chrome keeps using more memory". It says how far it went and how fast, and that it hasn't come back down. The bell in the title bar keeps it for 30 days. On the Processes page, open a browser or another app made of many processes, and RigSight splits its memory into its tabs, its extensions and the app itself, with its recorded history beside it. You can end an app there too, with a warning before you end a part of Windows. RigSight is free and open source. Why is my memory usage high on Windows 11 with nothing running? Usually it's apps that start with Windows and sit in the tray, a browser that keeps running after you close its window, and memory Windows keeps as a cache. Cached memory is handed back as soon as an app needs it, so it isn't a problem. Check Task Manager's Startup apps page and turn off what you don't need. Why is high memory usage not showing in Task Manager's list? The Processes list only shows what apps hold. Memory used by drivers, the Windows kernel and hardware such as integrated graphics isn't listed there. If the Non-paged pool figure on Performance > Memory keeps climbing for hours, a driver may be leaking memory, and Microsoft's free RAMMap tool shows where it went. Is high memory usage at idle bad? Not by itself. Windows uses spare RAM to cache files you might open again, and gives it back the moment an app asks. It's a problem when Available memory is close to zero, the PC stutters or Windows warns that it is low on memory. Why does Chrome use so much RAM? Chrome runs each tab and extension as its own process, so its memory adds up quickly with many tabs open. Turn on Memory Saver in Settings > Performance, and press Shift + Esc in Chrome to open its own task manager and see which tab or extension holds the most. Why is my memory usage high after a Windows update? Right after a big update Windows often does background work, such as indexing files again. Give it a few hours and a restart before you go looking. If one process still holds far more than it used to, update or reinstall that app or driver.

t: GPU thermal throttling, and how to tell if yours is
d: In 5,128 minutes of heavy load my GPU never passed 73°C, so it never had a reason to slow down. What GPU thermal throttling is, how RigSight tells it apart from normal boost and power limits, and how to check and fix it.
l: PC problems Temperatures gpu thermal throttling is my gpu thermal throttling how to check if gpu is throttling gpu thermal throttling temp gpu thermal throttling symptoms gpu thermal throttling fix how to check if gpu is power throttling
b: In 5,128 minutes with my GPU at least 80% busy, the hottest it got was 73°C, in No Man's Sky on 7 October. RigSight starts looking for GPU thermal throttling at 83°C, so my card never had a reason to slow itself down. That's what most healthy PCs look like. Throttling is worth knowing about because when it does happen, it looks like the game got slower for no reason. What GPU thermal throttling is Every GPU has a maximum temperature set by its maker. NVIDIA lists 85 to 93°C for its recent GeForce GPUs, depending on the model. As a card gets close to its limit, it lowers its clock speed and power so it makes less heat. The card stays safe, but it does less work, so the frame rate falls. Normal GPU temperature while gaming has the usual ranges and each maker's limits. The usual symptoms are these. The game runs well for the first few minutes, then the frame rate drops and stays lower. The GPU's temperature sits near its limit, and the fans run fast. The clock speed falls while the load stays the same. Power throttling is a different thing. A card at its power limit lowers its clocks at normal temperatures, which is how cards are designed to run. A card that eases its clocks a little as it warms from 60 to 75°C is doing its normal boost, not throttling. How to check if your GPU is throttling Start a demanding game and play for 15 minutes, so the card is fully warm. Watch the GPU's temperature and clock speed together, with an overlay or a monitoring app. If the temperature reaches the high 80s and the clock falls while the load stays near 100%, that's thermal throttling. GPU-Z's Sensors tab has a PerfCap Reason line that names what is holding the clocks back, such as temperature or power. How to fix GPU thermal throttling Check every fan on the GPU spins under load. A stopped fan is the fastest way to a throttling card, and GPU fan not spinning covers how to tell. Clean the dust out of the GPU's heatsink and the case filters with short bursts of compressed air, holding the fans still. Give the case airflow. Air in at the front or bottom, out at the back or top, and room around the PC. Cap the frame rate a little under your screen's refresh rate. The card does less work for frames you never see, and runs cooler. Raise the GPU's fan curve a little in the card maker's app, then test again. On an older card, new thermal paste can help. A big gap between the GPU's temperature and its hot spot is a sign, as GPU hotspot temperature explains. Opening a card can affect the warranty, so check that first. For the whole PC running hot, PC overheating while gaming has the full list. Your next step is the 15-minute check above. If the clocks hold while the temperature stays below the high 80s, your GPU isn't throttling. How RigSight catches it A GPU's clock speed moves all the time, so a lower clock on its own proves nothing. As a card warms up, its boost lets the clock ease down a step or two. A heavier scene draws more power and can hit the card's power limit. A different game runs at different clocks altogether. None of that is the card slowing down to stay cool. So RigSight compares the GPU with itself, inside one stretch of one game at heavy load. It takes the clocks from that same stretch while the GPU was cooler, and looks for minutes where the GPU sat at 83°C or more with its clocks below 88% of that, without drawing more power than before. Three minutes or more of that counts as throttling. Since version 1.7.0, when it happens you get a notification afterwards, such as "Your GPU slowed itself for 12 minutes to stay cool", with how far the clocks fell and the temperature it started at. RigSight also tells you after a game when it ran hotter than usual at the same power. The bell in the title bar keeps every notification from the last 30 days. RigSight is free and open source. At what temperature does a GPU thermal throttle? It depends on the card. NVIDIA lists maximum temperatures of 85 to 93°C for its recent GeForce GPUs, and cards start lowering clocks as they get close to that. Check the maker's page for your model. What are the symptoms of GPU thermal throttling? The game runs well for the first few minutes, then the frame rate drops and stays lower. The GPU's temperature sits near its limit, the fans run fast, and the clock speed falls while the load stays the same. How do I check if my GPU is power throttling? GPU-Z's Sensors tab has a PerfCap Reason line that names what is holding the clocks back, such as power or temperature. A card at its power limit lowers its clocks at normal temperatures, which is how the card is designed to run, not a fault.

t: GPU fan not spinning? When it's normal and when it's a fault
d: My GPU's fans stood still 42% of the time since late September, and never once above 52°C. When a GPU fan not spinning is normal, how RigSight tells it apart from a stuck fan, and what to check when it really is a fault.
l: PC problems Fans gpu fan not spinning gpu fan not spinning while gaming gpu fan not spinning on startup gpu fan not spinning when idle why is one gpu fan not spinning gpu fan not spinning under load
b: Since 29 September, RigSight has recorded about 29,700 minutes of my GPU's two fans. They stood still for 42% of that time. They were never still with the GPU above 52°C, and from 52°C up they spun every single minute. A GPU fan not spinning is usually the card doing what it was built to do. What matters is whether the fan stays still when the GPU is hot, and here's how to tell the two apart. Why most GPU fans stop on purpose Most GPUs made in the last several years have a fan stop mode. NVIDIA card makers call it things like zero RPM, 0dB or fan stop. AMD calls it Zero RPM and says it is on by default. The idea is simple. When you're on the desktop or watching a video, the heatsink alone can keep the GPU cool, so the fans stay off and the card is silent. The fans start once the GPU warms past a set point. On many cards that's somewhere around 50 to 60°C, but the exact number is set by the card maker, so it differs between models. Once started, cards often keep spinning until the GPU drops a few degrees below that point. That gap stops the fans from flicking on and off every few seconds. So these are all normal. A GPU fan not spinning when idle, with the GPU at 30 to 50°C. A GPU fan not spinning on startup, because the card is cold. Fans that start and stop a few times while you browse, as the GPU drifts around its start point. One fan of three stopping before the others at light load, on cards that do that. How to tell if it's a fault The test is heat. A healthy fan with fan stop spins once the GPU is warm. A broken one doesn't. Here's how to check. Open a tool that shows both GPU temperature and fan speed. For AMD cards, AMD Software has this under Performance > Metrics . For any card, MSI Afterburner or HWiNFO show both. Start a demanding game or a benchmark, windowed so you can watch the numbers. Watch the fan speed as the temperature climbs past 60°C. If the temperature reaches about 70°C or more and the fan still reads 0 rpm, close the game. That's a GPU fan not spinning under load, and it needs fixing before you play again. If the fans spin up and the GPU settles at a normal gaming temperature, the card is fine. The post on normal GPU temperature while gaming has the ranges. A GPU that runs hot with no fan won't usually break at once. It will throttle, which means it slows itself down to stay under its limit. You'll see lower frame rates and the clock speed dropping. If it gets too hot it can shut the PC off. Either way, don't keep gaming on it. What to check when the GPU fan is not spinning while gaming Try these in order. The first ones are the most common causes and the safest to fix. 1. A fan curve or tool that holds the fans back Fan tools like MSI Afterburner, EVGA Precision X1, ASUS GPU Tweak and AMD Software can all set their own fan curve. A curve copied from another card, a profile that loads at startup, or a fixed speed of 0% can keep the fans still at any heat. Two of these tools running at once can also fight over the fans. Open the fan tool you use and choose its default or auto fan setting. In AMD Software, open Performance > Tuning and reset the tuning to default. The fan tuning there also has the Zero RPM switch. Close any second fan tool, then test again in a game. Turning fan stop off is a fair test. If the fans spin with it off and never with it on, the card's fan stop isn't waking up. A driver can cause that, which is the next step. 2. The graphics driver Fan control on modern cards goes through the driver. A bad install, or a driver release with a fan bug, can leave the fans still. Restart the PC first, since that clears a stuck state. If it keeps happening, install the latest driver from NVIDIA or AMD, or go back one version if the trouble started right after an update. 3. Something blocking the fan Shut the PC down and switch the power supply off at its switch. Then look closely for these. A cable resting against the blades. Cables tied near the card can drift into them. Thick dust or pet hair around the hub, which can stall a weak fan. A blade that rubs the shroud, often after a card was dropped or the shroud bent. Turn each fan gently with a finger. It should spin freely and coast for a moment. If it feels gritty, stiff or stops at once, the bearing is worn. When you clean it with compressed air, hold the blades still so the air doesn't spin them too fast. 4. Power and the fan's own cable Each fan connects to the card's board through a small cable under the shroud. If the card was opened, repasted or cleaned, one may have come loose. That's the usual reason one GPU fan isn't spinning when the others are. If you're not comfortable opening the shroud, leave it to the maker's support, since opening it can affect the warranty on some cards. If no fan spins and you get no display, the card likely has no power at all. Check that the PCIe power cables are pushed fully into the card and the power supply, with no gap at the latch, and that the card is seated in its slot. 5. Laptops Laptop GPUs usually share fans and heat pipes with the CPU, and the laptop's maker sets how they behave. Silent or quiet modes in the maker's app can hold the fans low. Switch to its balanced or performance mode and test again. If the fans never come on and the laptop gets hot, contact the maker. 6. When it's the fan itself If the fan stays still in a game after all of the above, it has failed. Contact the card maker about a repair or replacement under the warranty. Until it's fixed, don't game on the card. If your GPU fan isn't spinning right now, start with the heat test above. Five minutes in a game with the temperature and fan speed on screen tells you whether you have a quiet card or a broken fan. How RigSight caught it RigSight records every fan's speed each minute next to the temperature of the part it cools. On the Fans page, a GPU fan at 0 rpm with a cool GPU shows as "Resting while cool". The same fan at 0 rpm with the GPU at 70°C or more shows as "Stopped while hot" and counts as needing a look. For a card with fan stop, the page also works out where the fans start, and says it as "Silent below that, faster as it warms". It shows how long they stood still and how many times they started up, for a day, a week, a month or a year. My fans also stop between about 42 and 50°C some of the time and spin the rest. That's the gap cards keep on purpose. Once spinning, they keep going until the GPU has cooled a few degrees, so they don't flick on and off. RigSight once read a stopped fan as a clogged one, and that story is in The day RigSight told me my healthy fan was clogged . Since then it compares a fan only with itself at the same heat. Since version 1.7.0 you don't have to be watching. If a GPU fan shows 0 rpm for 3 minutes or more with the GPU at 70°C or more, and it always turns at that heat, you get a notification titled "Your GPU fan stopped". It says how long, from when and how hot the GPU was, and ends with "Check it isn't blocked or unplugged." RigSight also tells you when fans spin slower than usual at the same heat. The bell in the title bar keeps every notification from the last 30 days, so one you missed while gaming is still there. GPU fans show without admin rights. RigSight is free and open source. Is it normal for GPU fans to not spin? Yes, at idle. Most current NVIDIA and AMD cards have a zero RPM or fan stop mode that keeps the fans still while the GPU is cool, often below somewhere around 50 to 60°C. The exact point depends on the card. The fans start once the card warms past that point. Why are my GPU fans not spinning on startup? When the PC first starts, the GPU is cold, so a card with fan stop has no reason to spin. Some cards give the fans a short spin at power on and some don't. As long as they start once you game, nothing is wrong. Why is one GPU fan not spinning? Some cards stop one fan before the others at light load, and some run only part of their fans until the card is warm. If one fan stays still while the others spin hard in a game, it may be stuck, unplugged at its small connector on the card, or worn out. What should I do if my GPU fan is not spinning while gaming? Watch the GPU temperature. If it climbs past about 70°C and the fan still reads 0 rpm, close the game. Reset any custom fan curve to default, update the graphics driver, and check the fan isn't blocked by a cable or dust. If it still won't spin, contact the card maker about the warranty. Can a GPU fan not spinning and no display be the same problem? Often, yes. If the fans don't move and there's no picture, the card may not be getting power. Check that the PCIe power cables are pushed fully into the card and the power supply, and that the card sits firmly in its slot.

t: Should RigSight be rewritten in Rust? I measured first
d: RigSight felt slow to open, and I wondered whether parts of it should be rewritten in Rust. Measuring every part said no. The slow parts were drivers, Windows and the way the window started, and fixing those made it open in about 1.1 seconds instead of 1.9.
l: Building RigSight
b: In early November RigSight started to feel slow to open. I click it in the tray, and there's a pause before the window shows. So I asked a big question. Should parts of RigSight be rewritten in Rust, a language known for fast programs? Before rewriting anything, I wanted to know where the time actually went. Where the 1.9 seconds went On my PC, with my real history, the window took about 1.9 seconds to show. I traced every part of that time. Reading the settings file took about half a second. Setting up the pages took nearly another half second, including pages I hadn't opened yet. Building the window itself took about 0.4 seconds. The app had grown a lot in a month. The main window's layout file went from about 800 lines in mid October to over 2,100, and the settings had more than doubled. None of that was slow code. It was just more to load before the window showed, and all of it was loaded up front. The fixes were about doing less at the start, not about a faster language. Each page is now built the first time you open it, not when the app starts. The settings are read while the window is still loading, instead of before it. More of the app is compiled ahead of time, so less of it has to be compiled while it starts. Things you only see later, like the welcome screen and the plans, wait until they're needed. 1.1 s How long RigSight's window now takes to show on my PC, down from about 1.9 seconds. Home shows today's history in about 1.3 seconds instead of 2.2. Checking everything else The next morning I measured the rest of the app the same way, page by page and thread by thread, to see whether anything else would gain from Rust. Nothing would. When you switch pages, most of the time goes to laying out and drawing text, which is the window framework's own work, not RigSight's. RigSight's own code was about 25 ms of each visit. The history is stored in SQLite, which is already written in C. The Storage page's cleanup scan is slow because reading a whole drive's folders is slow, whatever language asks for them. The recorder that runs all day was the most interesting part. On my PC it used about 2.2% of one CPU core, while the test copy used under half a percent. Of the recorder's busiest thread, about 90% of the time was spent inside Windows' kernel and drivers, reading sensors. All of RigSight's own code together came to about 0.4% of a core. A faster language can't make a driver answer faster. The bug the numbers found So why did my recorder use five times more than the test copy? I tried one taskbar reading at a time. With the CPU temperature in the taskbar, the recorder used about 1.1% of a core. With the GPU temperature, it used 2.4%. RigSight has a fast way to read an NVIDIA card's temperature, load and power, straight from NVIDIA's own library. But when any reading on the NVIDIA card was being watched live, for the taskbar, a widget or the overlay, a rule switched that fast way off and read everything the slow way instead. Version 1.6.2 keeps the fast way on. Before 1.6.2 With a GPU reading in the taskbar, the recorder used about 2.2% of a CPU core. Since 1.6.2 The same settings use about 1.1%, half as much, all day. If I had rewritten the recorder in Rust, it would have called the same drivers the same slow way, and nothing would have changed. The numbers said where to look, and it was one rule, not the language. The lesson I'm keeping is boring, and that's fine. When something feels slow, measure where the time goes before deciding what to rewrite. Most of the time, the answer is doing less, not doing it in another language.

t: 1% low FPS meaning, and why my 116 was really 69
d: Four hours of Risk of Rain 2 at 187 FPS. Each minute's 1% low, averaged, said 116. Counting every frame together, it was 69. The 1% low FPS meaning in plain words, what a good gap to the average looks like, and how to see and fix it.
l: PC problems FPS and games 1 low fps meaning what is 1 low fps 1 low fps explained 1 low fps drops 1 low fps fix 1 low fps msi afterburner does low fps cause lag
b: On 28 October I played Risk of Rain 2 for about four hours, at an average of 187 FPS. If you take the 1% low of each minute and average them, you get 116, which looks fine. Counting every frame of those four hours together, the real 1% low was 69, and RigSight found 3,281 stutters. Two numbers from the same hours of play told different stories. Here is the 1% low FPS meaning in plain words, why the way it's measured matters, and what to do when yours is bad. 1% low FPS meaning, and why it tells you more than the average A game doesn't make frames at an even pace. Some frames take 7 ms, some take 9 ms, and now and then one takes 30 ms. Average FPS hides that. It adds all the frames up and divides by the time. The 1% low looks only at the slowest frames. Take every frame from a stretch of play, sort them from fastest to slowest, and look at the slowest 1%. Turn that frame time into a frame rate, and you have the 1% low. A frame rate is 1,000 divided by the frame time in milliseconds, so these frame times give these frame rates. 16.7 ms per frame is 60 FPS. 25 ms per frame is 40 FPS. 50 ms per frame is 20 FPS. So a 1% low of 40 means that one frame in every hundred took 25 ms or longer. In a game running at an average of 100 FPS, that is about one slow frame every second. Your eyes notice changes in pace more than the pace itself. A steady 60 FPS feels smooth. A game that runs at 140 FPS but drops a few frames to 30 every second feels worse, even though its average is more than double. Each slow frame is a tiny freeze, and you feel it as a hitch when you turn the camera. That is why reviewers show the 1% low next to the average. Tools work it out in slightly different ways. Some take the frame time at the 99th percentile, the point that 99% of frames are faster than. Others average all the frames in the slowest 1%. The second way gives a lower number. An average of several short windows' lows, the way RigSight used to do it, gives a higher one. Compare 1% lows only between runs measured with the same tool. The 0.1% low is the same idea for the slowest one frame in a thousand, and it catches rare big hitches. What is a good 1% low? There isn't an official number. What matters is the gap to your average. This is RigSight's own rule of thumb, not an industry standard. A 1% low at 70% of the average or higher plays smoothly. 100 average with 75 lows is fine. Between 50 and 70% of the average, you may feel the odd stutter. Below half of the average, the game stutters. 100 average with 40 lows feels rough. Two more checks help. If you have a G-Sync or FreeSync monitor, try to keep the 1% low above the bottom of its variable refresh range, which is in the monitor's specs. And for fast shooters, a higher 1% low is usually worth more than a higher average. How to see your 1% low and fix 1% low FPS drops These are the common ways to see it. MSI Afterburner with RivaTuner Statistics Server. In Afterburner's settings, open Monitoring , tick Framerate 1% Low and turn on Show in On-Screen Display . RivaTuner must be running to draw the overlay. MSI notes the 1% low may only update while benchmark recording runs, so set a benchmark hotkey on the Benchmark tab and press it in game. CapFrameX, a free tool that records a run and shows the averages, the lows and a frame time graph. Many games' own benchmark modes, which print average and lows at the end. Measure the same stretch of play each time, and play it for a minute or more. A 1% low from ten seconds of play swings a lot from run to run. When the 1% low is far below the average, look for something that interrupts the game now and then. Try these in order. Close background work. Launchers downloading updates, browsers playing video and cloud sync all grab CPU and disk time at random moments. Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc and sort Processes by CPU and Disk . Check graphics memory. If video memory sits at your card's full size, the game swaps data in and out, and you get spikes. Lower Texture quality first. Check for a CPU limit. Poor lows with low GPU load in busy scenes usually mean the CPU is the limit. GPU not at 100% usage but low FPS shows the test. Set a frame cap. A cap a little below what your PC holds in busy scenes trades a few frames of average for a much steadier pace. With G-Sync or FreeSync, cap a few frames below the refresh rate. VSync vs an FPS cap explains why. Give it a second session after updates. After a new graphics driver or game patch, many games rebuild their shaders while you play, and the first session hitches. If it stays bad, see FPS drops in games . Rule out heat. A GPU or CPU at its limit slows down in bursts. Normal GPU temperature while gaming has the numbers. Set Windows to Best performance in Settings > System > Power & battery > Power mode , and play laptops on the charger. For finding what causes the hitches themselves, see games stuttering on PC . Next time a game feels off, look at the 1% low before the average, and check how your tool works it out. If the 1% low is under half the average, work through the fixes above in order. How RigSight caught it Before version 0.35.0, RigSight's 1% low was an average of RivaTuner's own 1% lows, each worked out over the last 1,024 frames. Averaging lows from short windows smooths the worst moments away, the same way my minutes averaged out to 116. On 25 October I asked for something better, a record of every frame instead of an average. Since 0.35.0, RigSight keeps every frame's time from RivaTuner, sorted into narrow bands each minute. That takes about 60 bytes a minute, and it lets RigSight work out the true 1% and 0.1% lows for any stretch of play, from a single minute to a whole month. It also counts stutters. A stutter is one frame that took at least 2.5 times as long as the frames just before it, and at least 20 ms. A game running at 144 FPS that jumps from 7 ms frames to 20 ms is a hitch you feel, while 8 to 12 ms isn't. Nothing is counted while a game runs under 20 FPS overall, so loading screens don't count. When five or more stutters bunch up within 15 minutes, RigSight names what else was busy at that time, like another app reading the disk hard. On the Games page, each game says how smooth it plays, as Smooth, Mostly smooth or It stutters, from how many stutters an hour it had, with the 0.1% low beside it. My Risk of Rain 2 day had about 780 stutters an hour, so it stutters. The Can it run better? card compares the 1% low with the average. At 70% of the average or above, it says the game plays smoothly. Between 50 and 70% it says you may feel the odd stutter, and below 50% it says it stutters. My 69 against 187 is 37%. The How it runs chart draws each play's average as a line with a dot for each play, and the 1% low dashed under it. Graphics driver installs and game updates are marked between plays, so a gap that grew after one of them stands out. Every play below lists its stutters. While you play, the overlay and widgets can show the 1% low live next to the frame rate. Frame times come from RivaTuner Statistics Server, which has to be running before the game starts, and the Games page has a button to install or start it. RigSight is free and open source. What is 1% low FPS? It is the frame rate your game stays above for 99% of its frames. Take every frame time you measured, find the slowest 1%, and turn that time into a frame rate. A 1% low of 40 means one frame in a hundred took 25 ms or longer. What is a good 1% low FPS? There is no official number. RigSight's own rule of thumb compares it with your average. A 1% low at 70% of the average or more usually feels smooth, and below half of it you will feel stutter. It also helps if the 1% low stays above your monitor's lower G-Sync or FreeSync limit. Why are my 1% low FPS drops so big? Big gaps usually come from the CPU being the limit in busy scenes, graphics memory running out, shaders compiling during play, or background apps grabbing CPU or disk time. A first session after a driver or game update often has worse lows than later ones. Does low FPS cause lag? Low FPS makes the picture update less often, so the game feels slower to respond, but it isn't network lag. Ping and packet loss cause network lag. A low 1% low feels like a short freeze or hitch, which people often call lag too. How do I see 1% low FPS in MSI Afterburner? In Afterburner's settings, open the Monitoring tab, tick the Framerate 1% Low entry and turn on Show in On-Screen Display for it. RivaTuner Statistics Server must be running, since it draws the overlay. MSI notes the 1% low may only update while benchmark recording runs, so set a benchmark hotkey on the Benchmark tab and press it in game.

t: Games stuttering on PC? Find out if it's the game or the PC
d: My worst stutter burst was 369 hitches in 15 minutes of Risk of Rain 2, and nothing else on the PC was busy. How RigSight counts every stutter and names what else was running, why games stutter on PC, and how to fix it.
l: PC problems FPS and games games stuttering on pc game stuttering but high fps games stuttering on pc all of a sudden why do my games stutter on pc micro stutters in games stuttering in games fix games stuttering on pc windows 11
b: On 28 October, in one stretch of Risk of Rain 2 starting at 10:35 PM, RigSight counted 369 stutters in 15 minutes. That's more than one hitch every three seconds. My first guess was something in the background. But in those 15 minutes nothing else on the PC was busy. Steam used about 3 MB a second of disk, and no other app used more than about 1% of the CPU. The stutter was coming from the game itself. When games keep stuttering on PC, that's the question to answer first, because the fixes for each side have nothing in common. Why games stutter on PC A stutter is one frame, or a few, that take far longer than the ones around them. The average frame rate barely moves, which is why a game can show 180 FPS and still feel rough. The 1% low FPS post explains the numbers. The causes split into two sides. The game itself can be busy. Many games build shaders the first time they need them, especially after a graphics driver or game update. Open-world games load new areas as you move, and busy scenes can make the CPU the limit for a moment. Something else on the PC can grab a resource at the wrong moment. A launcher updating, an antivirus scan, cloud sync or a browser tab can take the disk or CPU. A game that fills the GPU's memory has to swap data in and out. Overlays and capture tools hook into the game and add their own work every frame. Heat makes a CPU or GPU slow down in bursts once it reaches its limit. How to fix games stuttering on PC First find the side. In RigSight, open the game on the Games page, open the play frame by frame, and read the line about when its stutters bunched up. Without RigSight, run the game with Task Manager open on a second screen, or play a while, then check Processes sorted by Disk and CPU while it stutters. Then work through these in order. Give it a second session after any driver or game update. If the stutter is shaders being built, the second session is smoother. Close background work. Pause launcher downloads, cloud sync and browser video while you play. Lower Texture quality one step if the GPU's memory is nearly full. Turn overlays off one at a time, including Discord's, Steam's and the NVIDIA or AMD overlay, and see whether the stutters drop. Set a frame cap a little below what your PC holds in busy scenes. A steadier pace hides small hitches, and with G-Sync or FreeSync cap a few frames below the refresh rate. Use your launcher's verify or repair option for the game's files. Check temperatures while you play. Normal GPU temperature while gaming has the limits. Set Windows to Best performance in Settings > System > Power & battery > Power mode , and play laptops on the charger. If nothing else on the PC was busy and the stutter survives all of that, it's likely the game's own. Look for a patch, or check the game's forums for others with the same hardware. How RigSight caught it Since version 0.35.0, RigSight reads every frame's time from RivaTuner Statistics Server while you play. It counts a stutter when one frame takes at least 2.5 times as long as the frames just before it, and at least 20 ms. A game at 144 FPS jumping from 7 ms frames to 20 ms is a hitch you feel, while 8 to 12 ms isn't. Nothing counts while a game runs under 20 FPS overall, so loading screens stay out. When you open a play frame by frame and five or more stutters bunched up within 15 minutes, RigSight looks at what else was going on in those minutes, against the rest of the play. It names another app reading or writing the disk heavily, the GPU's memory nearly full, another app busy on the CPU, or Windows nearly out of memory. If none of those stood out, it says so. That last answer is useful too, because it tells you to look at the game. On the Games page, each game says how smooth it plays, as Smooth, Mostly smooth or It stutters, from how many stutters an hour it had, with the 0.1% low beside it. Every play lists its stutters. My Phantom Blade Zero days have run at between about 160 and 270 stutters an hour, so that game reads as It stutters too. RivaTuner has to be running before the game starts, and the Games page has a button to install or start it. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to catch the next bad session and see what was running when the stutters bunched up. If it's another app, close it. If it's nothing, the game is the place to look. Why do my games stutter even with high FPS? Average FPS hides slow frames. A game can average 180 FPS and still have one frame in a hundred take 15 ms or more, which you feel as a hitch. Look at the 1% low and the frame times, not the average. Why are my games stuttering on PC all of a sudden? Look at what changed. A new graphics driver or game patch makes many games rebuild their shaders during the first session. A new background app, a Windows update installing, or a launcher downloading can also start it. If it stays after a second session, work through the fixes in order. What are micro stutters in games? Micro stutters are single frames that take several times longer than the ones around them, often only tens of milliseconds. They're too short to show in an FPS counter, but you feel them as small hitches when you move the camera.

t: How to check VRAM usage in games, and what too high looks like
d: On my 12 GB card, one game used up to 7.2 GB of graphics memory and another about 2. How to check VRAM usage in games on Windows 11, how much games really use, when it's too high, and what RigSight shows.
l: PC problems FPS and games how to check vram usage how to check vram usage in game how to check vram usage while gaming how to check vram usage windows 11 vram usage in games vram usage too high how much vram do games use
b: My GPU has 12 GB of memory. Playing Phantom Blade Zero, the game itself used up to 7.2 GB of it, usually about 6. Playing Risk of Rain 2 on the same PC, it used about 2 GB. Same card, about three times the difference. That's why a list of how much VRAM games use only goes so far. Here's how to check VRAM usage for your own games on Windows 11, and how to tell when it's really too high. VRAM usage in games, and when it's too high VRAM is the GPU's own memory. Games keep textures, models and the frames being drawn there, because the card can reach it much faster than the PC's main memory. Higher texture settings, higher resolutions and ray tracing all take more of it. The PC's own memory works differently, and normal RAM usage while gaming covers it. When it runs out, the card can have to fetch data from the PC's main memory instead, which is far slower. That shows as stutters when you turn into a new area, textures that appear blurry and sharpen late, and in bad cases crashes. Nearly full without any of that is fine. A game that keeps 10 GB of a 12 GB card filled may just be using the room it has. How to check VRAM usage on Windows 11 Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager. Open Performance and click your GPU, usually GPU 0 . Dedicated GPU memory is the card's own memory in use, out of its total. To see one game's use, open Details , right-click a column heading, choose Select columns and tick Dedicated GPU memory . Sort by it while the game runs. Shared GPU memory is main memory the card can borrow. On a gaming card with its own memory, a lot of it in use can be a sign the card ran short. To check VRAM usage while gaming, you need it on screen or recorded, because tabbing out changes what the game is doing. An overlay that shows GPU memory, or a tool that records it, works better than Task Manager for that. How to fix VRAM usage that's too high Lower Texture quality one step first. It usually saves the most memory for the least visible change. Turn down ray tracing, or turn it off. It needs extra memory on top of everything else. Lower the resolution, or use your card's upscaling, such as DLSS, FSR or XeSS, which draws at a lower resolution and scales it up. Close other apps that use the GPU, like browsers with video or capture tools, before you play. Update the game and the graphics driver, since games sometimes fix memory use in patches. How RigSight caught it RigSight records the GPU's memory every minute, both the whole card and the game in front. On the Games page, each game shows its graphics memory as "up to" its highest of the card's total, for the game's own use when Windows reports it, or for the whole card and all apps when it doesn't. That's where my two numbers came from. RigSight doesn't treat nearly full as a problem by itself, because many games fill the card on purpose. It only speaks up when memory ties in with something that went wrong. When a game crashes with the card's memory nearly full, at least 90%, and at least 1 GB and 15% above what that game usually uses on your PC, the opened crash says so. It's careful about it, because running out of memory can crash a game, but a game that simply loaded more looks the same. And when stutters bunch up while the card's memory is 95% full or more, the play's frame-by-frame view names that as what was going on. You can also put GPU memory used in the overlay, a widget or the taskbar. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to check your heaviest game's VRAM usage against your card's total. If it sits near the top and the game stutters, lower textures first. If it sits near the top and plays fine, leave it alone. For stutters with plenty of memory free, see games stuttering on PC . How much VRAM do games use? It depends on the game, the resolution and the texture setting. On my 12 GB card, Risk of Rain 2 used about 2 GB and Phantom Blade Zero up to 7.2 GB. Check your own games, since a number for someone else's settings tells you little. Is VRAM usage too high when it's nearly full? Not by itself. Many games load as much as the card has room for and keep it, because it makes them faster. It's too high when nearly full comes with stutters, textures that load late, or crashes. How do I check VRAM usage while gaming? Keep Task Manager open on a second screen, or use an overlay that shows GPU memory, like RigSight's or MSI Afterburner's with RivaTuner. A tool that records it lets you look back after the game instead.

t: Internet keeps disconnecting on PC? Find which side drops
d: My PC lost the internet six times since October, once for 44 minutes, and every time the PC's own connection was fine. How RigSight tells you when the internet drops and which side it was, why it happens, and how to fix it on Windows 11.
l: PC problems Internet and screen time internet keeps disconnecting on pc pc internet keeps disconnecting windows 11 internet keeps disconnecting and reconnecting internet keeps disconnecting every few minutes why does my internet keep dropping internet drops while gaming wifi keeps disconnecting windows 11
b: Since October my PC has lost the internet six times. The longest was 44 minutes on the morning of 2 October, and two came within ten minutes of each other on 4 November. In every one, the PC's own connection to the network was fine. The internet went somewhere past it. When your internet keeps disconnecting on PC, that's the first thing to find out, because the fix for each side is different. Why the internet keeps disconnecting These are the usual reasons, split by side. On the PC's side, the Wi-Fi signal can be weak, especially through walls or from another floor. Windows can put the network card to sleep to save power, and some cards don't wake up cleanly. An old or broken network card driver can drop the link, often after a Windows update. A loose or damaged Ethernet cable drops the link when it's moved. Past the PC, the router can overheat, restart on its own or need a firmware update. The provider's line can drop too, and then every device in the house loses the internet together. How to fix internet that keeps disconnecting on PC Start by finding the side. When it drops, look at the network icon in the taskbar. A disconnected Wi-Fi or Ethernet icon means the PC's own link went. A connected icon with no internet means it went past the PC. If you want a record, open Command Prompt , run ipconfig to find your Default Gateway , then run ping with that address and -t , and leave it running. If the router keeps answering while the internet is gone, it's the provider's side. If the PC's own link drops, try these in order. Run the network troubleshooter in the Get Help app, which checks the common problems for you. Forget and re-join the Wi-Fi network. Go to Settings > Network & internet > Wi-Fi > Manage known networks , select your network, choose Forget , then connect again with the password. Turn off the card's power saving. In Device Manager , expand Network adapters , open your card's Properties , and on the Power Management tab clear Allow the computer to turn off this device to save power . Some cards don't have that tab. Update the network card's driver from your PC or motherboard maker's support page. Try a cable, or move closer to the router, to rule out a weak signal. Reset Windows' network settings. In Command Prompt as administrator, run netsh winsock reset , netsh int ip reset , ipconfig /release , ipconfig /renew and ipconfig /flushdns , then restart. As a last step, use Network reset under Settings > Network & internet > Advanced network settings . It removes and reinstalls your network adapters, so you'll need to set up any VPN or custom adapter settings again. If the PC stays connected but the internet goes, look past it. Check whether other devices drop at the same moment. If they do, it isn't your PC. Restart the router and the modem, and check that the router has room to breathe and isn't hot. Look for a firmware update in the router's own settings page. Write down when each drop happened and how long it lasted, and call your provider. A list of dates and times gets taken more seriously than "it keeps dropping". How RigSight caught it RigSight watches the connection the same way the taskbar's network icon does, and checks it against what actually moved. A "drop" while apps were still downloading is Windows' check being wrong, so it doesn't count. Drops under 10 seconds don't count either, since Windows' own check flickers now and then. Neither does the first minute and a half after the PC starts or wakes, while the network is still coming up. Each drop gets one of two kinds. Either the cable or Wi-Fi itself went, or the PC stayed connected and the internet went past it, at the router or the provider. All six of mine were the second kind. That rules out my network card, its driver and my cable in one go. Since version 1.4.0 RigSight also tells you as it happens. Once a drop has lasted 15 seconds you get "Your internet is down", and when it comes back, how long it was gone. If the third drop comes within 10 minutes, you get one "Your internet keeps dropping" instead of a pile of notices. RigSight also pings your router every 5 seconds. During a drop where the router still answers, the notice says "Your router is reachable, but there's no internet connection". That points straight at the provider or the line into your home. You can turn the alerts off with Internet drop alerts in Settings. On the Network page, a strip under the graph shows when the internet was up and when it dropped, with Windows' own icon for each kind. Every drop is also listed under What happened, so you have the dates and how long each lasted when you call your provider. My pings to the provider also showed short spikes while big downloads ran, which is a different problem covered in ping spikes while gaming . RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to catch the next drop and see which side it is. Once you know that, you only have half the list to work through. Why does my internet keep disconnecting and reconnecting? Either the PC's own link to the network keeps dropping, which points at Wi-Fi signal, the network card, its driver or its power saving, or the link stays up and the internet beyond the router goes. Watch whether Windows shows the Wi-Fi or Ethernet as disconnected, or connected with no internet. Why does my internet keep disconnecting every few minutes? Regular drops every few minutes often come from the network card being put to sleep to save power, a weak Wi-Fi signal, or a router that keeps restarting. Turn off the card's power saving in Device Manager, try a cable, and check whether other devices drop at the same moment. How do I fix internet that keeps disconnecting on Windows 11? Start with Windows' own network troubleshooter in the Get Help app. Then forget and re-join the Wi-Fi network, update the network card's driver, turn off its power saving, and as a last step use Network reset under Advanced network settings, which reinstalls your network adapters. Why does my internet only drop while gaming? Often it doesn't drop more while gaming, you just notice it more then. If it really does, a big download or upload at the same time can make the connection look dead, and a network card with power saving or an old driver can also give up under load.

t: PC restarts randomly while gaming? Rule things out first
d: My PC went off eleven times in two weeks with no blue screen, and the minutes before each one ruled out heat and the power supply. How to check why a PC randomly restarts while gaming, and how to tell heat, the power supply, tuning and Windows apart.
l: PC problems Crashes pc restarts randomly while gaming check why pc randomly restarts pc restarts randomly no blue screen pc randomly shuts off while gaming not overheating pc restarts randomly after windows update pc restarts randomly when idle pc shuts down randomly while gaming
b: Between 17 and 29 September my PC went off eleven times without shutting down properly, five of them on 29 September alone. There was no blue screen and nobody touched the power button. When your PC restarts randomly while gaming, the first job is the one I had. Before you replace anything, use what happened in the minutes before to rule causes out. Why a PC restarts randomly while gaming These are the usual causes, and how to tell them apart. Heat. CPUs and GPUs protect themselves by slowing down, and if that isn't enough the PC switches off. A part close to its maker's limit in the minute before is your answer. Recent desktop CPUs list limits around 89 to 100°C. Intel gives 100°C for the Core i9-14900K, and AMD 95°C for most Ryzen 7000 chips and 89°C for the X3D ones. Check the page for your model. Dust in the filters, a dead fan or a pump that stopped are the common reasons. The power supply. If temperatures were fine, this is the top suspect for a PC that randomly shuts off while gaming. Games push the GPU and CPU to full power at once, and modern cards can draw short spikes above their rated power. A supply that is too small or worn out trips its protection and the PC goes off, exactly like a power cut. The signs are that it only happens under heavy load, often in the same demanding games or scenes, never at the desktop. Tuning. An overclock, an undervolt, Curve Optimizer or an XMP or EXPO memory profile can be stable for months and then not, after a BIOS update or on a warm day. Unstable tuning can reset the PC with no blue screen at all. This is the cheapest thing to rule out. Windows itself. Restarts after an update come from Windows Update, and you'll see an event 1074. Restarts at shutdown, sleep or wake point to Fast Startup, sleep settings, the BIOS or chipset drivers rather than to your game. The mains. A power cut or dip switches everything off at once. If the lights flickered or other devices lost power too, it wasn't the PC. How to check why your PC randomly restarted, and fix it First make sure it really was a crash.
