Windows restarts on purpose for updates, and a PC that "turned off" might have gone to sleep. Right-click Start and open Event Viewer . Go to Windows Logs > System and click Filter Current Log . Type 41,1001,6008,1074 in the event IDs box and click OK . Look at the entries around the time it restarted. Event 1074 from User32 is a planned restart. It names the program that asked for it, often Windows Update. It is not a crash. Event 1001 from BugCheck is a blue screen, with its stop code. Read blue screen of death causes next. Event 41 from Kernel-Power means Windows started again after not shutting down cleanly. Open its Details tab. A BugcheckCode of 0 with no 1001 means the PC lost power or was reset. Kernel-Power 41 explains every field. Event 6008 from EventLog gives the time Windows last noted it was running before the sudden shut-off. Treat it as roughly right, since it can be some minutes early. Reliability Monitor shows the same thing on a calendar. Type reliability into Start and open View reliability history . Then turn off automatic restart, so a hidden blue screen stays on screen. On current Windows 11 the crash screen is black and stays up for only about two seconds, so in a fullscreen game you may only see black and then the boot logo. Open Settings > System > About and click Advanced system settings . Under Startup and Recovery , click Settings . Clear Automatically restart under System failure and click OK . If the next one still goes straight to black with no blue screen, Windows never got the chance, and you're looking at power, heat or a hard reset. Then work through the fixes in this order. Reset all tuning. Load the BIOS defaults, turn off XMP or EXPO for a test, and reset any GPU tool such as MSI Afterburner to default. Play the game that restarts most. Watch temperatures in that same game. If they're high, clean the dust filters and check that every fan and the pump are running. Plug the PC straight into a wall socket. Reseat both ends of the power supply's cables, and the GPU's power plugs. If the card takes several 8-pin plugs, check the manuals for the card and the power supply. Some ask for a separate cable for each plug. Compare your power supply's wattage with what your GPU maker recommends for the card. If it's close, or the supply is old, test with another one. Set Active hours in Settings > Windows Update > Advanced options so update restarts don't land on your evenings. If the restarts are at idle or overnight, turn off Fast Startup in Control Panel > Hardware and Sound > Power Options > Choose what the power buttons do > Change settings that are currently unavailable and see whether they stop. Check for hardware errors. Filter the System log by the event source WHEA-Logger . Errors the hardware couldn't correct point at the CPU, memory or motherboard, or at tuning that's too tight. Turn off automatic restart now, then reset your tuning to defaults and play the game that restarts most. If it still goes off with no blue screen and your temperatures were normal just before, the power supply is the part to test next. How RigSight caught it RigSight's Crashes page lists every sudden shut-off and blue screen, read from Windows' own records, and on its first run it reads them from up to 90 days back. Each shut-off is timed by the last minute RigSight recorded, not by Windows' own guess, which can be some minutes early. For six of my eleven, RigSight had already been recording the minutes before. In every one the GPU was between 1 and 18% busy, drawing 33 to 55 W. The CPU was under 65° and the GPU around 50°. So whatever switched my PC off, it wasn't heat, and it wasn't a power supply struggling under a game. Windows' record of all eleven shows no blue screen code and no power button press. That's as far as the records go, and RigSight doesn't claim more than that. Each shut-off gets a cause with one word for how sure RigSight is. A shut-off under heavy load reads Possibly mains or power supply, because from inside the PC those two look the same. One while a part was above your alert temperature reads Possibly heat. An error the hardware couldn't correct, logged around it, makes it Likely a hardware fault. A held power button reads Confirmed. Only a shut-off while the PC was doing little, with no button press and nothing logged, is called Likely a power cut. Those are counted apart, so they don't hide the PC's own problems. A PC running again within two minutes reads as a power dip or a reset. Open a shut-off to see the 45 minutes before it, minute by minute. It shows CPU and GPU temperatures, load, how many watts the GPU was drawing, memory and fans, with the game in front. A shut-off at 300 W and normal temperatures points at power, and one at 90° points at heat. The Temperatures graph leaves a gap where nothing was recorded and says whether the PC was off, shut off suddenly, crashed or was asleep. On the Games page, the play itself says it ended in a shut-off or a power cut. CPU temperature and power need RigSight running with admin rights. RigSight is free and open source. Why does my PC restart randomly with no blue screen? Either Windows had no time to show one, because power was lost, or it showed one and restarted straight away. Turn off Automatically restart under Startup and Recovery to catch the second kind. If Kernel-Power 41 has a BugcheckCode of 0, it was a real loss of power or a reset, not a blue screen. My PC randomly shuts off while gaming but it's not overheating. Why? Then the power supply and tuning are the main suspects. A supply that can't handle the GPU's short power spikes switches off to protect itself, and an unstable overclock, undervolt or XMP or EXPO profile can reset the PC with no blue screen. Reset tuning to defaults first, since it costs nothing. Why does my PC restart randomly after a Windows update? Look for event 1074 from User32 in the System log at that time. If it's there, Windows restarted on purpose to finish an update. Set your Active hours in Windows Update so it doesn't happen while you play. If it's a Kernel-Power 41 instead, a new driver from the update is worth suspecting. Why does my PC restart randomly when idle? Restarts at idle point away from heat and the power supply's limit and toward the mains, sleep and wake problems, or memory and CPU tuning that is unstable at low load. Check whether other devices flickered, turn off Fast Startup for a test, and try with XMP or EXPO off.

t: Ping spikes while gaming, and the download behind mine
d: My ping to my internet provider jumped to 155 ms in the minute Steam pulled 175 MB, while my own router stayed under a millisecond. How RigSight shows where ping spikes while gaming start, why they happen, and how to fix them.
l: PC problems Internet and screen time ping spikes while gaming lag spikes while gaming lag spikes while gaming pc random ping spikes while gaming high ping in games but good internet ping spikes on wifi ping spikes on ethernet packet loss meaning internet drops while gaming
b: On 5 November at 10:32 PM, RigSight's ping check to my internet provider's first router came back in 155 ms. A minute before it was 1 ms, and a minute after it was 1 ms again. My own router answered in under a millisecond the whole time. In that minute Steam pulled 175 MB, more than thirty times what it pulled the minute before. I wasn't in a game, but it's a common story behind ping spikes while gaming. Something else fills the connection, and the game's packets wait in line behind it. Why ping spikes happen Ping is how long one small packet takes to reach a place and come back. A game sends small updates many times a second, so when one waits, you see players jump or your shots land late. A speed test doesn't show this. It measures how much your connection can move, not how quickly one packet comes back. These are the usual reasons for spikes. Something else fills the connection. A launcher updating a game, Windows Update, a cloud backup uploading photos, or someone streaming in another room can fill the line. Routers and modems can hold the extra traffic in a queue, and the game's packets wait in that queue too. Network researchers call this bufferbloat, and a ping during a big download is the classic way to see it. Wi-Fi is struggling. It shares the air with other networks and devices, and walls and distance make it resend packets. That shows as spikes on the home side, in pings to your own router. The route to the game server is busy or long. Busy hours on the networks in between can add delay, and a server in another region adds distance you can't remove. The provider's line has trouble. Spikes on the provider's side with nothing downloading, at any hour, point there. How to find and fix ping spikes while gaming Find which side the spike is on. Open Command Prompt , type ipconfig and note the Default Gateway , which is your router. Run ping 192.168.1.1 -t with your router's address in one window, and ping 1.1.1.1 -t in a second window. The -t keeps it going until you press Ctrl + C. Play for a while and watch both. If both jump together, it's your Wi-Fi or cable. If only the second one jumps, it's the line or something filling it. Stop background downloads while you play. In Steam, the setting for downloads during gameplay is under Settings > Downloads , and each game's Properties > Updates can override it. Check your other launchers for the same kind of setting. Cap Windows' own update downloads. Go to Settings > Windows Update > Advanced options > Delivery Optimization > Advanced options and set a limit for background downloads. Microsoft notes the limit only covers automatic update downloads, not ones you start yourself. Pause cloud backups and sync, like OneDrive or Google Drive, during a match. Uploads fill the line just as downloads do, and on many connections upload is much smaller. Try a cable. If pings to your router jump around, plug the PC into the router with Ethernet and test again. If you have to stay on Wi-Fi, move closer to the router or use its 5 GHz network. Look for a queue setting on your router. Some routers have a setting for this, often called QoS or Smart Queue Management. It keeps the queue short while something downloads, so game packets don't wait as long. Your router's manual says whether it has one. Restart the router, and update your network card's driver from the PC or motherboard maker. If the spikes happen in only one game, check which server region it puts you on. A closer region usually means lower ping. If the provider's side spikes with nothing else using the internet, write down the times and call your provider. A record of when it happened helps more than "my internet is bad". How RigSight caught it Since version 1.4.0, RigSight checks the line every 5 seconds in two places. One ping goes to your router, which is the home side of the line, your cable or Wi-Fi. The other goes to your internet provider's first router after it, which is the provider's side. RigSight finds that router the way a traceroute does, without asking any outside server. The pings leave from the network card itself, so a VPN in between doesn't hide the real line. A ping that isn't back within a second counts as lost. Since version 1.14.0, while a game or a call is online, RigSight also checks the server it's talking to, so a slow route past your provider shows too. Two pings at once tell you where a spike starts. If the router is slow, the problem is inside your home. If the router is quick and the provider's side is slow, the problem is on the line, at the provider, or in whatever is filling the line. On my PC the router never went past 3 ms in the 484 minutes of checks so far, and 4 of 5,767 pings to the provider got no reply. The Network page shows it in a few places. Right now has your speeds, whether the connection is working well, its ping and packet loss, and every app using it. The graph of each hour has a Ping view, and any hour that went past 80 ms is marked, because that's where online games start to feel it. On a line that's never that fast, the mark starts at twice its usual. A sentence above the graph gives the usual ping and how many hours went past the mark. When the same app was uploading a lot in most of them, it names that app. Mine was a download, so the sentence doesn't name it, but the hour does. Click the marked hour and Steam is at the top of its apps, with 334 MB downloaded. The second spike in my history was the same kind. At 7:16 AM on 6 November the provider's side hit 105 ms. In that hour Epic's installer pulled 292 MB and Ubisoft Connect 216 MB, and those two were the top of the list. Drag across the graph to zoom into a busy evening. If the internet drops altogether, RigSight tells you when it went and when it's back, and a strip under the graph shows each drop. Internet keeps disconnecting on PC covers that side. You can pause the ping checks under the graph or in Settings. Seeing each app's internet use needs RigSight running with admin rights. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is the two ping windows from the first step, left running during your next match. One look at which one jumps tells you whether to fix your Wi-Fi or your downloads. Why do I get ping spikes while gaming? Often something else on your connection is downloading or uploading at the same moment, like a launcher update, Windows Update or a cloud backup, and the game's packets wait behind it. Wi-Fi trouble and a busy route to the game server are the other usual reasons. Pinging your router and the internet at once tells you which side it's on. Why is my ping high in games but my internet is good? A speed test measures how much data your connection can move each second. Ping is how long one small packet takes to get there and back. A fast connection can still have high ping when the game server is far away, the route to it is busy, or something else is filling the line while you play. Are ping spikes worse on Wi-Fi than on Ethernet? They can be. Wi-Fi shares the air with other networks and devices, and walls and distance make it resend packets. If pings to your own router jump around, try a cable. If the spikes happen on a cable too, look past your home network. What does packet loss mean? Packet loss means some packets never arrive. In a game it shows as rubber-banding or actions that don't register. A lost ping now and then is normal. RigSight only mentions it once 1% or more of its pings get no reply.

t: Rewriting all 5,445 sentences RigSight shows
d: On 5 November I wrote down how RigSight should talk, then checked every one of the 5,445 texts the app shows against it. The rule that mattered most was to say what happened and never guess at why.
l: Building RigSight
b: RigSight had grown fast. In six weeks it picked up crash findings, a Games page, an AI helper, a rebuilt Network page and dozens of notifications. Each was written on its own day. Read together, the app didn't always sound like one person, and a few lines guessed at things the records couldn't show. On 5 November I wrote down how RigSight should talk. It's the voice of someone who knows PCs, explaining something about yours, then stopping. The rules Write in plain, everyday English, the way a person would say it. Keep it short by cutting words, not the useful part. Never repeat the title in the line under it. Lead with what happened, then what it means, then what to do, if there's anything to do. Say what was seen. An observation is not a diagnosis, and two things at the same time are not cause and effect. Stay calm. Save urgent words for when the evidence earns them. No marketing or AI phrases. Every notification has to teach something you can't already see. Say what happened, not why you think it happened The rule I care about most is the fourth one. The example I wrote down uses RigSight's own notification for when the internet drops. With a guess added Your internet is down. Your router is reachable, but there's no internet connection. This is usually your internet provider. Saying what was seen Your internet is down. Your router is reachable, but there's no internet connection. The last sentence on the left sounds helpful. But RigSight doesn't know it's the provider. It knows the router answered and the internet didn't. You can work out the rest yourself, and if the guess would have been wrong, the app hasn't told you something false. Every text, one by one Then I checked everything the app shows against the rules. Every page title, button, tooltip, notification, error and line of What's new came to 5,445 texts. Most were fine. The rest came out as 55 sets of changes, and all of them went out in version 1.5.0. 55 Sets of changes from checking 5,445 texts, all in 1.5.0. Most were small, and a few removed a guess about a cause the records can't show. Precision matters as much as tone. An SSD reporting 4% available spare is not a drive almost out of space, so RigSight says what the drive reports. Notifications now give durations in words, like "for about 3 minutes", instead of figures to decode. The update screen gives one time for the restart, about 15 seconds, because that's what the real updates took. The app also moved to US spelling, so it says color and license everywhere. The Spanish translation was redone for every changed line too, and the app's tests now fail if a retired phrase comes back. Writing rules down sounds like busywork. In practice it changed how I build. Every new feature's mock-up now shows its real final words, already checked against the rules, so the words get reviewed with the design instead of after it. The blog follows the same idea. The posts say what RigSight recorded, and when the records don't say why, the posts don't either.

t: Blue screen of death causes on Windows 11, and the three on my PC
d: My PC had three blue screens in four weeks, each with a different stop code. Two were the graphics driver and one a USB audio driver. The common blue screen of death causes on Windows 11, how to find the stop code and the driver Windows names, and the fixes.
l: PC problems Crashes blue screen of death causes windows 11 blue screen of death causes blue screen of death causes and solutions why do i keep getting blue screen how does the blue screen of death happen blue screen of death common causes
b: Between 11 August and 9 September my PC hit three blue screens, and each one had a different stop code. The usual advice says that different codes every time point at hardware. The real answer was in the drivers Windows named. Two of the three were the graphics driver, and the third was a USB audio driver. The blue screen of death causes on Windows 11 are fewer than they seem, and Windows writes down which one it was if you know where to look. Blue screen of death causes on Windows 11 Microsoft calls a blue screen a stop error or bug check. Drivers and the core of Windows run with full access to the system. When one of them does something that could corrupt memory or your files if it carried on, Windows stops everything on purpose. It saves a dump file and shows a stop code that names the kind of fault. On current Windows 11 that screen can be a plain black one with the same "Your device ran into a problem" message, and it only stays up for about two seconds. Microsoft estimates that about three quarters of stop errors are caused by faulty drivers. In its own breakdown, hardware problems are about one in ten, and a share can't be traced at all because the memory was too damaged to read. That's why the driver Windows names matters more than whether the codes match. How to find the stop code and the driver yourself The stop code is on the blue screen itself, such as Stop code: VIDEO_TDR_FAILURE , and sometimes a line saying What failed: nvlddmkm.sys . That second line is the driver Windows blames. If the PC restarts too fast to read it, turn off the automatic restart. Open Settings > System > About and click Advanced system settings . Under Startup and Recovery , click Settings . Clear Automatically restart under System failure , and check that Write debugging information isn't set to (none) . For crashes that already happened, you don't need any extra tool. Windows keeps the details in a few places. In Reliability Monitor, type reliability into Start and open View reliability history . A blue screen shows as "Shut down unexpectedly" with the problem name BlueScreen. The BCCode line is the stop code in hex. In Event Viewer, open Windows Logs > System and look for event 1001 from the source BugCheck. It reads "The computer has rebooted from a bugcheck" with the code, its four parameters and where the dump was saved. Kernel-Power 41 has the same code in decimal, and the Kernel-Power 41 post shows how to convert it. Right beside it in the same log, some crashes also get event 1019 with "Possibly related driver" and a file name. That's where my nvlddmkm.sys and RtUsbA64.sys came from. In Windows Logs > Application , the Windows Error Reporting event for a BlueScreen has a "Fault bucket" line. Once Windows has looked at the dump, that line can carry the driver's name, as it did for my 11 August crash. To find the driver behind an old crash without WhoCrashed or other third-party tools, use Microsoft's own debugger. Install WinDbg . Microsoft offers it from its WinDbg download page and the Microsoft Store. Open it as administrator, choose File > Start debugging > Open dump file , and pick the newest file in C:\Windows\Minidump . Type !analyze -v and press Enter. Give it a minute to download symbols. Look for MODULE_NAME , IMAGE_NAME and the line "Probably caused by". A file ending in .sys is the driver. If it names ntoskrnl.exe , that's Windows itself, and the real cause is usually a driver or hardware further back. Common stop codes and what they point to 0x124 WHEA_UNCORRECTABLE_ERROR means the hardware reported an error it couldn't recover from. It's usually CPU or memory tuning, so undo overclocks, undervolts, Curve Optimizer and XMP or EXPO, and update the BIOS. 0x101 CLOCK_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT means a CPU core stopped answering. It's usually unstable CPU tuning. 0x1A MEMORY_MANAGEMENT, 0x50 PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA, 0x4E PFN_LIST_CORRUPT point to memory. Test with XMP or EXPO turned off and run Windows Memory Diagnostic. 0x116 VIDEO_TDR_FAILURE and 0x119 VIDEO_SCHEDULER_INTERNAL_ERROR point to the graphics driver. Clean-reinstall it and undo any GPU overclock. 0xD1 DRIVER_IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL and 0xA IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL mean a driver touched memory it shouldn't. Network, audio and graphics drivers are frequent culprits. 0x133 DPC_WATCHDOG_VIOLATION means a driver took too long. Often storage, chipset or network drivers, or SSD firmware. 0x7A KERNEL_DATA_INPAGE_ERROR and 0x154 UNEXPECTED_STORE_EXCEPTION mean Windows couldn't read from the drive. Check the drive's health and its cable. 0x9F DRIVER_POWER_STATE_FAILURE means a driver failed during sleep or wake. Update chipset and graphics drivers. 0x3B SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION, 0x7E SYSTEM_THREAD_EXCEPTION_NOT_HANDLED and 0x139 KERNEL_SECURITY_CHECK_FAILURE mean a driver crashed. Anti-cheat and recently installed software are common causes, and so is a driver for something you plug in, like my USB audio one. 0xEF CRITICAL_PROCESS_DIED means a core Windows process stopped. Run sfc /scannow and check the drive. Microsoft's Bug Check Code Reference lists every code with its parameters, if yours isn't here. Fixes, safest first Undo what changed last. For a new driver, open Device Manager , double-click the device, then Driver > Roll Back Driver . Take out new hardware and test without it. Uninstall new software, especially anything with its own driver. Install updates from Settings > Windows Update , then get the newest drivers for the device the stop code, event 1019 or WinDbg named, from its maker. Put all tuning back to default. Load BIOS defaults, turn off XMP or EXPO for a test, and reset GPU tools. Run Windows Memory Diagnostic from Start. Several memory codes in a row deserve a longer test with MemTest86. Repair Windows files by running sfc /scannow in Terminal (Admin) . If it can't fix everything, run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth followed by sfc /scannow again. Check the drive's health with its maker's tool, and keep 10 to 15% of it free, as Microsoft suggests. Check temperatures under load against your CPU and GPU maker's limit for your model. If Windows won't stay up long enough, start in Safe Mode. Go to Settings > System > Recovery > Advanced startup > Restart now , then Troubleshoot > Advanced options > Startup Settings > Restart and press 4. From there you can roll back drivers or use System Restore . Updating the BIOS can fix 0x124 and 0x101 crashes on some boards, but a failed BIOS update can leave the PC unable to start. Only do it with your motherboard maker's instructions, on a stable PC, and never during a storm or on a laptop without its charger. How RigSight caught it RigSight reads Windows' own crash records, and when it is first installed it reads them from up to 90 days back. So all three blue screens are on my Crashes page, each with its stop code named and explained. On 22 August it was 0x116 VIDEO_TDR_FAILURE. At the next start Windows named nvlddmkm.sys as the driver involved. RigSight says "Windows crashed inside nvlddmkm.sys, the NVIDIA driver" and marks it Confirmed, because Windows' own record says so. It was the worst moment of the graphics driver hangs I wrote about in display driver stopped responding and has recovered . On 9 September it was 0x3B SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION, and Windows named RtUsbA64.sys . RigSight doesn't keep its own name for that file, so it reads the description the file carries and says Windows crashed inside the Realtek USB audio driver. That one is Confirmed too, and it adds "It wasn't the graphics driver", so the NVIDIA driver doesn't get the blame for all three. On 11 August it was 0x119 VIDEO_SCHEDULER_INTERNAL_ERROR, and Windows named no driver at the next start. RigSight says the graphics scheduler hit an error, which is usually the graphics driver, and marks it only Possibly. Under what's still unknown it says which driver or part was at fault, because Windows didn't name one. The error report Windows filed later does name nvlddmkm in its fault bucket line, which I found in Event Viewer. So two of my three codes were the same driver, and the codes themselves are from the same family. 0x116 and 0x119 are both graphics stop codes. There hasn't been a blue screen since 9 September, as of 5 November in Windows' own log. Each opened crash also checks the things you would otherwise check by hand. It looks for a driver or Windows update installed in the 7 days before. It names that update, or rules it out when the same blue screen had already happened before it. It also shows any hardware errors handed over at the next start, says whether the CPU or GPU was over your alert limit, and counts how many times the same blue screen has happened before. A 0x124 or 0x101 with no driver named reads Likely a hardware fault. Open a crash for the 45 minutes before it, minute by minute, and use Copy report to paste the whole thing into a forum post. CPU temperature and power need RigSight running with admin rights. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to find the BCCode of your last blue screen in Reliability Monitor, then look for event 1019 beside it in the System log. If your last few crashes share a code or a named driver, fix that one thing first. If the codes differ and no driver repeats, start with memory and tuning. Why do I keep getting blue screens? Repeated blue screens with the same stop code, or with the same driver named, point to that driver, so update it or roll it back. Different codes with no driver in common point toward hardware, such as unstable memory or CPU tuning, a failing drive or heat. Compare the codes and the named drivers of your last few crashes before changing anything. How does the blue screen of death happen? Windows stops on purpose when something running with full system access, usually a driver, does something that could damage your files or the system if it carried on. It saves a dump file, shows the stop code and restarts. Can overheating cause a blue screen? It can, but more often an overheating PC slows itself down or switches off with no blue screen. A blue screen during heavy load with high temperatures is worth checking with the fans, dust filters and the CPU or GPU maker's temperature limit for your model. Can a blue screen damage my PC? The blue screen itself doesn't damage anything. It's Windows stopping to avoid damage. Unsaved work is lost, and frequent crashes can corrupt files, which is why running sfc /scannow after a run of blue screens is a good idea.

t: Checking ping without asking anyone's server
d: The rebuilt Network page checks your ping every 5 seconds, and it doesn't ask any outside server to do it. How RigSight finds your provider's first router, the router that ignored empty pings, and the colour rule the page follows.
l: Building RigSight
b: Until November, RigSight's Network page only counted data. How much each app downloaded and uploaded, what moved while you were away, when the connection dropped. I had left ping out on purpose. On 4 November I rebuilt the page, and this time ping went in, because ping is what you actually feel in a game. Whose server? Measuring ping means sending something somewhere and timing the answer. Many tools ping a big public server, such as one run by Google or Cloudflare. My first plan did the same. Then I asked why RigSight should talk to anyone's server at all, when the internet you use already starts at your provider's own equipment. So RigSight pings two places, and neither is a public server. The first is your router, the home side of the line. The second is your internet provider's first router after it, where your provider's side starts. Between the two, a spike tells you whether the trouble is in your home or past it. Finding the provider's router takes a small trick. RigSight sends pings that may only travel a few hops before they expire, the way a traceroute does. Each one dies at a router along the way, and that router sends back a note saying so. The first note that comes from outside your home is your provider's router. The pings are aimed at an internet address only to pick the way out, and they never get there. 5 s How often RigSight pings your router and your provider's first router. It looks for the provider's router again every half hour, in case it moved. The router that ignored empty pings The first build didn't work on my own router. The pings to it went unanswered every time, while Windows' own ping command got answers straight away. The difference turned out to be what was inside the ping. RigSight's were empty, filled with zeros, and Windows fills its pings with letters. My router simply ignored the empty ones. Now RigSight fills its pings the way Windows does. There was one more catch on my PC. I use a VPN, Cloudflare WARP, which routes traffic through its own tunnel. Pings sent the normal way would go into the tunnel and measure the VPN instead of my line. RigSight sends its pings from the network card's own address, so a VPN can't hide the real line. Usage is never a warning In the first mock-up of the new page, a line said that OBS sent 4.1 GB in an hour, coloured amber. It was wrong. Using the internet isn't bad, and on RigSight amber already means stutters on the Games page. So the page has a rule. Usage is never shown in warning colours. Ping peaks are marked in the ping line's own blue. Amber is kept for drops and for data that got lost. Two more things changed after trying the mock-ups. The live view went to the top of the page and stayed open, because hiding what's using your internet right now behind a click made it worse. And usage and ping became one graph with a switch, instead of two graphs stacked on top of each other. The rebuilt page went out in version 1.4.0, along with alerts when the internet drops. The ping checks have already caught real spikes on my own line. There's more on reading them in ping spikes while gaming , and on drops in internet keeps disconnecting on PC . Later, the servers games and calls use One evening Discord showed lost packets and high ping while both checks stayed at 1 ms. The call was on a server in Singapore, about 97 ms away, and nothing RigSight checked was that far. So from version 1.14.0, while a game, a call or remote play is online, RigSight also checks the server that app is already talking to, every 5 seconds. It only asks servers your apps already use, it needs admin rights to see which one that is, and Settings has a switch for it. Your router and your provider are still checked the same way.

t: How to check GPU temperature history without being misled
d: RigSight's own chart once showed a GPU topping out at 68° on a day that hit 74°. How to check GPU temperature history on Windows with HWiNFO, GPU-Z or Afterburner logs, or a temperature monitor with history, and how to read it.
l: PC problems Temperatures check gpu temperature history temperature monitor with history pc temperature history cpu temperature history gpu temperature logger windows temperature history check gpu temps how to check temp on gpu when should i worry about gpu temp
b: In the first week of October, RigSight's own temperature chart showed a GPU topping out at 68° on a day whose highest reading was 74°. Both numbers were right, and the chart still told the wrong story. If you want to check GPU temperature history in Windows, that's the trap to know about. First you need a history at all, because Windows doesn't keep one. Then you need to read it in a way that doesn't hide the moment the card got hot. Why Windows keeps no temperature history Windows records crashes, updates and errors in its logs, but not temperatures. Task Manager can show the temperature of a dedicated GPU, and that's the only temperature Windows itself shows. It has no CPU temperature reading at all, and it saves neither. That means you can only look back at times when some app was already recording. If nothing was running last night, last night's temperatures are gone. The useful habit is to set up recording before you need it. How to check GPU temperature history yourself Check GPU temps right now in Task Manager Task Manager gives a quick look at the current reading in Windows 10 version 2004 or later, and in Windows 11. Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager. Open the Performance tab. Click your GPU, usually GPU 0 or GPU 1 . Read GPU Temperature under the graphs. Integrated graphics built into the CPU don't show a temperature here. The graphs on this tab cover only the last minute, and they aren't temperature graphs. Log it with HWiNFO HWiNFO is a free sensor app that reads nearly every chip in a PC, CPU included, and can write the readings to a CSV file you open in a spreadsheet. Download HWiNFO from its official site and run it. Tick Sensors-only and click Start . At the bottom of the sensors window, click the logging button, the icon with a green plus. Pick a folder and a file name for the CSV log. Play as you normally would. Click the same button, now a red cross, to stop. Open the CSV in Excel or Google Sheets and find the column for GPU Temperature , or the CPU column for your chip. Sort it or make a quick line chart. You can lower HWiNFO's polling interval for finer detail, but the default is fine for temperatures. The catch is that it only records while HWiNFO is open and logging. You have to remember to start it, and a log left running for days grows into a very large file. Other GPU temperature loggers GPU-Z has a Log to file box on its Sensors tab. It records the GPU only. MSI Afterburner draws a monitoring graph of the last few minutes, and its Settings > Monitoring tab has a Log history to file box that saves it. With RivaTuner Statistics Server it can also show the temperature on screen while you play. All of them have the same limit as HWiNFO. They only know about the time they were running and logging. For a temperature monitor with history that records whether you remembered or not, you need one that runs in the background, like RigSight. There's more on how these tools compare in free PC monitoring software . Check GPU temps while you play Tabbing out to Task Manager mid game changes what you're measuring, because the card relaxes as soon as the game is in the background. An overlay shows the reading while the game keeps running. The NVIDIA app and AMD Software each have a performance overlay that can include GPU temperature. MSI Afterburner can show it too, drawn in the game by RivaTuner Statistics Server, which installs alongside it. An overlay is good for watching, but it's still only now. Glance at it once the game has run for 10 minutes, then let a log or a background recorder keep the rest. What to look for in a temperature history A pile of numbers is only useful if you know what to ask of it. Look at the highest reading in a session and when it happened, not only the average line. Compare it with your card's maximum. NVIDIA lists 85 to 93°C for its recent GeForce cards depending on the model, for example 90°C for the RTX 4070 family. Check for gaps. A stretch with no readings isn't a cool stretch, so make sure your tool shows where it wasn't recording. Watch where the temperature levels off. A short spike to the high 80s is less worrying than an hour spent there. Compare the same game over weeks. If one game settles 6 or 8 degrees hotter than it did last month, at the same settings, dust or paste may be building up. Note the temperature at rest. A PC idling warmer than it used to, with the room the same, points the same way. For what counts as normal, see normal GPU temperature while gaming and normal CPU temperature while gaming . If the history shows a real problem, PC overheating while gaming has the fixes. Whichever tool you pick, start recording today. The next time a game stutters or the PC shuts off, you'll have the hour before it to look at instead of a blank. How RigSight caught it The line on the chart showed each minute's average. Inside one of those minutes the GPU had touched 74° for a few seconds, and an average of sixty seconds smoothed that away. The day's high said 74°, and the line never got there. That's confusing when you're looking for the moment it got hot. So since version 0.18.0, the Temperatures chart has a switch for each minute's Average , Highest or Lowest . Pointing at a minute shows all three. The average stays the default because it shows the trend, and the highest is one click away when you're hunting a spike. The same week, someone on X pointed out a second problem. A stretch where RigSight recorded nothing looked exactly like a PC that had stayed cool. Now any stretch with nothing recorded is shaded and labelled "Not recorded". Pointing at it gives the times and, when Windows' own log says, the reason, such as the PC being off or asleep. The whole story, with a third way the chart misled people, is in Three ways my temperature chart was lying . Today RigSight records CPU, GPU, GPU hot spot and GPU memory temperatures all day, with no log to start, and the Temperatures page shows them. Its range menu goes from the last 5 minutes to the last 12 months, plus a custom range. Week, Month and Year are the last 7 days, 30 days and 12 months. Drag across any stretch to zoom in. The same page shows the warmest hours of the past week and the CPU's and GPU's resting temperature over the last 30 days. Motherboard and drive temperatures show live on the page but aren't kept. CPU temperature, motherboard and drive readings need RigSight to run with admin rights. RigSight keeps the history as long as you choose, and it's free and open source. Reports covers any day, week, month, year or custom range. For a single day, its minute by minute graph lines temperatures up with the app in front. For any period, Peaks lists the highest CPU, GPU and GPU hot spot readings with the app that was running. If you want the raw numbers, the Export button on the page saves what it shows, and the Export in Settings can save temperatures as CSV files for a spreadsheet. Does Windows keep a history of GPU or CPU temperature? No. Task Manager shows the GPU's temperature at this moment, and Windows has no CPU temperature reading of its own. Neither is saved. To look back, you need an app that was recording at the time. How do I check my CPU temperature history? Use a sensor app that logs to a file, such as HWiNFO, and start the log before you play. Open the file afterwards in a spreadsheet and look at the highest values. Apps that record all day, like RigSight, keep it without you starting anything, though CPU temperature needs admin rights. How do I check my GPU temps while gaming? Task Manager's Performance tab shows the GPU temperature, but you have to tab out of the game. An on-screen overlay from MSI Afterburner with RivaTuner Statistics Server, or your graphics driver's own overlay, shows it during play. A log shows how hot it got afterwards. When should I worry about GPU temp? Worry when the card sits at its maker's listed maximum, which is 85 to 93°C on recent NVIDIA cards depending on the model, when the frame rate drops as it gets there, or when the same game runs clearly hotter than it did a few weeks ago. A history is what shows you that last one.

t: PC overheating while gaming, or just warm? How RigSight tells
d: How RigSight tells a PC overheating while gaming from one that is only warm, by setting each game against its own usual. Why PCs get hot in games, and how to stop it, from dust and airflow to frame caps, fan curves and thermal paste.
l: PC problems Temperatures pc overheating while gaming how to stop computer from overheating when playing games how to prevent pc from overheating while gaming is it normal for pc to get hot when gaming why does my pc get hot when i play games laptop overheating when gaming cpu overheating while gaming
b: Your fans roar, the case is warm to the touch, and the frame rate sags after twenty minutes of play. That feels like a PC overheating while gaming, but a hot PC and an overheating PC are different things. A PC is meant to get warm in games. The question is whether yours runs hotter than it used to in the same game, and RigSight answers that from your PC's own history. Why a PC is overheating while gaming A GPU can draw a few hundred watts in a game, and nearly all of that power turns into heat inside the case. Warm air out of the back and fans that speed up are signs the cooling is working. Each part has a maximum temperature set by its maker, and it changes from model to model. NVIDIA lists 85 to 93°C for its recent GeForce cards. AMD lists 89 to 95°C for recent Ryzen CPUs, and Intel lists 100°C for the Core i9 14900K and 105°C for the Core Ultra 9 285K. The posts on normal GPU temperature while gaming and normal CPU temperature while gaming list the figures by model. Your PC is really overheating when one of these is true. A part sits at its maker's maximum during play and the frame rate drops as it gets there. On the GPU that's GPU thermal throttling . The PC shuts off or restarts in games, and the temperatures just before were at the limit. The same game, at the same settings, runs clearly hotter than it used to. When it is, the cause is usually one of these. Dust packed into a cooler's fins is the most common reason a PC that used to run cool now runs hot. A case that can't move air out, a game drawing far more frames than the screen shows, a fan that has stopped, a quiet fan curve, a badly mounted cooler, motherboard power settings past the maker's guidelines and old thermal paste make up most of the rest. If none of the signs fit, your PC is probably just warm. Loud fans alone aren't a sign of overheating, and PC fans loud while gaming covers that case. If the frame rate drops but temperatures are fine, see FPS drops in games instead. How to stop your computer from overheating when playing games Do these in order, and change one thing at a time, so you know what helped. Clean out the dust. Shut down Windows, switch off the power supply and unplug the PC. Take out and rinse or brush the dust filters, usually at the front, top and bottom of the case. Blow dust out of the CPU cooler, the GPU and any radiator with compressed air, and hold each fan still while you do so it doesn't spin up. Let anything you washed dry fully before it goes back in. Give the case room to breathe. Air should come in at the front or bottom and leave at the back or top. Most fans have small arrows on the frame that show the airflow. Pull the PC out of a desk cubby, keep it a hand's width from the wall, and don't put it on carpet if the power supply draws air from underneath. For a quick test, play with the side panel off for 20 minutes. If temperatures drop a lot, another intake fan or a clearer path will help more than anything you do to the coolers. Cap your frame rate. If a game runs at 250 frames per second on a 144 Hz screen, your GPU is working flat out for frames you never see. A cap a little under your screen's refresh rate often cuts the heat noticeably. Many games have a frame rate limit in their own video settings, so use that first. On NVIDIA, open the NVIDIA Control Panel, go to Manage 3D settings and set Max Frame Rate . On AMD, Radeon Chill in AMD Software lowers the frame rate when there's little movement on screen, and AMD says it saves power and helps lower GPU temperature. Check every fan spins. Look through the side panel while a game is running. Every case fan, the CPU cooler fan and every fan on the GPU should be turning. Many GPUs stop their fans when cool, so check under load. If one stays still, see GPU fan not spinning . Set a better fan curve. A fan curve decides how fast fans spin at each temperature, and some motherboards ship with quiet curves that let the CPU get hot before the fans react. Change the case and CPU fan curves in the BIOS or the motherboard maker's app, and the GPU's curve in the card maker's app. Raise the speed a little at the temperatures you see in games, then test again. Check the cooler and BIOS settings. Intel's own checklist for a CPU that runs hot asks you to confirm the cooler is rated for your CPU, that it's mounted properly with the protective film removed from its base, and on a liquid cooler that the pump and radiator fans are plugged into the right headers. Intel also notes that some motherboards ship with power settings that go past its guidelines, and loading the BIOS defaults can bring the temperature down. Change BIOS settings only if you're comfortable, and note what you change. Replace the thermal paste last. Paste dries out over years. If the PC is old and the steps above didn't help, new paste on the CPU can bring the temperature down. Repasting a GPU is a bigger job and can void the warranty, so check that first. A big gap between the GPU's main reading and its hot spot is the clearest sign a card needs it, as explained in GPU hotspot temperature . Laptops run hotter than desktops by design, and the maker sets their limits. For a laptop overheating when gaming, play on a desk, not a bed or your lap, so the vents underneath stay open. Clean the vents with short bursts of compressed air. Cap the frame rate, and try the maker's balanced mode to see whether the temperature falls more than the frame rate does. A stand that lifts the back edge helps the fans pull in air. Test each fix like for like. Use the same game, the same settings and the same scene or map. Play long enough for temperatures to level off, about 10 to 15 minutes, and note how warm the room is, because a room 5°C warmer makes every part run warmer too. A light game in winter against a heavy one in summer will always look like your PC got worse. Start with the dust and the frame cap tonight. Then play your usual game for 15 minutes and compare the highest temperatures with what you had before. How RigSight caught it The picture at the top is RigSight's demo PC, not mine. Its Reports page for October has a table called Against your usual. In Counter-Strike 2, the game it played most that month, its GPU ran at 65° in steady play. Its usual in that game was 66 to 71°, from 46 days and 132 hours of play before. RigSight called that "3° cooler, too little to count". The CPU in the same minutes read the same way, the fans were at their usual speeds and PC problems were as usual. That PC gets warm in games. It isn't overheating. The comparison is strict on purpose. It only uses steady play. That means the GPU at least 80% busy, after the first 10 minutes, so the cooler has warmed up. Both sides need the same GPU power, within 15%. If the game ran much heavier, RigSight doesn't compare it at all. It reads the PC at rest on both sides, so a warmer room isn't blamed on the PC. A game only reads hotter when it is at least 5° warmer, and at least 3° more than the change at rest, with an hour of play now and two hours over three days before. I built it that strict after RigSight once warned me that a healthy fan was clogging. That story is in The day RigSight told me my healthy fan was clogged . When a game does run hotter, RigSight says so in a few places. The PC health card on Home gets one line naming the game, the part, how many degrees hotter at the same power, and the usual range. With no change it says "Temperatures as usual". On the Games page every play keeps its GPU temperature and power, and a play at the usual power says how far it was from that game's usual. So you can see which evening it started. If the PC shut off in a game, the crash's close-up says whether it was running hot just before. It also points out that a power cut at the same moment would look the same. You can turn on Temperature alerts under Notifications in Settings to get a warning that names the game when a part stays over your limit. CPU temperature needs RigSight running with admin rights. RigSight is free and open source. Is it normal for a PC to get hot when gaming? Yes. Games load the GPU and CPU hard, and both turn that power into heat. GPU temperatures in the 60s to 80s °C and CPU temperatures in the 60s to mid 80s °C are common. It's overheating when a part sits at its maker's maximum and slows down, or the PC shuts off. Why does my PC get hot when I play games? A GPU can draw a few hundred watts in a game, and almost all of it ends up as heat inside the case. If the case can't move that heat out fast enough, everything inside warms up. Dust, blocked vents and uncapped frame rates make it worse. How do I stop my laptop overheating when gaming? Play on a hard, flat surface so the vents underneath aren't blocked, clean the vents, cap the frame rate and use the maker's balanced or quiet mode. A stand that lifts the back edge helps air reach the fans. Can overheating make my PC shut off while gaming? Yes. When a part reaches a temperature it can't safely run at, the PC can switch itself off to protect it. A sudden power cut looks the same afterwards, so check the temperatures just before the shut-off before blaming heat.

t: Free PC monitoring software, and why I built an HWiNFO alternative
d: HWiNFO showed me every sensor but not what my PC did yesterday, so I built RigSight. Free PC monitoring software compared, from Task Manager and HWiNFO to MSI Afterburner, LibreHardwareMonitor and RigSight, and which one answers your question.
l: PC problems Tools pc monitoring software free pc hardware monitoring software free hwinfo alternative hwinfo alternative free hwinfo alternative open source msi afterburner alternative msi afterburner alternative for monitoring msi afterburner alternative to show fps pc temp monitoring software free
b: Before RigSight existed, I used HWiNFO. It's a great tool, and it shows almost every sensor in a PC. What it didn't give me was the history I wanted. I could see what my PC was doing right now. I couldn't easily see what it did yesterday, or last week, or how this month compared with the one before. That gap is why I built RigSight. Search for free PC monitoring software, or an HWiNFO alternative, and you get the same few names every time. They aren't really rivals. Each one answers a different question about your PC. How RigSight came out of HWiNFO HWiNFO can keep a record. You switch on logging, it writes every sensor to a CSV file, and you open the file in a spreadsheet afterwards. That works when you know a problem is coming. It doesn't help with the evening you didn't plan for, like the game that stuttered at 11 PM or the PC that shut off while you were away. To look back at those, something has to have been recording all along. So RigSight is two programs. A small recorder starts with Windows and writes readings all day. The window you open is only for looking back, and you can close it whenever you like. The full story of that first day is in Day one, and 25 versions before midnight . What you get from that is history in plain words. Home says each day's CPU and GPU peak with the app that was in front at the time. The Temperatures page shows the CPU and GPU from the last 5 minutes up to the last 12 months, or any custom range. The Crashes page lists app crashes, blue screens, driver resets and sudden shut-offs with what most likely caused each one. The Timeline lists what changed on the PC, such as drivers and Windows updates, and whether things ran hotter or less stable afterwards. RigSight keeps the history as long as you choose in Settings, from 3 months up to forever. It also keeps time per app, internet use per app, fan speeds over months, and each game's frame rate and 1% low for every play. Live readings can go in the taskbar on tiles, where a click shows that reading's last ten minutes. They can also go in desktop widgets and an in-game overlay. Everything can be exported as CSV. RigSight is free and open source. It falls short in a few places too. It reads its sensors with LibreHardwareMonitor's library, so it shows fewer sensors than HWiNFO. It can't overclock, undervolt or control fans. Afterburner and your motherboard's software do that. FPS readings and the overlay in exclusive full screen games need RivaTuner Statistics Server. CPU temperature and power, motherboard fans, drive health and per-app internet use need RigSight to run with admin rights. It runs on Windows 10 and 11 only. Why every monitoring tool answers a different question Most sensor apps are built to show what is happening now, because that's what you need while you tune or test. Keeping everything is a different job. It needs a recorder that runs all the time without getting in the way, and a way to read months of numbers without a spreadsheet. So the tools split by question. Is my CPU or GPU too hot right now, and what is every sensor saying? Use HWiNFO. Can I overclock or undervolt my GPU, set a fan curve and see FPS in game? Use MSI Afterburner with RivaTuner Statistics Server. Do I want a small open source sensor reader? Use LibreHardwareMonitor. What did my PC do last night, last week or before it crashed? Use RigSight. Which app is eating CPU or memory right now? Task Manager is already on your PC. Free PC monitoring software, tool by tool Task Manager It's built into Windows, so there's nothing to install. Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc and open Performance for graphs of CPU, memory, disk, network and GPU use. On many PCs with a dedicated GPU it also shows the GPU temperature, as long as the driver supports it. It doesn't show CPU temperature, fan speeds or voltages, and its graphs only cover the last minute. It's good for finding which app is busy, not for checking temperatures. HWiNFO HWiNFO reads more sensors than any other tool here. It reads nearly every sensor on the CPU, GPU, motherboard and drives, down to individual voltages, power limits and memory timings, and it is updated often for new hardware. It can log every sensor to a CSV file, raise alerts on any reading, show readings in the tray and on screen, and share its sensor data with other apps. It is free for personal and non-commercial use. Commercial use needs the paid Pro licence. In the free version, the shared memory feature that lets other apps such as overlays read HWiNFO's sensors switches itself off after 12 hours, and you turn it on again by hand. It isn't open source. Where it falls short is the sensor window, which is a long list of numbers that doesn't tell you which ones matter or what is normal for your PC. It only logs while you have logging switched on, and you read the CSV files yourself. If you are diagnosing a fault and know what you are looking for, nothing beats it. MSI Afterburner and RivaTuner Statistics Server MSI Afterburner is a free GPU tool that works with cards from other makers too, not only MSI. It is the usual choice for overclocking and undervolting a GPU, setting your own fan curve and watching GPU readings on a graph. Its in-game overlay comes from RivaTuner Statistics Server, a separate free tool that installs alongside it. RivaTuner also has a frame rate limiter that many players use on its own. Its weak spot is that it is built around the GPU. CPU and motherboard readings are thinner than HWiNFO's, and the graphs show the recent past while the app is open. Unless you turn on its log file, it keeps no record of how a game ran last week, and it doesn't tell you what the numbers mean. MSI recommends downloading it only from msi.com or Guru3D, because fake copies exist. If you only want an MSI Afterburner alternative to show FPS, you may not need Afterburner at all. RivaTuner can show a frame rate counter by itself. NVIDIA's and AMD's own apps have performance overlays, and the Xbox Game Bar, opened with Win + G, has a Performance widget with FPS. LibreHardwareMonitor LibreHardwareMonitor is free and open source, under the MPL 2.0 licence. It reads temperatures, fan speeds, voltages, load and clocks from motherboards, Intel and AMD processors, NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs, drives and network cards. Some sensors need it to run as administrator. Its library is also used inside other apps, RigSight among them, which makes it the usual pick when someone wants an open source HWiNFO alternative. Its weak spots are that it reads fewer sensors than HWiNFO, and it shows what is happening now unless you turn on Log Sensors , which saves the readings to a file. Get it from the project's GitHub page. The project warns that librehardwaremonitor.com is not its site. Side by side Tool Best at Keeps history Open source Task Manager Which app is busy right now Last minute only No HWiNFO Every sensor, alerts, CSV logs While logging is on No MSI Afterburner with RivaTuner GPU tuning, fan curves, FPS overlay Recent graph while open, optional log file No LibreHardwareMonitor Open source sensor readings While Log Sensors is on Yes, MPL 2.0 RigSight History in plain words for heat, crashes, changes, app time and internet Yes, all day, kept as long as you choose Yes, MIT A common setup is RigSight running all the time for the history, with HWiNFO or Afterburner opened when you need a closer look or want to tune something. That's how I still use HWiNFO today. Pick the tool for the question you have right now. If it's about heat, see how to check your GPU temperature history . If your PC crashed and you don't know why, start with how to find out why your PC crashed . What is the best free PC monitoring software? It depends on the question. HWiNFO reads the most sensors, MSI Afterburner is the usual choice for GPU tuning and an in-game overlay, and RigSight keeps a history so you can look back. Many people run one of each. Is there an open source HWiNFO alternative? LibreHardwareMonitor is open source under the MPL 2.0 licence and reads CPU, GPU, motherboard, drive and network sensors. RigSight is open source under the MIT licence and reads its sensors with LibreHardwareMonitor's library. Neither reads as many sensors as HWiNFO. What is an MSI Afterburner alternative to show FPS? RivaTuner Statistics Server, which installs with Afterburner, can show a frame rate overlay on its own. NVIDIA's and AMD's own apps have performance overlays, and the Xbox Game Bar has a Performance widget. RigSight shows FPS in its overlay and records it per game, reading it from RivaTuner. Is HWiNFO free? Yes, for personal and non-commercial use. Commercial use needs the paid Pro licence. The free version's shared memory feature, which other apps use to read HWiNFO's sensors, switches off after 12 hours until you turn it on again. Can I run more than one monitoring program at once? Usually yes. Many people keep one running in the background and open another when they need a closer look. If readings look odd or a tool reports conflicts, close one of them and compare.

t: Taskbar tiles worked on my taskbar, not on theirs
d: A GitHub issue asked for more colourful taskbar readings. RigSight 1.2.0 gave every reading a tile and a look of its own, and a bug report 94 minutes later showed a fallback I had never told anyone about.
l: Building RigSight
b: On 2 November someone opened an issue on RigSight's GitHub . They asked for taskbar readings that were more colourful and cleaner, with different graphs, and pointed me at Pulsar , an open source app that puts PC stats on the taskbar. Until then, RigSight's taskbar readings were plain numbers with a short name under each, and a small graph behind the name if you turned it on. Pulsar is under the GPL licence and RigSight is under MIT, so Pulsar's code can't go into RigSight. I could still borrow its ideas, and it had plenty of them. A day of tiles I built it on 3 November. Every reading now sits on a tile of its own, in its part's colour or any colour you pick. Each reading gets its own look too. There's a filled, line or bar graph, and for temperatures and loads a level, blocks or a ring. Width makes the strip Compact, Standard or Roomy. I picked those names after looking at what Gmail and Outlook call the same kind of setting. Two decisions took me longer than the code. The first was who gets tiles. Everyone who already had readings in the taskbar got them, and anyone with none got nothing added. Setting Background to None on the Taskbar page brings back the old look. The second was room. My first mock-up ran the readings over the app buttons in the middle of the taskbar. When I checked, the real strip had the same flaw with enough readings, because it never looked at where the apps were. Now, when room runs out, the graphs first narrow to the width of their words. Then the last readings wait in a +N tile that names them when you point at it. Pulsar also stacks readings in two rows, and my first thought was why I had never done that. Halfway through building it I stopped, because I had the readings pair up in the order they were listed. Download and upload belong in one box, and only you know which two of your readings go together. So in Two rows you choose the pairs, and any reading can sit on its own. The two icon styles got bigger in Windows 11 too, 24 pixels instead of Windows' 16, each on a tile in its part's colour. RigSight 1.2.0 went out that evening, and I replied on the issue with what I had added. Ninety-four minutes later The same person opened a new issue with a picture of their taskbar. Level, Blocks and Ring didn't work. They also asked whether clicking a reading could show more about it. Their taskbar uses Windows 11's smaller taskbar buttons, so it is 32 pixels tall instead of the usual 48. On a taskbar that short there's no room for the name under the number, so RigSight puts each reading on one line. And on one line, I had Level, Blocks and Ring fall back to a filled graph. It was worse than that, because a reading with one of those three looks doesn't keep the history a graph needs. The graph had nothing to draw, so all they saw was the number. 32 px How tall their taskbar was. I had only tested the looks on my own, which is 48 px. That fallback came from one of my early mock-ups. I wrote it down as a detail and then forgot it. Nothing on the Taskbar page said it would happen, and the page's own preview kept showing Blocks and Ring. On my taskbar every look drew as picked, so I never saw it. In 1.2.0 On a 32 px taskbar, Level, Blocks and Ring showed only the number, and nothing said why. Since 1.2.1 Whatever height your taskbar is, the look you pick is the look you get. The fix, and the card they asked for RigSight 1.2.1 went out a little after 9 AM the next morning. On one line, Level is a band behind the words, Blocks are a row under the line, and a ring leads the tile like an icon, the way Pulsar draws its own. Every reading on that short taskbar sits on a tile of the same height. Two rows leaves room above, between and below its two lines instead of filling the box edge to edge. Clicking a reading now opens a card above it. It shows the last ten minutes on a small graph with the low, average and high, that part's other readings, the apps using it most right now and a button to the page it belongs to. For fans it lists what they are cooling instead of apps. Click a box in Two rows, or an icon per part, and the card shows both readings side by side. I closed both issues with a note of what changed. The bug itself was small. What bothered me was the kind of bug it was. RigSight dropped something you picked and didn't tell you. That's the same mistake as a page saying "nothing recorded" while it is still loading, which I wrote about in The tests said 15 milliseconds. The app froze. I have one PC with one taskbar size, so 1.2.1 also added a test for a 32 pixel taskbar. A picked look now has to draw there before a release can go out.

t: Games crashing after a graphics driver update, and how to tell why
d: Two apps crashed on my PC within ten seconds of a new NVIDIA driver going in. How RigSight tells a crash during the install from a bad driver, why games crash after a graphics driver update, and how to roll back or clean install.
l: PC problems Drivers and updates games crashing after graphics driver update game crashing after nvidia driver update nvidia driver causing crashes games crashing after amd driver update nvidia driver causing game crashes latest nvidia driver causing crashes why does my graphics driver keep crashing
b: On 7 October at 5:40 PM I installed a new NVIDIA driver. Within ten seconds, two programs on my PC had crashed. Cloudflare WARP went down seven seconds after Windows put the new driver in, and RigSight's own recorder went down three seconds after that. Neither crash meant the new driver was bad. Games crashing after a graphics driver update can mean two different things, and each one has its own fix. Why games crash after a graphics driver update A graphics driver sits between every game and the GPU. A new version changes that layer for every game at once, so a bug in it can crash one game and leave the rest alone. NVIDIA lists the problems it knows about as open issues in each driver's release notes, and often ships a hotfix driver for the worst ones. Not every crash after an update is the new driver's fault, though. These are the other usual reasons. The install itself can crash apps. Programs that are open can crash while Windows swaps the driver under them, as my two did. Your screens can also flicker or go black for a moment. Neither means the driver is bad. Leftovers from older drivers can clash. Settings and profiles from earlier versions can conflict with the new one, and a clean install removes them. Windows Update sometimes installs a graphics driver on its own, so the driver can change without you running anything. Tuning that was borderline can fail. An overclock or undervolt that was stable on the old driver can fail on the new one. A driver that lets the card boost higher can show up a weak power supply or a card that runs hot. Something else changed the same week. A game patch, a Windows update or a new overlay can look exactly like a driver problem. After a driver change, the first launch of a game can also take longer while the game rebuilds its shader cache. That is a slow start, not a crash. How to fix games crashing after a graphics driver update Start with the checks, then the safest fix. Each step rules something out. Check that the driver is the change. Open Settings > Windows Update > Update history and look under Driver updates . This catches drivers Windows installed by itself. Then open Device Manager , expand Display adapters , right-click your GPU, pick Properties and read the version and date on the Driver tab. Check your game launcher for a game update on the same day too. Find the file the game crashed in. Open Event Viewer > Windows Logs > Application and find the Error from Application Error at the time of the crash. The line Faulting module name says which file it crashed in. Files like nvwgf2umx.dll or nvd3dumx.dll belong to the NVIDIA driver, and files starting with amdxx or atiumd belong to AMD's. A crash inside one of those points at the driver. A crash inside the game's own files points at the game. Crashes in the minute or two while the driver was installing don't count. For more on reading these logs, see how to find out why your PC crashed . Roll the driver back. This is Microsoft's own way to put the previous driver back, and it is safe. Sign in as an administrator, open Device Manager , expand Display adapters , right-click your GPU and pick Properties . On the Driver tab, press Roll Back Driver , pick a reason, press Yes and restart if Windows asks. If the button is greyed out, Windows didn't keep an older version. Download the driver you had before from NVIDIA's driver page or AMD's support page, where older versions are listed for each card, and install it with the clean install option below. Play the games that crashed for a few sessions. If they now run fine, the new driver was the problem. Stay on the old one until a newer driver lists your game as fixed in its release notes. If Windows Update keeps putting the newer driver back, Microsoft's Show or hide updates troubleshooter, a small file called wushowhide.diagcab, can hide that one driver update. Microsoft made it for Windows 10, and guides report it still works on Windows 11. A newer version of the same update can still install later. If the old driver crashes too, or you want to keep the new one, do a clean install. Settings left from older versions can clash with the new driver, and a clean install puts it in fresh. For NVIDIA, download the driver for your card, run the installer, pick Custom (Advanced) , tick Perform a clean installation and restart when it finishes. The exact screens can differ a little between driver versions. A clean install resets your NVIDIA Control Panel settings, so note any per-game settings first. For AMD, AMD's advice is to remove AMD Software from Settings > Apps > Installed apps , then install the new version from AMD's support page. The AMD installer's Factory Reset option removes all earlier versions as part of the install, and AMD notes you can't roll back to the old driver after that. Use DDU only when a clean install isn't enough. Display Driver Uninstaller, usually called DDU, removes every trace of a graphics driver, and its own developer says it was designed for cases where the normal uninstall fails. Follow the developer's guide. Download the driver you want first, back up anything important, and have your BitLocker recovery key to hand if the drive uses BitLocker. Disconnect from the internet so Windows Update can't slip its own driver in, run DDU in Safe Mode as the developer strongly recommends, then restart, install the driver you downloaded and reconnect. For AMD, the AMD Cleanup Utility does a similar job for problems an uninstall can't fix. If it still crashes, look past the driver. Reset MSI Afterburner or your card maker's tool to default and test at stock clocks. Turn the Steam, Discord, NVIDIA and RivaTuner overlays off one at a time, since they all hook into the game. Use your launcher's verify or repair option for the game's files. If the crash comes after a long stretch under load, check GPU temperatures and look at your power supply. If every game crashes and the screen goes black before Windows recovers, you are probably seeing graphics driver resets rather than ordinary game crashes. For those, read display driver stopped responding and has recovered . How RigSight caught it That evening RigSight couldn't tell me much, because it was one of the two programs that crashed. The recorder had been asking the GPU for its temperature through NVIDIA's own library. The old driver went away in the middle of that call, and the call landed on memory that wasn't there any more. WARP crashed in dcomp.dll, a part of Windows that draws app windows. Both programs were open while the driver was swapped under them. The full story of my bug is in The driver update that knocked RigSight out . Since version 0.17.1, RigSight stops reading the GPU while its driver changes. That night also changed how RigSight reads crashes. It now checks every app crash and freeze against the graphics driver installs Windows logged. A crash within two minutes of one gets "Likely the driver install" on the Crashes page. A line names the driver, says it "was being installed at that moment" and gives the time of the install and of the crash. The advice is to do nothing. An app that crashed while a driver was replaced under it says nothing about the new driver. Crashes in the days after are the ones that point at the driver. When a game crashes inside a graphics driver file, RigSight names it in plain words, such as "The NVIDIA graphics driver failed while running Crimson Desert". It marks that Confirmed, because Windows named the file. The picture at the top is that example from RigSight's demo PC, not a crash of mine. Then the opened crash looks at the week before it. If a new graphics driver, Windows update or BIOS went in during those seven days, RigSight checks whether the same game crashed in the same file in the 30 days before that install. If it did, the crash says the driver didn't cause it, with how many times it happened before the install and since. If it didn't, the crash says how many days before the driver went in, and that this crash hadn't happened in the 30 days before it. If nothing new went in, it says "Nothing new was installed". On the Games page, each game lists every play and how it ended, newest first. The graphics driver, Windows and game updates that came between plays sit in the same list. The How it runs chart marks every driver and game update against the frame rate. Frame rates need RivaTuner Statistics Server running. The Timeline lists every graphics driver install with its time, the new version and the one it replaced. Its "This PC now" panel shows the driver you're on and since when. When a driver made a measurable difference, the Before and after filter shows it. That filter counts graphics driver resets, blue screens inside a graphics driver and shut-offs after the GPU hung. It doesn't count game crashes, so for those the Games and Crashes pages are where to look. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is the rollback. It takes about five minutes and answers the question directly. If the old driver crashes too, look at the game, your clocks and your temperatures. If the game just closes with no message at all, read why a game crashes to desktop with no error . Why are games crashing after an NVIDIA driver update? A new driver changes how every game talks to the GPU, and a bug in it can crash some games and not others. NVIDIA lists known problems as open issues in each driver's release notes and often ships a hotfix driver for the worst ones. Why does my graphics driver keep crashing? The usual causes are a bad driver version, leftovers from older drivers, an unstable GPU overclock or undervolt, heat, or a power supply that can't hold up under load. Rolling back and doing a clean install rules out the driver. If it still crashes on a driver that used to work, look at clocks, temperatures and power next. Should I use DDU every time I update my graphics driver? No. Its own developer says DDU was designed for cases where the normal driver uninstall fails, and its guide also covers switching between NVIDIA and AMD cards. For an everyday update, the installer's clean install option is enough. Is it safe to roll back a graphics driver? Yes. Roll Back Driver puts back the version Windows kept from before the update, and you can update again whenever you like. If the button is greyed out, Windows didn't keep one, and you install the older version from NVIDIA or AMD instead.

t: GPU not at 100% usage but low FPS? Find what your card waits for
d: How RigSight tells whether a frame cap, VSync or the CPU keeps your GPU under 100% usage, why the card waits, and how to check a CPU bottleneck yourself.
l: PC problems FPS and games gpu not at 100 usage but low fps why is my gpu not at 100 usage cpu bottleneck symptoms cpu bottleneck cpu and gpu usage not at 100 but low fps cpu bottleneck vs gpu bottleneck
b: Your GPU is not at 100% usage but your FPS is low, and that feels wrong. Why would the GPU rest while the game struggles? The card is waiting. Something else decides how many frames get made, and the GPU finishes its share early. RigSight works out what it waits for from every play you've recorded, and below is how it does that and how you can check it yourself. Why a GPU is not at 100% usage In most games, a GPU that works as hard as it can sits at 95 to 100% load. Below that, it finishes each frame and then waits for the next one. That waiting is fine when you have the frames you want. It only matters when FPS is also lower than you expect. There are four usual reasons the card waits. A frame cap or VSync tells the game to stop at a set number of frames. The CPU can't prepare frames fast enough. This is a CPU bottleneck. The game engine has a limit of its own, such as a capped menu, a physics tick or one busy thread. Windows or the laptop runs the card in a power saving mode, or the game runs on the wrong GPU. Some games are simply limited by their engine. Older games and many simulation games lean on one thread, and no PC runs them much faster. If the same game is CPU limited on every PC you read about, that is likely the case. How to check it yourself and fix it First, rule out a frame cap or VSync Look at the FPS counter first. If the frame rate sits flat on a round number like 60, 120, 144 or 165 while GPU load is low, it is a cap. The card makes those frames easily and then stops. In the game's display or graphics menu, turn off VSync and any Frame rate limit for the test. In the NVIDIA Control Panel, open Manage 3D settings and check Max Frame Rate and Vertical sync . On AMD, check Radeon Chill and Frame Rate Target Control in AMD Software. Check that RivaTuner, if you use it, has no frame limit set for this game. If FPS climbs and GPU load rises with it, the cap was the reason, and nothing is wrong. You can keep the cap if you like it. A cap is often the better choice with a G-Sync or FreeSync screen, as VSync vs an FPS cap explains. Second, try the resolution test for a CPU bottleneck This is the clearest test, and it takes two minutes. Stand in the same busy spot in the game and note your FPS. Lower the resolution or the resolution scale a lot, for example from 1440p to 1080p or to 50% scale. Look at the FPS again.
