Lower resolution makes the GPU's job much smaller but leaves the CPU's job the same. If FPS rises a lot, the GPU was the limit. If FPS barely moves, the CPU or the engine is the limit. That is also why people see a CPU bottleneck at 1080p that disappears at 4K. At 4K the card becomes the slower part again. CPU bottleneck symptoms GPU load stays well below 95% while FPS is lower than you want, and no cap is set. FPS barely changes when you lower resolution or graphics settings. FPS dips in crowded places, big fights or large open areas, and recovers in quiet ones. The total CPU usage looks modest, often 30 to 60%, but one or two threads are close to 100%. The 1% low FPS is far below the average, so the game feels uneven. See 1% low FPS meaning . The total CPU number fools many people. A game can max out two threads and leave the rest idle, and Task Manager shows a low total. Here is how to see each thread. Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc and open the Performance tab. Click CPU , then right-click the graph and pick Change graph to > Logical processors . Play in a window or on a second screen and look for one or two graphs pinned near the top. Third, check power mode and the right GPU A card in a power saving state runs at low clocks and can look half busy. Set Settings > System > Power & battery > Power mode to Best performance , and play a laptop on its charger. If your plan changes by itself, see power plan keeps changing. On laptops and PCs with built-in graphics, make sure the game runs on the dedicated card. Open Settings > System > Display > Graphics . Find the game in the list, or add it with Browse . Open its options and choose High performance , then restart the game. What to do about a CPU bottleneck vs GPU bottleneck If the GPU is the limit, you are in the normal state. Lower graphics settings or resolution scale for more frames, or turn on DLSS, FSR or XeSS if the game has them. If the CPU is the limit, graphics settings give little back. These steps help more. Raise the resolution or graphics quality. It sounds backwards, but if the card is waiting anyway, better visuals cost you almost nothing. Lower the settings that load the CPU. Those are view distance, crowd or traffic density, physics, shadows from many lights, and simulation detail in strategy games. Close background apps that use CPU time. Sort Task Manager's Processes tab by CPU . Set a frame cap near the frame rate your PC holds in busy scenes. An even frame rate often feels better than a higher average that jumps around. Check that the CPU isn't hot and slowing down. See PC overheating while gaming . What the numbers mean GPU load at 95 to 100% means the game is GPU bound. That is normal. GPU load under 95% with FPS flat at a round number means a cap or VSync. GPU load under 95% with uneven FPS and one or two CPU threads near 100% means the game is CPU bound. GPU load and GPU clock both low on a laptop point to the power mode, the battery, or the wrong GPU. These are rules of thumb. Some games never quite reach 99% even when the card is the limit, so read the trend rather than one number. One session can mislead you too, which is why RigSight looks at every play. For a live look while you play, its overlay can show frame rate, GPU load, CPU load and clock speeds in a corner of the game, through RivaTuner in exclusive fullscreen games. Do the resolution test tonight in your most demanding scene. It takes two minutes and tells you which part to spend money or settings on. How RigSight caught it Here is Dota 2 on the example PC that RigSight's site uses for its pictures. Over its plays the GPU averaged 68% busy and never reached full load. On a live counter that looks like a card being held back by something. RigSight's Can it run better? card on the game's page reads it the other way round. The frame rate sat flat at 236 fps across the plays, so a frame cap or VSync set the pace, and the card had room to spare. Its answer is that you can raise the settings and keep 236 fps. The card works from all your plays together, once a game has three plays with frame rates. When the frame rate stays flat at one number across them, it says a cap sets the pace. It says what share of the time your GPU spent at full load, counting 95% and up as full. The cut-offs are RigSight's own rules of thumb. At full load 70% of the time or more, it says lower settings would give more frames. From 30%, it says the card is the limit in busy scenes. Below 30% with a cap in play, it says you can raise the settings and keep that frame rate, as with Dota above. Below 30% with no cap, it says something else sets the pace, most likely the CPU. RigSight also reads the game's own saved graphics settings and shows them on the game's page under How it's set . That lets the card name the cap. It says when the game's own frame limit or VSync holds the frame rate, and it says when a game runs with no limit and VSync off faster than your screen can show. Reading those files right took some care. My own Cyberpunk 2077 settings file stores its frame limit as a number with a separate on or off switch, and RigSight first read the number and missed the switch. A limit I had turned off came through as 30 fps. I found it while testing the AI on pretend PCs and fixed it in RigSight's reading. The lesson carries over to anyone checking by hand. A cap can hide in more than one place, so check every one. The FPS readings come from RivaTuner Statistics Server, which needs to be running before the game starts. RigSight's Games page has a button to install or start it. RigSight is free and open source. Why is my GPU not at 100 usage? Because it has nothing more to do. Either a frame cap or VSync stops it after the target frame rate, or the CPU can't prepare frames fast enough to keep it busy. Low usage on its own is not a fault, it only matters when your FPS is also lower than you want. What are CPU bottleneck symptoms? The usual signs are GPU load well under 95% with no frame cap, FPS that barely changes when you lower resolution or graphics settings, dips in crowded scenes and big fights, and one or two CPU threads near 100% in Task Manager while the total CPU usage looks modest. CPU bottleneck vs GPU bottleneck, which is better to have? Being limited by the GPU is the normal, healthy state in most games. The card runs at 95 to 100% and you trade settings for frames. A CPU limit is harder to fix with settings, and it often shows as uneven frame rates in busy moments. Is GPU usage at 100% bad? No. A GPU is built to run at full load for hours while you play. What matters is its temperature and whether the fans keep it within the maker's limits.

t: Normal CPU temperature while gaming, and why yours jumps around
d: How RigSight shows a CPU temperature that jumps around in games, what a normal CPU temperature while gaming is on Ryzen, Intel, an AIO and laptops, and the limits AMD and Intel give.
l: PC problems Temperatures normal cpu temperature while gaming normal cpu temperature while gaming ryzen normal cpu temperature while gaming with aio normal cpu temperature while gaming laptop normal cpu temperature while gaming fahrenheit cpu temperature monitor windows 11
b: A RigSight user on a laptop once wrote to me that the peaks on the one hour temperature chart jumped around every second. Part of that was my bug. The other part is something every gamer runs into when they ask what a normal CPU temperature while gaming is. A CPU's temperature doesn't sit still. It can go from 55 to 80°C and back within a second, and the number you happen to look at decides whether you worry. Normal CPU temperature while gaming on a desktop On a desktop with a decent cooler, most CPUs sit somewhere between 60 and 85°C in a game. Games rarely load every core at once, so they run cooler than a stress test or a long video export. Look at where the temperature settles over a few minutes of play, not at single spikes. Why CPUs run as hot as they do Modern CPUs boost their clock speed until they run into a limit on power or temperature. A chip that reaches the high 80s isn't always struggling. Some are built to use all the room they have. Readings also jump more than a GPU's, because a CPU has a small surface to move heat through and a game's load on it changes from one moment to the next. Every CPU has a maximum temperature in its spec, often called Tjmax or TJunction. At that point it slows itself down to protect the chip. Intel describes this throttling as the processor lowering its clock speed when it goes above that figure. There is no single number that fits every CPU. Here are the makers' figures for some common chips. The AMD Ryzen 5 5600X is rated to 95°C. AMD has said up to 95°C is typical and by design at full load on this chip. The AMD Ryzen 7 5800X, Ryzen 9 5900X and 5950X are rated to 90°C, which AMD called typical at full load. The AMD Ryzen 7000 X series, such as the 7700X, is rated to 95°C. The AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D is rated to 89°C, lower than the other Ryzen 7000 chips. The AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D is rated to 95°C. The Intel Core i9 14900K is rated to 100°C. The Intel Core Ultra 9 285K is rated to 105°C. For any other chip, search its name on AMD's or Intel's own site and look for "Max. Operating Temperature" or "TJUNCTION". Ryzen Ryzen chips have a reputation for running hot, and AMD has been open that this is on purpose. Soon after the Ryzen 5000 series came out, AMD's technical marketing director said temperatures up to 90 or 95°C at full load were typical and by design, because a higher allowed temperature lets the chip boost for longer before it backs off. In games, most Ryzen desktops with a reasonable cooler sit in the 60s to 80s. The Ryzen 7 7800X3D is the one to watch more closely, with a ceiling of 89°C. With an AIO An all-in-one liquid cooler moves heat to a radiator, which usually gives you lower peaks than a small tower cooler. Readings in the 60s and low 70s are common in games. The liquid takes time to warm up, so an AIO can look very cool for the first few minutes and then rise to a steady level. On a laptop Laptop CPUs share a small cooler with the GPU, and readings in the 80s and low 90s are common in games. They also tend to jump around the most, as that user's chart showed. The laptop maker decides the power limits and how fast the fans spin, so a laptop that sits at 90°C may be doing exactly what it was tuned to do. Intel points laptop owners to the maker for this. How to check your CPU temperature and fix it when it runs hot Windows' Task Manager shows your GPU's temperature, but not your CPU's. The BIOS shows it only at rest, which tells you little about gaming. AMD's Ryzen Master and Intel's Extreme Tuning Utility read their own chips, and a sensor app such as HWiNFO can log readings to a file while you play. Whichever you use, look at the highest reading during a session, because the number you see after you alt-tab out can be lower than the peak was. If it does run hot, Intel's support checklist is a good order for any brand. Make sure the cooler is rated for your CPU. Intel's rule is that the cooler's rated wattage should be at least the processor's base power. A small cooler that came with a 65 W chip won't keep up with a 125 W one. Check the cooler is mounted firmly and the protective plastic film was removed from its base. It's an easy thing to miss on a new build. Check the thermal paste. If the PC is several years old, or the cooler has been taken off and put back, fresh paste can help. Check that every fan spins, including the CPU cooler's own fan or the AIO's radiator fans. Intel's checklist also says to make sure an AIO's pump and fans are plugged into the right motherboard headers. A pump on a header that slows it down at idle, or a pump that has failed, can make an AIO CPU hit its limit in games. Check case airflow, so the cooler isn't breathing air the GPU already heated. Look at the BIOS settings. Intel notes that some motherboards ship with settings that run beyond Intel's guidelines, and suggests loading the BIOS defaults or asking the motherboard maker whether overclocking settings are turned on. Change BIOS settings only if you're comfortable there, and write down what you change. On a laptop, play on a hard surface, keep the vents clean, and try the maker's quieter or balanced mode to see whether the temperature falls more than the frame rate. A frame cap helps the CPU too, because fewer frames means less work per second. For every fix for the whole PC, see PC overheating while gaming . For the GPU side, see normal GPU temperature while gaming . Next, look up your exact CPU's maximum on AMD's or Intel's site, then play for half an hour and note where the temperature settles. If it stays 10 degrees or more under the limit, you're fine. If it sits at the limit, start with the cooler mount and the fans. How RigSight caught it The laptop's chart was grouping readings by where they landed on the screen. Every time the chart slid along, the groups changed, and a CPU that jumped around a lot changed the line's shape each second. The whole story is in Three ways my temperature chart was lying . Since 0.16.1 RigSight gives each minute one point, the same minute every time, so a minute that already happened keeps its shape. That left the real question. If a CPU spikes for a few seconds, what should you look at? In RigSight's temperature chart each minute can be shown as its average, its highest or its lowest, and hovering a minute shows all three. The average shows where the CPU settles in a game. The highest shows the short spikes that an average hides. RigSight records the CPU temperature all day and keeps it as history, so you can see how hot it got during last night's game without starting a log first. The Temperatures page shows today's lowest and highest under the gauge and a chart for any range up to the last 12 months. Since 1.12.0, its Over the months card shows how far the CPU climbs above its resting temperature under the same load, week by week or month by month. A warmer room lifts load and rest together, so that gap shows the cooling itself, and a slow climb there points to dust or old paste. Reports puts each peak next to the app that was doing the work. For a week, a month or a custom range, its Against your usual card compares the CPU in the game you played most with your own usual in that game from the weeks before. That tells you whether 83°C is normal for your PC, which matters more than any range online. Under Notifications > Temperature alerts in Settings you can set a CPU limit from 60 to 100°. It starts at 85°, and Reports tells you how many minutes the CPU spent at it. Like most tools that read the CPU's own sensors, RigSight needs admin rights for CPU temperature and power, and it says so when they're missing. RigSight is free and open source. What is a normal CPU temperature while gaming on Ryzen? Most Ryzen desktops sit somewhere in the 60s to 80s °C in games. AMD has said that up to 90°C on the Ryzen 7 5800X and 95°C on the Ryzen 5 5600X is typical and by design at full load, and games are usually lighter than full load. The Ryzen 7 7800X3D has a lower limit, 89°C. What is normal CPU temperature while gaming with an AIO? An AIO liquid cooler usually gives lower peaks than a small air cooler, and the 60s and low 70s °C are common in games. If an AIO CPU reaches its limit, check that the pump runs and is plugged into the right header, and that the radiator fans spin. What is normal CPU temperature while gaming on a laptop? Laptop CPUs run hotter than desktop ones, and readings in the 80s and low 90s °C are common in games. The laptop maker sets the limits and the fan behaviour, so their support page has the right numbers for your model. What is normal CPU temperature while gaming in Fahrenheit? 60 to 85°C is 140 to 185°F. AMD's 95°C limit is 203°F, and Intel's 100°C limit is 212°F. Why is my CPU hotter than my GPU while gaming? CPUs have a smaller surface to move heat through, and many are tuned to boost until they reach a set temperature. A CPU that reads hotter than the GPU in the same game is common and not a fault on its own.

t: Why my display driver stopped responding and has recovered
d: "Display driver stopped responding and has recovered" means the GPU took too long to answer and Windows reset its driver. How RigSight caught the resets on my own PC, what LiveKernelEvent 141 and nvlddmkm events mean, and how to fix it.
l: PC problems Crashes display driver stopped responding and has recovered how to fix display driver stopped responding and has recovered display driver stopped responding and has recovered windows 11 display driver stopped working and has recovered nvlddmkm crash nvlddmkm nvidia corporation video_tdr_error why does my graphics driver keep crashing
b: The screen goes black for a second, the game freezes or closes, and a note in the corner says "display driver stopped responding and has recovered". You may not see the note at all, only the flicker. Either way, Windows just reset your graphics driver. It happened on my own PC more often than I knew, and finding out how often changed what RigSight reads. Why the display driver stops responding Windows has a safety net called Timeout Detection and Recovery, or TDR. When the GPU takes on a task, Windows expects it done or paused within a time limit. Microsoft gives the default as two seconds. If the card misses it, Windows treats the card as frozen, resets the graphics driver, clears the graphics memory and redraws the desktop. That reset is the flicker you see. Most of the time the desktop comes back fine. The game that was running often doesn't, because it lost its connection to the GPU. Some games recover, some show a black screen, and many simply crash. If resets pile up quickly, Windows stops trying. By default, once the card has hung and recovered five times within a minute, the next hang ends in a blue screen. A recovery that fails also ends in a blue screen, called VIDEO_TDR_FAILURE, stop code 0x116. It often names nvlddmkm.sys on NVIDIA cards or amdkmdag.sys on AMD cards. The card misses the deadline for a handful of reasons. The driver can have a bug, or a new version can clash with a game. An overclock or undervolt that is almost stable makes the card stall under a certain load. A card that overheats slows itself down, and if that isn't enough it can hang. A power supply that dips for a moment when the card's power use jumps can stall it too. Less often, the card itself is failing. Where Windows records the resets Windows logs a reset in a few places, and the names are worth knowing, because forum answers use them all. In Event Viewer, under Windows Logs > System , a reset can be an entry from source Display with Event ID 4101, saying the display driver stopped responding and has recovered. As on my PC, it can also be missing. On NVIDIA cards, the System log also holds entries from source nvlddmkm . Event 153 usually reads as a TDR reset on the GPU. Event 13 is a graphics exception with an error code in its data. Reliability Monitor has them too. Search Start for reliability and open View reliability history . A reset shows as Hardware error , and its details say LiveKernelEvent with code 141 or 117. 141 means one graphics engine stopped answering. 117 means the whole card did. In both cases Windows recovered it. Write down the times. Whether the resets happen in one game or in everything, at idle or only under load, tells you more than the error itself. How to fix display driver stopped responding and has recovered Try these in order. The first ones are the easiest to test. Update, roll back or clean install the graphics driver. The driver is the most common cause and the easiest to test. If the resets started right after a driver update, roll it back. Open Device Manager > Display adapters , right-click your card, and pick Properties > Driver > Roll Back Driver . If you have been on the same driver for months, update it. Either way, use the clean install option. On NVIDIA, pick Custom (Advanced) and tick Perform a clean installation . On AMD, use the installer's Factory Reset option, which removes earlier versions of AMD Software and means you can't roll back to them afterwards. The full steps, and when DDU is worth it, are in games crashing after a graphics driver update . Put the GPU back to stock clocks. Reset MSI Afterburner or your card maker's tool to default and turn off any automatic tuning. Some cards ship with a factory overclock, and some have a switch for a quiet BIOS that runs lower clocks. Try it if yours has one. Check the GPU's temperature while you play, using a monitor that keeps a history. NVIDIA lists a maximum GPU temperature on the specification page for many of its cards, and it differs by model. The hot spot, which AMD calls junction temperature, normally runs well above the main GPU reading, so judge each against its own limit. If your card sits at its limit, clean the dust out, check the fans spin and give the case more airflow. Check the power. Make sure every power plug on the card is fully seated. If your card takes two or three power plugs, check the manuals for the card and the power supply. Some ask for a separate cable from the power supply to each plug instead of one cable with two plugs on it, and with a card that draws a lot of power that is the safer choice where your supply has enough cables. If resets only come at the heaviest moments of a game, the power supply is a real suspect. If it is always the same game, look at that game. Update it, verify its files in the launcher, turn off its overlays, and try a lower graphics preset or a frame rate cap. A different graphics mode, such as DirectX 11 instead of DirectX 12, is worth a try if the game offers one. Leave TdrDelay alone. Many old answers tell you to raise it in the registry so Windows waits longer. Microsoft documents those registry keys only for testing and debugging during driver development, and says end users shouldn't change them. A longer wait can hide the message, but the card still hangs, and now the PC sits frozen for longer. Wrong registry edits can also stop Windows working. If resets carry on with a clean driver, stock clocks, normal temperatures and a solid power supply, the card itself may be failing. Testing it in another PC, or another card in yours, settles it. If it is under warranty, the error codes and times you wrote down are what the maker will ask for. How RigSight caught it For months, RigSight's Crashes page counted zero graphics driver resets on my PC. It was reading the entry most answers tell you to look for, the Display event 4101 in Event Viewer. My PC had never written one. When I dug into Windows' error reports instead, the resets were there. Windows had filed a LiveKernelEvent 141 report, a graphics hang it recovered from, once on 13 July and six times on 30 July. On 22 August and 22 September the card hung and the PC went down with it, and the August one ended in a blue screen. So from version 0.25.0, RigSight reads those hang reports as well as the Display event. The first time it runs, it goes back 90 days, so resets from before you installed it show up too. A hang that is followed within minutes by a sudden restart isn't counted as a reset. It goes on that shut-off instead, because the card took the whole PC down. On 22 October I needed it. My NVIDIA driver reset five times in twenty minutes, between 5:13 and 5:33 PM, while I was running RigSight's tests. The NVIDIA kernel driver, nvlddmkm, logged each one as event 153, and Windows filed a LiveKernelEvent 141 report for two of them. I restarted the PC, and Windows has logged no resets since. Without the count, I would have remembered a couple of flickers and nothing more. Graphics driver resets have their own tile on the Crashes page. Open one and it says "The GPU stopped answering and Windows reset its driver", marked Confirmed, because Windows itself recorded it. It names the driver file from Windows' report and the app that was in front. Under Still unknown it says why the GPU stopped answering, since that can be the driver, heat, power or the card itself. Windows records the reset, not the reason. To help with the reason, RigSight shows the minutes around each reset. You get the last five minutes up close, a reading every 2 to 3 seconds, and the 45 minutes before with GPU temperature, hot spot, power and load. You can see whether the card was hot or pulling hard at that moment. With two or more resets, What they have in common says whether they all came in one game or across different apps. On the Games page, each game counts the resets during its plays. On the Timeline, a graphics driver update that brought clearly more resets than before can be marked as having made things worse. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to open Reliability Monitor and count the Hardware error entries for the last few weeks. One reset after hours of play is rarely worth worrying about. If there are several, start with a clean driver install and stock clocks, then check the temperature and power at the moments they happen. What does "display driver stopped responding and has recovered" mean? It means the GPU didn't finish a task within Windows' time limit, about two seconds by default, so Windows reset the graphics driver instead of letting the whole PC freeze. Your screen usually flickers or goes black for a moment and then comes back. The game running at the time often crashes or shows a black screen. What is LiveKernelEvent 141? It is the report Windows writes when part of the GPU stopped answering and Windows recovered it. You see it in Reliability Monitor as Hardware error, with LiveKernelEvent and 141 or 117 in its details. 141 means one graphics engine timed out, 117 means the whole GPU did. Both are graphics hangs that Windows recovered from. What is nvlddmkm event 153? nvlddmkm is the NVIDIA kernel driver. Event 153 in the System log usually says a TDR reset occurred on the GPU, so it is NVIDIA's own record of the same reset. Event 13 from nvlddmkm logs a graphics exception, and its data line holds the error code. Should I increase TdrDelay in the registry? Not as a fix. Microsoft documents the TDR registry keys for testing and debugging during driver development and says end users shouldn't change them. A longer delay can stop the message, but whatever made the card hang is still there, and the PC can sit frozen for longer instead of recovering. Can display driver resets damage my GPU? The reset itself is Windows protecting the PC, and it doesn't harm the card. The cause can matter, though. Heat or a struggling power supply are worth fixing before they get worse.

t: Game crashes to desktop with no error? How RigSight finds why
d: When a game crashes to desktop with no error, Windows still logs the crash. How RigSight reads that record and names the cause, why games crash with no message, and how to find and fix it yourself.
l: PC problems Crashes game crashes to desktop no error game randomly crashes to desktop without error games crashing to desktop windows 11 why does my game keep crashing pc every game crashes to desktop what causes a game to crash on pc
b: You're mid-match, the screen flicks, and you're looking at your desktop. There's no message and no report. The game is just gone. A game that crashes to desktop with no error feels like it left nothing behind, but Windows almost always wrote down what happened. RigSight reads that record for you, and you can read it yourself too. Why a game crashes to desktop with no error When a program hits a fault it can't handle, Windows ends it at once and logs an Application Error. The game often has no time to show its own message. So the crash looks silent, but the record is there. The fault can come from several places, and the file Windows names is the best clue to which one. If it's the game's own .exe, UnityPlayer.dll , GameAssembly.dll or an Unreal Engine file, the crash was inside the game. Bugs, broken files and mods live here. nvwgf2umx.dll , nvd3dumx.dll and nvlddmkm.sys belong to the NVIDIA driver. amdxx64.dll and atiumd64.dll belong to the AMD driver. Files starting with igd belong to the Intel graphics driver. d3d11.dll , d3d12.dll , dxgi.dll and vulkan-1.dll are the graphics layer. The fault is usually the driver's or the game's, not DirectX itself. gameoverlayrenderer64.dll is the Steam overlay and DiscordHook64.dll is Discord's. RTSSHooks64.dll is RivaTuner Statistics Server, which MSI Afterburner uses for its overlay. nvspcap64.dll is the NVIDIA overlay. Overlays hook into the game, so a fault in one ends the game. KERNELBASE.dll and ntdll.dll are parts of Windows every program uses. The fault is most often still the game's, so treat it like the first case. If it says unknown, Windows couldn't tell. Use the exception code instead. The exception code says what kind of fault it was. These are the common ones. 0xc0000005 is an access violation. The game touched memory it wasn't allowed to. Bugs, mods, overlays and unstable memory all cause it. 0xc0000409 is a stack buffer overrun. The game found that part of its memory had been overwritten, or stopped itself on purpose after a serious error. 0xc0000374 is heap corruption. Memory got damaged, often by a mod, an overlay or a bug. 0xc000001d is an illegal instruction. The CPU hit an invalid instruction, which can point to an unstable overclock or undervolt. The pattern matters as much as the file. If the game crashes at the same place in the same file every time, it's the game or a mod. If it crashes in different files at random moments, or every game crashes, it's the PC. Then look at memory, tuning, heat and power. How to find the crash yourself Right-click Start and open Event Viewer . Go to Windows Logs > Application . Click Filter Current Log , type 1000,1002 in the event IDs box and click OK . Find the entry at the time of the crash, with your game's .exe as the faulting application. Event 1000 is a crash. Event 1002 is a freeze that ended with the game being closed. In a 1000, three lines matter. Faulting application name is the game's .exe and its version. Faulting module name is the file the crash happened in, and it's your best lead. Exception code is the kind of fault, from the list above. Reliability Monitor shows the same thing as a calendar. Type reliability into Start, open View reliability history , and look for "Stopped working" under the game's name. A .NET game may also leave a .NET Runtime 1026 entry with the error's name, just before the 1000. If there's no 1000 at all and the whole PC restarted, it wasn't a game crash. See PC restarts randomly while gaming instead. How to fix a game that crashes to desktop Try these in order. The first ones are the safest. Verify the game's files. In Steam, right-click the game in your Library and choose Properties > Installed Files > Verify integrity of game files . Epic, EA, Ubisoft and Battle.net have a Verify or Repair option in each game's menu. If it crashes within seconds of starting, also repair its anti-cheat if it has one. Easy Anti-Cheat, for example, has a Repair Service button in the setup file inside the game's folder. Turn off overlays one at a time. That means Steam, Discord, the NVIDIA app or AMD Software, and RivaTuner. If the faulting module is one of their files, start with that one. Remove mods, reshade files and injected tools, then test the plain game. Update or clean-reinstall the graphics driver if the faulting module belongs to it. If the crashes began after a new driver, try the one before. Undo tuning. Reset GPU overclocks, and in the BIOS turn off XMP or EXPO for a test. A memory profile that's slightly unstable is a classic cause of random crashes across several games. Test memory. Open Start, type Windows Memory Diagnostic , and pick Restart now and check for problems . The result appears in the System log under the source MemoryDiagnostics-Results. Check temperatures and memory use while playing. A GPU near its limit or RAM nearly full can both end a game. Windows logs event 2004, Resource-Exhaustion-Detector, in the System log when it's running out of memory. Repair Windows files. Open Terminal (Admin) and run sfc /scannow . If it finds problems it can't fix, run DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth and then sfc /scannow again. How RigSight caught it The picture on this post is an example from RigSight's demo PC, not a crash of mine. Crimson Desert closed at 10:06 PM with no message. RigSight put it on the Crashes page as "The NVIDIA graphics driver failed while running Crimson Desert", marked Confirmed, with "Update the NVIDIA driver" as the first thing to try. That headline comes from the same entry you'd find in Event Viewer. Windows named nvwgf2umx.dll as the file the game crashed in. RigSight knows that file belongs to the NVIDIA driver, so it says so in plain words. It does the same for AMD and Intel drivers, DirectX, Vulkan, Unity, Unreal, and the Steam, Discord, RivaTuner and NVIDIA overlays. Every crash carries one word for how sure the cause is. Confirmed means Windows named a file RigSight knows. Likely means the evidence points one way. Possibly means other causes fit too. Not enough to say means it can't tell, and it says that instead of guessing. RigSight also looks for patterns across crashes. A game that crashes within a minute of starting reads "crashed as it was starting", which points at its files, an add-on or its anti-cheat, not at heat. Three crashes at the same place in the same file read "crashes at the same spot every time". That's a fault in the game, not your hardware. A crash while a graphics driver was being installed is put down to the install. Open a crash and you see the 45 minutes before it and the 10 after. You see temperatures, load, power, memory, fans and network, and which app was using the CPU and GPU. For a game, RigSight also keeps the last five minutes before the crash at a reading every 2 to 3 seconds. In the example, What it wasn't says "It wasn't overheating" and "Memory wasn't full", so you can stop worrying about those two. RigSight also says when graphics memory was well above that game's usual. You get a notification with the game's name the moment it happens, and the play on the Games page says it ended in a crash. CPU temperature needs RigSight running with admin rights. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to find the Application Error 1000 for your last crash and read its faulting module. If it's the game's own file, verify the files first. If it's an overlay's file, turn that overlay off and play again. Why does my game keep crashing on PC? Most often it's the game itself, its files or mods, an overlay hooking into it, or the graphics driver. If one game crashes in the same file every time, look at that game. If every game crashes, look at the whole PC. Check memory settings, overclocks, temperatures and the power supply. Why does every game crash to desktop? When several games crash, the cause is usually something they share. That can be the graphics driver, an overlay that hooks every game, an unstable overclock or XMP or EXPO memory profile, or heat. Turn overlays off, reset tuning to defaults and run Windows Memory Diagnostic before reinstalling games. What causes a game to crash on PC with no error message? A crash to desktop means the game hit a fault it couldn't handle and Windows ended it, often too fast for the game to show anything. Windows still logs it as event 1000 in the Application log, with the faulting module and an exception code such as 0xc0000005. Are games crashing to desktop on Windows 11 different from Windows 10? No. The logs, the fields and the fixes are the same on both. Windows 11 just moves some settings, and the steps here use the Windows 11 names.

t: Why did my PC crash? How RigSight caught one on mine
d: How to find out why your PC crashed on Windows 11 or 10, from a crash RigSight caught on my own PC. It covers what Windows records, why PCs crash, and where to look.
l: PC problems Crashes how to find out why pc crashed windows 11 how to find out why my pc crashed how to find out why pc keeps crashing event viewer crash logs windows 11 how to find out why pc just crashed how to determine why my pc crashed
b: On 7 October I updated my NVIDIA graphics driver. Ten seconds after the new driver started, a program on my PC crashed. It happened to be RigSight's own recorder, caught asking the GPU for its temperature at the exact moment the old driver disappeared. Windows wrote it down like any other crash, as one line in a log I'd never have opened. That's the problem when you try to find out why a PC crashed on Windows 11. The record is there, but nobody shows it to you. Why PCs crash "Crash" covers a few different things, and each one has its own usual causes and leaves a different trail. A blue screen with a stop code. Windows itself hit an error it couldn't recover from and saved a report. On current Windows 11 it's a black screen that says your device ran into a problem, with the stop code in small text, and it only stays up for a couple of seconds. Microsoft estimates that about three quarters of stop errors come from faulty drivers. The PC just went off or restarted with no blue screen. Windows had no time to write anything, so the record is thin. Power is the usual suspect, whether that's the mains, the power supply or a held power button. Heat and unstable tuning can also do it. One game or app closed and the rest of Windows kept running. That's an app crash, logged separately. A bad update, a mod, an overlay or a driver change is the usual cause, like my driver install. The screen went black for a few seconds and came back. That's a graphics driver reset, a different problem again. If you didn't see it happen, the tools below will tell you which one it was. How to find out why your PC crashed in Reliability Monitor Reliability Monitor is the easiest place to start. It puts every crash of the last year on a calendar. Click Start and type reliability . Open View reliability history . You can also press Win+R and run perfmon /rel . Click the column for the day it crashed. Red X marks are critical events. Double-click an entry in the list below the graph to see the technical details. These are the entries that matter. "Windows was not properly shut down" means Windows didn't get to shut down cleanly. On its own, that means the PC lost power, was switched off by holding the power button, or froze so hard that Windows wrote nothing. After a blue screen you see it too, next to the BlueScreen entry below. "Shut down unexpectedly" with the problem name BlueScreen is a blue screen. The BCCode line is the stop code, such as 124 or 116 . "Stopped working" under an app's name means that app crashed. The details name the file it crashed in. Read the crash logs in Event Viewer Event Viewer has the same events with more detail, and exact times. Right-click Start and choose Event Viewer . Open Windows Logs > System . In the right pane, click Filter Current Log . In the box that says <All Event IDs> , type 41,1001,6008,1074 and click OK . Now you only see the events that matter. Event 41 from Kernel-Power says "The system has rebooted without cleanly shutting down first." Windows writes it when the PC starts again. Click it and open the Details tab. If BugcheckCode is not 0, it was a blue screen. If it's 0, the PC lost power or was switched off. Kernel-Power 41 goes through every field. Event 1001 from BugCheck says "The computer has rebooted from a bugcheck." This one gives the stop code in hex and the path of the dump file Windows saved. Event 6008 from EventLog says "The previous system shutdown was unexpected." It gives the time Windows last knew it was running. That time can be stale by some minutes. Event 1074 from User32 is a normal restart that a person or a program asked for. If you see one at the time of a "random" restart, it wasn't a crash. Windows Update is a common source. For a game or app that closed, switch to Windows Logs > Application and filter for 1000 and 1002 . Event 1000, Application Error, names the program, the faulting module and an exception code. Event 1002, Application Hang, is a program that froze and was closed. Games crashing to desktop goes through those fields. Look for the minidump file After a blue screen, Windows usually saves a small memory dump in C:\Windows\Minidump , one file per crash with the date in its name. Opening it takes a debugger. WinDbg is free from Microsoft. Open the file, run !analyze -v , and look for the line "Probably caused by". It often names a driver file such as nvlddmkm.sys . You don't always need the dump. The stop code alone, from Reliability Monitor or Event Viewer, often says enough. If the Minidump folder is empty, open Settings > System > About > Advanced system settings , then Startup and Recovery > Settings , and set Write debugging information to Small memory dump or Automatic memory dump . The next blue screen will be saved. The small dumps go to the Minidump folder. The others are saved as C:\Windows\MEMORY.DMP . What the evidence points to A stop code that names a driver. Update or reinstall that driver. If the crashes began after a new driver, roll it back. Blue screen causes lists the common codes. Codes like 0x124 WHEA_UNCORRECTABLE_ERROR or 0x101 CLOCK_WATCHDOG_TIMEOUT. The hardware reported the error. Undo any overclock or undervolt, including XMP or EXPO memory profiles, and check temperatures. Kernel-Power 41 with a code of 0. No blue screen was saved. Power is the usual suspect, then heat and tuning. Random restarts while gaming walks through it. The same app crashing in the same file. That program, a mod or an overlay is at fault, not the PC. Different apps crashing at random, with different codes each time. That leans toward memory, the drive or heat. Run Windows Memory Diagnostic from Start and check your drive's health. Also look at what changed. Reliability Monitor lists installs under Informational events , and Settings > Windows Update > Update history shows what Windows installed. A crash that began right after a new driver arrived has a likely suspect, as mine did. How RigSight caught it RigSight is a free, open-source Windows monitor. Its Crashes page reads the same Windows records this post walks through, for blue screens, sudden shut-offs, app crashes and freezes, and graphics driver resets. It lists them on one timeline with the stop codes and file names already pulled out. When it first runs, it reads up to 90 days back from Windows' logs, as far as they still reach. My crash taught it something. Since 0.17.1, when an app goes down within two minutes of a graphics driver install, the Crashes page says which driver was being installed at that moment. That's the answer I had to work out by hand that day. Every crash gets a plain sentence for the most likely cause and one word for how sure that is. The words are Confirmed when Windows' own record says so, Likely, Possibly, and Not enough to say. A blue screen whose driver Windows named reads as Confirmed. A shut-off that neither Windows nor RigSight has anything on says Not enough to say, rather than guessing. Open one and you get what Windows can't give you. RigSight shows the 45 minutes before the crash and the 10 after. You see temperatures, load, power, memory, fans and the network, with the apps doing the work. It lists what it ruled out, such as "It wasn't overheating", and any driver, Windows update, BIOS or hardware change from the week before. Copy report puts it all in a block of text for a forum post, and the Event Viewer button opens Windows' own log. CPU temperature and power need RigSight running with admin rights. The readings only exist from when RigSight started recording, so older crashes from Windows' logs show without them. Your next step is to open Reliability Monitor now and find the red X for your crash. If it says BlueScreen, take the stop code to blue screen causes . If it says Windows was not properly shut down, go to Kernel-Power 41 . How do I find out why my PC just crashed? Open Reliability Monitor right away and look at today's column. A red X with Windows was not properly shut down means Windows didn't shut down cleanly. If a Shut down unexpectedly entry with the problem name BlueScreen sits next to it, Windows crashed, and its BCCode is the stop code. If it's alone, the PC lost power, was switched off or froze. Where are the crash logs in Event Viewer on Windows 11? Right-click Start, open Event Viewer, then go to Windows Logs, System for the PC going down and Windows Logs, Application for apps and games crashing. Use Filter Current Log and type 41,1001,6008 in the event IDs box to see only the crash entries. How long does Event Viewer keep logs? Each log has a size limit, often 20 MB for System and Application, and the oldest entries are dropped when it fills. On a busy PC that can be a few weeks or a few months. Reliability Monitor keeps about a year of its own history. How do I figure out why my PC keeps crashing? Write down the time of every crash and compare them. The same stop code or the same faulting file each time points to one driver or program. Different codes every time, or sudden shut-offs with no code at all, point more toward hardware, heat or power.

t: Why Kernel-Power 41 happens, and how RigSight caught mine
d: My PC logged Kernel-Power 41 again and again. How RigSight caught and explained it, what causes Kernel Power 41, including while gaming, and how to fix it.
l: PC problems Crashes kernel power 41 kernel power 41 while gaming kernel-power 41 (63) what causes kernel power error 41 how to fix kernel power 41 kernel power 41 windows 11 what is kernel power 41 critical error
b: In the 30 days up to 1 October, my own PC logged Kernel-Power 41 again and again. There were 22 shutdowns that didn't finish cleanly, against 7 that did. I don't switch my PC off at the wall, and my lights weren't flickering 22 times a month. RigSight is what put that number in front of me, and working out what it really meant changed how RigSight reads this event for everyone. Why Kernel-Power 41 happens When you shut down normally, Windows closes everything and marks the shutdown as clean. When it starts and finds no clean mark, it logs event 41 from the source Kernel-Power, with the text "The system has rebooted without cleanly shutting down first." So the event is written at the next start, not at the moment the PC went down. It sounds like a diagnosis. It isn't. It only says the last shutdown wasn't clean. Anything that stops Windows without a proper shutdown leaves one behind. That's why searching the event ID alone gets you every possible answer. These are the usual causes when the event shows no blue screen. A power cut or dip. If the lights flickered or other devices lost power too, it was the mains. A battery backup, called a UPS, stops these. A power supply that can't keep up. This is the classic cause of Kernel Power 41 while gaming. Modern GPUs can draw short spikes above their rated power, and a tired or undersized supply switches off to protect itself. It looks exactly like a power cut from inside the PC. Overheating. CPUs and GPUs switch the PC off when they pass their limit, rather than burn out. The limit is on the maker's page for your model and differs between models. Intel lists 100°C for the Core i9-14900K, for example, AMD 95°C for most Ryzen 7000 chips and 89°C for the X3D ones. An unstable overclock or undervolt. That includes XMP or EXPO memory profiles, Curve Optimizer and GPU tuning tools. Tuning that is too tight can reset the PC with no blue screen. A held power button after a freeze. The timestamp usually records it, but Microsoft notes it can stay at 0 when the frozen PC couldn't write to its drive. A shutdown that didn't finish, often with Fast Startup, like mine. With Fast Startup on, a normal shutdown goes through hibernate, so an unfinished one leaves a 41 behind. These are usually harmless. A loose cable. Check the power cable at the wall and at the supply, and the GPU's own power plugs. How to read Kernel-Power 41 yourself Right-click Start and open Event Viewer . Go to Windows Logs > System , click Filter Current Log and type 41 in the event IDs box. Double-click the event, then open the Details tab and pick Friendly View . These are the fields that matter. BugcheckCode is the blue screen's stop code, written in decimal. 0 means no blue screen was recorded. Any other number means Windows crashed with a stop error. Convert it to hex to look it up. Open Calculator, switch to Programmer , type the number with DEC selected and read the HEX line. Microsoft's own example, 159, is 0x9F, DRIVER_POWER_STATE_FAILURE. In PowerButtonTimestamp , anything other than 0 means someone held the power button to switch the PC off. For SleepInProgress , Microsoft's event 41 article only shows it as false or 0, and doesn't explain the other numbers for this event. They line up with Windows' list of power states, where 0 is none, 2 to 4 are sleep, 5 is hibernate and 6 is off. Read that way, a 5 or 6 most likely means a shutdown that never finished, not a crash in the middle of a game. Microsoft's own advice splits it the same way. A code above 0 is a stop error, so follow the stop code. See what causes a blue screen . A power button timestamp means the PC was switched off by hand, usually because it had frozen. When everything is 0, Windows had no chance to write anything, and Microsoft points to the power supply, overheating, memory and overclocking. How to fix Kernel-Power 41, in order Note when it happens. Only under load points to the power supply or heat. At idle or overnight points to the mains, sleep or Fast Startup. Undo all tuning. In the BIOS, load the default settings and turn off XMP or EXPO for a test. Reset any GPU overclock in its tool. If the restarts stop, the tuning was the cause. Check temperatures while gaming. If the CPU or GPU is near its limit just before it goes off, clean the dust filters and check every fan spins. Plug the PC straight into a wall socket, not a power strip or extension. Reseat the power supply's cables at both ends, and the GPU's power plugs. Check the power supply. Compare its wattage with your GPU maker's recommended supply. If the card takes two or three 8-pin plugs, check the manuals for the card and the power supply. Some ask for a separate cable from the supply for each plug instead of one cable with two plugs on it, and with a power-hungry card that is the safer choice anyway. If the 41s happen at shutdown, sleep or wake, turn off Fast Startup. Go to Control Panel > Hardware and Sound > Power Options > Choose what the power buttons do > Change settings that are currently unavailable , then clear Turn on fast startup and click Save changes . Update the BIOS and chipset drivers from your motherboard maker too. If it still happens under load with everything at defaults, test with another power supply. It's the part most often at fault, and the hardest to prove any other way. Also check whether the 41 is alone. Filter the System log for WHEA-Logger as the event source. An error the hardware couldn't correct around the same time points at the CPU, memory or motherboard, or at tuning that's too tight for them. How RigSight caught it RigSight reads Windows' crash records every time it starts, so every Kernel Power 41 shows up on its Crashes page as a sudden shut-off, with the time it happened and what the PC was doing in the minutes before. That's how I saw how often it was happening. Without it, each one was a single red line in Event Viewer that I would never have gone looking for. At first, RigSight called them power loss while the PC was asleep. That was my mistake, and it came from one field in the event. The full story is in My PC wasn't losing power in its sleep . In short, the field SleepInProgress holds the power state Windows was moving into, not a yes or no. On my PC it was a 6, switching off. These were shutdowns that never quite finished, not power cuts. Today, every sudden shut-off on the Crashes page gets a cause and one word for how sure RigSight is. A held power button reads as Confirmed. A SleepInProgress of 5 or 6 says Windows was already shutting down. An error the hardware couldn't correct, logged around it, makes it Likely a hardware fault. A shut-off is only "Likely a power cut" when the PC was doing little, nobody held the button and Windows logged no error. A shut-off under load is only "Possibly mains or power supply", because from inside the PC those two look the same. Open a shut-off and you see the 45 minutes before it. It shows temperatures, load, GPU power draw, memory and fans, with the game in front. If the GPU was drawing 320 W at normal temperatures when it went off, that points toward the power supply rather than heat. The shut-off is timed by the last minute RigSight recorded, not by Windows' 6008 time, which can be some minutes early. CPU temperature and power need RigSight running with admin rights. RigSight is free and open source. Your next step is to open the latest event 41 and read BugcheckCode and PowerButtonTimestamp . If both are 0 and it happens while gaming, start with tuning and the power supply. If SleepInProgress is 5 or 6 and it only happens at shutdown, you're probably looking at what I was. Those are shutdowns that didn't finish, and nothing to panic about. What is Kernel-Power 41 (63)? It's the same event. 41 is the event ID and 63 is its task category, which Event Viewer shows in brackets. The long number like (70368744177664),(2) is the event's keywords. None of these numbers say what caused the shut-off. The fields on the Details tab do. Why does Kernel Power 41 happen while gaming? Under a game the GPU and CPU draw the most power and run hottest, so a power supply that can't keep up, an unstable overclock or overheating shows up there first. If BugcheckCode is 0 and nobody touched the power button, start with the power supply and the temperatures in the minutes before. Is Kernel-Power 41 a hardware problem? Not always. It's logged after a power cut, a held power button, a blue screen caused by a driver, or a shutdown that didn't finish. If it keeps happening with a code of 0 while the PC is working hard, hardware, usually the power supply, is the most likely cause. How do I fix Kernel Power 41? Fix what caused it, since the event is only the record. Read the BugcheckCode first. With a code, follow the stop code. With all zeros, undo overclocks and XMP or EXPO, check temperatures, plug the PC straight into the wall, and test or replace the power supply if it only happens under load.

t: Normal GPU temperature while gaming: is 85°C too hot?
d: What a normal GPU temperature while gaming is, the limits NVIDIA and AMD give, and why RigSight only ever compares your card with itself, after it once told me my healthy fan was clogged.
l: PC problems Temperatures normal gpu temperature while gaming is 85 degrees hot for a gpu while gaming average gpu temperature while gaming normal gpu temperature while gaming laptop what temperature is normal for gpu when should i worry about gpu temp normal gpu temp while gaming gpu 85 degrees while gaming average gpu temp while gaming is 68 degrees hot for a gpu
b: On 29 September RigSight told me my GPU fan was running 1,473 rpm faster than usual at the same temperature, and that my cooler might be clogging. Nothing was wrong. It had compared minutes when my card's fans were stopped at rest with minutes in a game. That mistake is the best answer I have to "what's a normal GPU temperature while gaming?" Normal is what your own card does in the same game, at the same load. Charts of other people's cards give you a rough range and nothing more. GPU temperature while gaming What it means Under 60°C Cool. A light game, or a big cooler. 60 to 80°C Normal for most desktop cards. 80 to 85°C Warm, and still within spec for most cards. Above 85°C Close to the limit on many cards. Check airflow, dust and the fan curve. At the card's limit, 83 to 93°C on NVIDIA cards The card slows itself to stay there. Why a GPU runs as hot as it does A GPU turns almost all the power it draws into heat, and a demanding game asks it for nearly all it has. How hot it ends up depends on how much power the game pulls, how well the cooler moves that heat into the case, and how well the case moves it out into the room. A hotter room starts the whole chain higher. Normal GPU temperature while gaming On a desktop card with a working cooler, a demanding game usually puts the GPU somewhere between 60 and 80°C. Where yours lands in that span depends on the card, the cooler the maker put on it, the case and the room. A big card with three fans in a case with good airflow often stays in the 60s. A small card with one or two fans, or any card in a tight case, often sits in the high 70s. A card that stops its fans at rest will idle warmer than you expect, around 40 to 50°C. That's by design. Two things are normal and catch people out. First, the temperature climbs for the first 10 minutes or so of a game, then levels off. Judge the level, not the climb. Second, modern cards boost their clock speed as long as there is room under their limit, so a warm card is often a card that is boosting its clock. The limits NVIDIA and AMD give There is no one safe number for every GPU. Each maker publishes its own, and it changes from model to model. NVIDIA lists a "Maximum GPU Temperature" on each GeForce card's spec page. These are the figures for its own Founders Edition or reference designs. The RTX 3060, 3060 Ti, 3080 and 3080 Ti have a maximum of 93°C. The RTX 4070, 4070 SUPER, 4070 Ti, 4070 Ti SUPER and 4090 have a maximum of 90°C. The RTX 5090 has a maximum of 90°C. The RTX 5080 and 5070 Ti have a maximum of 88°C. The RTX 5070 has a maximum of 85°C. NVIDIA notes that card makers such as ASUS, MSI or Gigabyte may publish different specs for their own versions, so check your exact card's page too. When a card reaches its maximum, it lowers its clock speed to stay there. That protects the chip, and it also costs you frames. AMD talks about its limit differently. On Radeon cards the reading to watch against the limit is the junction temperature, also called the hot spot, which is the hottest of many sensors on the chip. In 2019 AMD said that a junction temperature of up to 110°C during typical gaming on the RX 5700 series was "expected and within spec". AMD Software shows this reading as GPU Junction Temperature, next to the main GPU temperature, which sits well below it. If you want to understand that second number, GPU hot spot temperature explains the gap between the two. Is 85 degrees hot for a GPU while gaming? 85°C is warm. For most current cards it is still inside the maker's limit. It is 5°C under the 90°C of an RTX 4070 or 4090, and 8°C under the 93°C of an RTX 3080. On an RTX 5070, which NVIDIA lists at 85°C, it is right at the line, and the card is already holding itself back. So the answer depends on your card. Look up its maximum, then ask yourself these questions. Does it level off at 85°C, or keep climbing the longer you play? Does your frame rate drop when it gets there? Did it used to run cooler in the same game, at the same settings? If it levels off and the frame rate holds, your card is doing what it was built to do. If it keeps climbing, loses frames, or runs hotter than it did a few months ago, something has changed and it's worth a clean and a look at the airflow. Normal GPU temperature while gaming on a laptop Laptops are their own case. The GPU and CPU often share one set of heat pipes and fans, in a body a couple of centimetres thick. Gaming laptops commonly run their GPU in the high 70s and 80s °C, and that is how many are tuned out of the box. The laptop maker, not NVIDIA or AMD alone, sets how hot it is allowed to get and how loud the fans may run, so the maker's support page is the place to look for your model's numbers. What helps most on a laptop is simple. Play on a hard, flat surface so the vents underneath can breathe, keep the vents free of dust, and use the maker's own performance mode app if it has one. A stand that lifts the back edge helps too. How to check your GPU temperature in Windows Windows 10 version 2004 and Windows 11 show the temperature of a dedicated GPU in Task Manager. Microsoft notes it needs a graphics driver that supports WDDM 2.4 or later, which any recent driver does. Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager. Open the Performance tab. Click GPU 0 or GPU 1 , whichever is your GPU rather than the graphics built into the CPU. Look for GPU Temperature in the details under the graphs. Task Manager only shows the reading right now. To see how hot the card got during a game, you need a tool that records it while you play. Checking GPU temperature history covers the options. What to do if your GPU runs hot Try these in order. The first ones are free and fix most cases. Clean the card and the case filters. Dust packs into the fins of the cooler and the front filter. Hold the fans still while you blow them out so they don't spin up. Check airflow. Cool air should come in at the front or bottom and leave at the back or top. A case pushed against a wall or into a desk cubby traps hot air. Cap your frame rate. If your game runs at 200 frames on a 144 Hz screen, the card is working hard for frames you never see. NVIDIA has Max Frame Rate under Manage 3D settings in the NVIDIA Control Panel. AMD Software has Radeon Chill, which AMD says lowers power and GPU temperature by lowering the frame rate when you aren't moving much. Check the fans. Make sure every fan on the card spins in a game. If one doesn't, see GPU fan not spinning . Look at the room. A card runs warmer on a hot summer day. That's normal, and it's why comparing this week with last winter can mislead you. Steps past this, like a new fan curve, undervolting or new thermal paste, are covered in PC overheating while gaming . If your fans are the problem rather than the heat, PC fans loud while gaming is the better read. Next, look up your card's maximum on the maker's spec page, then play your usual game for half an hour and note where the temperature levels off. If it's well under the maximum, you can stop worrying. If it's close, start with the dust. How RigSight checks your GPU temperature After that false alarm, every temperature comparison in RigSight became like for like. The full story is in The day RigSight told me my healthy fan was clogged . Here is what it does now for your GPU. RigSight is a free, open-source PC monitor for Windows that records your temperatures all day and keeps them as history. Its Temperatures page shows the GPU's temperature with its lowest and highest of the day under it, plus the hot spot and memory junction readings when the card reports them. Below that, the history graph covers any range from the last 5 minutes to the last 12 months, or a Custom range, and can show each minute's average, highest or lowest reading. So you can see the exact peak of last night's session, not only how warm the card is now. The part that answers "is this normal?" is that RigSight compares your card with itself. For a week, a month or a custom range, Reports has an Against your usual table. It takes the game you played most and sets its GPU temperature against your own usual in that game from the weeks before, at the same power, with the room taken out. If a game now runs hotter than usual, the PC health card on Home says so in one line. That answers the question better than any chart of other people's cards. If you'd rather be told than check, Settings has Notifications > Temperature alerts . The GPU limit starts at 83° and can be set from 60 to 100°. When the GPU stays over it for a few seconds, the alert names the app that was running. More on GPU temperatures GPU hot spot temperature , the warmest point on the chip and the gap to the main reading. VRAM temperature while gaming , the memory around the GPU. GPU thermal throttling , when a hot card slows itself. GPU fan not spinning , and when that's normal. Normal CPU and GPU temperature at idle . How to check GPU temperature history . PC overheating while gaming, or just warm . Is 85 degrees hot for a GPU while gaming? It's warm, but it's inside the limit for most current cards. NVIDIA lists a maximum of 90°C for the RTX 4070 and 4090 and 93°C for the RTX 3060 and 3080, though the RTX 5070 is listed at 85°C. If your card sits at 85°C, check its own maximum, then look at dust, airflow and the fan curve. What is the average GPU temp while gaming? There is no single average that fits every card. Most desktop cards with a clean cooler settle somewhere in the 60s or 70s °C in a demanding game. Small cases, hot rooms and laptops run warmer. Is 68 degrees hot for a GPU while gaming? No. 68°C sits inside the 60 to 80°C a desktop card usually reaches in a demanding game, and well under the maximum NVIDIA lists for its recent cards, 85°C or more. It's the kind of reading a big card with a good cooler often shows. What is a normal GPU temperature while gaming on a laptop? Laptops run hotter than desktops because the cooler is small and shared with the CPU. Readings in the high 70s and 80s °C are common on gaming laptops. The laptop maker sets the limits, so their support page is the place to check. What is normal GPU temperature while gaming in Fahrenheit? 60 to 80°C is 140 to 176°F. 85°C is 185°F, and the 90°C limit on many NVIDIA cards is 194°F. When should I worry about GPU temp? Worry when the card reaches its listed maximum and the frame rate drops, when temperatures climb over weeks in the same game, or when the hot spot runs far above the main reading. A one-off warm day in summer is usually the room.

t: Why GPU hotspot temperature runs high, and when the gap is bad
d: Why the GPU hotspot temperature always reads higher than the GPU, what gap is normal, when 100°C is a problem, and how RigSight watches the gap for you over weeks of play.
l: PC problems Temperatures gpu hotspot temperature gpu hotspot temperature vs gpu temp gpu hotspot temperature 100c gpu hotspot temperature range gpu hotspot temperature 110c is 85 degrees hot for gpu hotspot gpu hotspot temperature msi afterburner
b: Your monitoring app shows two GPU temperatures. One says 72°C and the other, labelled hot spot, says 94°C. The GPU hotspot temperature always reads higher, and that's by design. What tells you whether something is wrong is how far apart the two are, and whether that gap has grown. A gap that grows does it slowly, over weeks, which is exactly what nobody notices by glancing at a number. Why the GPU hotspot runs hotter A modern graphics chip has many temperature sensors spread across it. AMD explained this in 2019 for its RX 5700 cards. An array of sensors is spread across the chip, and the highest reading from any of them is the hotspot, which AMD also calls the junction temperature. The ordinary GPU temperature is a single, general reading for the chip. On AMD cards some apps call it the edge temperature. Some parts of the chip always work harder than others, so one spot is always warmer than the general reading. That warmest spot is the hotspot. GPU hotspot temperature vs GPU temp, and the normal gap Under load, the hotspot usually runs about 10 to 20°C above the GPU temperature. Some high-power cards sit a little past that and are still fine. This range is a rule of thumb from people who build and repair PCs. Neither NVIDIA nor AMD publishes an official figure for the gap. A gap of 10 to 20°C under load is common. A gap of 20 to 25°C can be normal on big, power-hungry cards. A gap past about 30°C often means the cooler isn't pressing evenly on the chip, or the thermal paste has dried out or spread unevenly. Two things make the gap meaningful. Compare at steady load, a few minutes into a game, because at idle both readings are low and close. And compare like for like, with the same game on the same card, before and after. A gap that was 15°C a year ago and is 30°C now tells you far more than one reading against a forum post. What the makers say about a GPU hotspot temperature of 100°C, 105°C or 110°C AMD has been clear about its own cards. In 2019 it said a junction temperature of up to 110°C during typical gaming on the RX 5700 series was "expected and within spec". AMD said the card keeps raising its clocks until any one sensor reaches 110°C. The RX 7900 XTX shows why the gap matters. After it launched, some owners of AMD's own reference cards saw the hotspot reach 110°C while the main temperature stayed much lower, and the cards slowed down. At the start of 2023 AMD said the problem was related to the thermal solution on a limited number of its reference cards, and asked affected owners to contact AMD Support. A hotspot at its limit with a normal main reading was the sign. NVIDIA publishes one figure per card, the "Maximum GPU Temperature", for example 90°C for the RTX 4070 family. It doesn't publish a separate hotspot limit. On a GeForce card, a hotspot of 100°C with the main reading in the high 80s is a normal spread on a hot card. A hotspot past 100°C with the main reading in the 60s or 70s is a big gap and worth looking into. Tom's Hardware reported an RTX 5070 Ti throttling with its hotspot at 107°C, which a repair technician traced to badly applied thermal paste. Why your card might not show a hotspot Not every card reports one, and not every app reads it. When the RTX 50 series launched in early 2025, NVIDIA stopped giving the hotspot reading to common monitoring tools, so apps such as HWiNFO and GPU-Z showed only the main temperature. The sensor was still on the chip. In 2026 HWMonitor, HWiNFO and GPU-Z 2.71.0 started to read the RTX 50 hotspot again, so update your app if it shows none. Older GeForce cards like the RTX 30 and 40 series show it, and AMD lists the hotspot for the Radeon VII, the RX 5000 series and newer. How to check your GPU hotspot temperature Task Manager shows only the main GPU temperature, so you need a sensor app. In GPU-Z, open the Sensors tab and look for Hot Spot . In HWiNFO, start it in Sensors-only mode and find GPU Hot Spot Temperature under your GPU. In MSI Afterburner, open Settings > Monitoring and see whether a hotspot entry is in the list for your card. On some cards it has a plain name such as GPU temperature 2. If there's no second GPU temperature, your card or version doesn't report it there, and HWiNFO or GPU-Z is the better choice. Play for 10 minutes or so, then note both readings at the same moment. That pair is your gap. What to do if the gap is too big Clean the card first. Dust in the cooler raises both readings, and a clean cooler gives you a fair baseline. Check the warranty before you open anything. If the card is still covered and the gap is past 30°C on a fairly new card, contact the card maker. Taking the cooler off can void the warranty on some brands. If the card is out of warranty and you're comfortable doing it, new thermal paste and, where the card has them, new thermal pads usually bring a large gap back down. Tighten the cooler screws evenly, a little at a time in a cross pattern. After any change, play the same game for the same time and compare the gap with what you saw before. If only the main GPU temperature is high and the gap is normal, the chip and cooler are in good contact, and the heat is a matter of airflow, dust or settings. Normal GPU temperature while gaming covers that side, and PC overheating while gaming has the full list of fixes. Next, write down your gap after 10 minutes in your usual game. If it's under 20°C, leave it alone. If it's past 30°C, clean the card, check the warranty and plan the repaste or the return. How RigSight spots a bad hotspot gap Here is what it looks like on the demo PC in RigSight's own pictures, an RTX 3080 Ti. The GPU reads 68° and its hot spot 78°, a 10° gap, which is healthy. RigSight keeps that gap as history, so a gap that creeps up shows in the history. RigSight is a free, open-source PC monitor for Windows that records your temperatures all day and keeps them as history. When your card reports a hotspot, the GPU card on the Temperatures page shows it as its own tile, next to the memory junction, with today's lowest and highest under it. The history graph draws GPU hot spot as a line beside the main GPU line, so you can see the gap across a whole evening of play. RigSight also watches the gap for you. When the hotspot runs 30° or more above the core over 20 minutes or more of steady heavy load, Reports says so and adds that the thermal paste or cooler contact may have worn. Reports' Peaks list includes the day's highest GPU hot spot reading and the app that was running. For a warning while you play, Settings has Notifications > Temperature alerts with a GPU hot spot limit. It starts at 100° and can be set from 70 to 110°, so a Radeon owner can set it just under AMD's 110°C. What is the difference between GPU hotspot temperature and GPU temp? The GPU temp is one general reading for the chip. The hotspot is the highest reading from a whole grid of sensors across the chip, so it's always the warmer of the two. What matters most is the gap between them, not the hotspot on its own. Is a GPU hotspot temperature of 100°C bad? On an AMD Radeon card, 100°C is below the 110°C AMD calls within spec. On any card, look at the gap. A hotspot of 100°C with the GPU temp at 85°C is a normal spread, while 100°C with the GPU temp at 65°C points to poor contact between the cooler and the chip. Is 85 degrees hot for a GPU hotspot? No. A hotspot of 85°C is an ordinary reading in a demanding game. It usually means the main GPU temperature is somewhere in the 60s or low 70s. What is a normal GPU hotspot temperature range? In games, hotspots in the 80s and 90s °C are common, and Radeon cards can go higher while staying within AMD's spec. The gap to the main GPU temperature tells you more. As a rule of thumb from builders, not a maker's spec, about 10 to 20°C is common, and past about 30°C deserves a closer look. Why can't I see the hotspot on my RTX 50 series card? When the RTX 50 series launched in early 2025, NVIDIA stopped handing the hotspot reading to common monitoring tools, so most apps showed only the main GPU temperature. In 2026 HWMonitor, HWiNFO and GPU-Z 2.71.0 added it back. If your app shows no hotspot, update it.

t: FPS drops in games and how to catch what causes them
d: FPS drops in games come from heat, background apps, power settings, drivers, a full graphics memory or a frame cap. How RigSight records every play so you can see which one, and how to fix it.
l: PC problems FPS and games fps drops in games fps drops in games all of a sudden fps drop in games after windows update why my fps drops in games fps drops in games windows 11 fps drops in game while streaming
b: A commenter told me their Windows power plan kept switching from High performance to Balanced on its own, and they couldn't tell when it happened. That is the trouble with FPS drops in games. The cause usually changes quietly, before you start looking. It can be a power plan, a driver, a Windows update, a background download or a warm room. By the time the game feels slow, the moment that caused it is gone. Why FPS drops in games happen FPS drops in games feel random, but they almost never are. Something takes a share of the PC away from the game. It may be heat, another app, a power setting, a driver, or settings that ask for more graphics memory than your card has. The fix depends on which one it is, so the first job is to measure, not to tweak. How to find the cause yourself by measuring first Turn on an FPS counter that also shows GPU load and GPU temperature. Steam, the NVIDIA app, AMD Software and Xbox Game Bar all have one. The steps for each are in how to show an FPS overlay . Then play the way you normally do for 20 minutes and watch the numbers when the drop comes. The pattern tells you where to look. FPS is fine at first and gets worse after 10 or 20 minutes. That is usually heat. The GPU or CPU warms up and slows itself down. FPS dips in busy scenes while GPU load is well under 95%. Something other than the GPU sets the pace, usually the CPU. See GPU not at 100% usage but low FPS . FPS sits on a flat line, such as exactly 60 or 30. That is a cap, often VSync. See VSync and FPS caps. FPS dropped all of a sudden, from one day to the next. Something changed that day. Start with updates and drivers below. The average looks fine but the game hitches. Watch the 1% low, not the average. See what 1% low FPS means . Check for heat throttling GPUs and processors protect themselves. When they reach their temperature limit, they lower their clock speed, and you lose frames. The limit depends on the model, so look up your card or CPU on the maker's site. A drop that comes back every session after the same amount of play is the classic sign. Watch the GPU temperature, the GPU hot spot if your card reports one, and the GPU clock speed together. If the clock falls as the temperature reaches its peak, heat is the cause. Clean the dust out of the case and the card, make sure the case fans pull air through, and give a laptop a hard flat surface. Normal GPU temperature while gaming has the numbers, and PC overheating while gaming has the fixes. Close what runs in the background A browser playing video, a launcher downloading an update, a cloud backup or an antivirus scan can each take CPU time and disk time from the game. Task Manager finds them. Press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager. On Processes , click the CPU column to sort by it, then do the same with Disk and GPU . Close anything heavy you don't need while you play. Pause downloads in other launchers. Several overlays at once can also cost frames and cause conflicts. Keep one FPS counter, not three. If you stream, your streaming app should use the hardware encoder on your GPU, which costs far less than encoding on the CPU. Set Windows to its best performance mode Windows can run your PC in a power saving mode, and some apps switch it without telling you. On a laptop, the battery makes this worse. Open Settings > System > Power & battery . On Windows 10, select the battery icon on the taskbar and move the slider instead. Under Power mode , pick Best performance . On a laptop, set it for when it is plugged in. Play on a laptop with the charger connected. Most laptops lower the GPU's power on battery. Microsoft notes that if you can't change the power mode, a custom power plan may be active, and picking Balanced in Control Panel > Power Options brings the slider back. If your plan keeps changing by itself, see power plan keeps changing. While you're in Settings, check that Settings > Gaming > Game Mode is on. It is on by default, and Microsoft says it holds off driver installs and restart prompts while you play. FPS drop in games after a Windows update or a driver If your FPS dropped from one day to the next, find what changed that day. Open Settings > Windows Update > Update history and look at the dates. A Windows update can bring its own graphics driver, reset a setting, or arrive at the same time as a game patch. Install the newest graphics driver straight from NVIDIA, AMD or Intel, even if Windows already installed one. If the drop started right after a new graphics driver, go back one version. In Device Manager > Display adapters , right-click your card, pick Properties , open the Driver tab and press Roll Back Driver . Or download the previous version from the maker's site.
