The first few minutes after a new driver or a game patch can stutter while the game builds its shaders again. Give it one full session before you judge. Remove a Windows update only as the last step. Go to Settings > Windows Update > Update history > Uninstall updates . Microsoft warns that removing a security update carries risks, so put it back once a fixed version is out. If the game also started crashing after the driver, games crashing after a driver update covers a clean driver reinstall. Check graphics memory When a game needs more graphics memory than your card has, it has to keep part of its data in system memory and swap it in, and you get sharp dips and hitches, often when you turn around or enter a new area. Show video memory in your overlay. If it sits at the card's full size, lower Texture quality first, then resolution scale or ray tracing. Texture settings are the biggest user of graphics memory in most games. Rule out a frame cap A drop to exactly 60, 30 or half your refresh rate isn't a drop in power. It is a limit. VSync, an in-game limiter, NVIDIA's Max Frame Rate , AMD's Frame Rate Target Control or Radeon Chill can all hold the frame rate down. NVIDIA also has a Background Application Max Frame Rate that applies when the game isn't the window in front. Check the game's display menu and your graphics driver's settings for any of these. What the readings mean GPU load at 95 to 100% means the GPU is the limit. Lower graphics settings give more frames. GPU load well under 95% with no cap means the CPU or the game engine is the limit. Graphics settings won't help much. A GPU clock that falls while the temperature climbs means heat throttling. Video memory at the card's full size means the settings ask for too much memory. A big gap between average FPS and 1% low means the game hitches even when the average looks fine. Start with the pattern. Play one normal session with a counter on, note when the frames fall and what the GPU load and temperature were at that moment, and work through the matching section of this post. How RigSight catches an FPS drop The power plan now has its own line on RigSight's Timeline. Every switch is listed with the day and time and what the plan was before, next to every driver, Windows update and setting change. So a drop that started on Thursday can be laid next to whatever changed on Thursday. RigSight is free and open source, and it records each play of each game on its Games page, so you can look back at a drop after it happened. A game's page shows How it runs, a chart of the average FPS and the 1% low of every play, with a mark wherever a graphics driver or a game update came between two plays. Since the last update compares the frame rate of the plays before and after the game's last update. The frame rate comes from RivaTuner Statistics Server, which has to be running before the game starts. The Games page has a button to install or start it. Under it, Every play lists each session with its FPS and 1% low, and puts Windows updates, graphics drivers, BIOS updates, hardware changes and game updates between the plays where they happened. If the numbers fell right after one of them, you know where to start. The Heat and power card shows the GPU and CPU temperature while playing against what is usual for this game, the hot spot peak, and how much graphics memory the game used, its own share where Windows reports it. The CPU temperature needs RigSight to run with admin rights. The Timeline lists every driver, Windows update and setting change by day, including the power plan. While you play, RigSight's overlay can show frame rate, GPU load, temperatures and video memory, inside exclusive fullscreen games too through RivaTuner. Why does my FPS drop in games all of a sudden? Look at what changed that day first, such as a Windows update, a new graphics driver, a game patch or a power setting. If nothing changed, check temperatures and background apps, since a hot GPU or an app updating itself can pull frames away mid game. Can a Windows update cause FPS drops in games? Yes, sometimes. An update can replace your graphics driver, reset a power setting or turn a setting back on. Check Settings > Windows Update > Update history for the date, reinstall your graphics driver from NVIDIA, AMD or Intel, and only remove the update if that doesn't help. Why my FPS drops in games when the PC is new or fast? Fast parts still slow down when they get too hot, when Windows runs them in a power saving mode or when a frame cap holds them back. A laptop on battery also runs slower than on the charger. Check power mode and temperatures before blaming the hardware. Why does FPS drop in game while streaming? Streaming adds a video encoder and often a browser or chat app on top of the game. Use the hardware encoder on your GPU in your streaming app, lower the stream resolution, and close anything else that plays video.

t: Testing an AI on PCs that don't exist
d: To check the helper's advice on games, I built pretend PCs with known problems. Most of what went wrong wasn't the AI. It was what I was feeding it.
l: The AI journey
b: "How do I make this game run better?" is probably the question people will ask the helper most. It's also a hard one to answer well. The right advice depends on the game, the GPU, the resolution, the game's own settings, and what is actually holding the frame rate back. So the helper needed two new things. It needed to know how each game is set up, and I needed a way to check its advice that didn't depend on me playing every game on every kind of PC. Reading how a game is set Games keep their settings in files, and every engine does it differently. Unreal games keep an INI file in one place, Unity games in the registry or next to the game, others in Documents, Saved Games or a Steam folder, in INI, JSON, XML or Valve's own format. RigSight now finds and reads these for the things that matter, like resolution, display mode, VSync, frame limit, quality, upscaling, frame generation and ray tracing. It also reads what Windows adds, like which GPU the game is set to use, Game Mode and the screen's refresh rate. On my own PC it read the settings for 16 of my 17 games. Five PCs with a known problem each RigSight already had a pretend PC for testing its insights, one that simulates temperatures, fans and loads over months. I extended it with games, adding frame rates minute by minute, stutters, drive activity, video memory and the game's settings file. Then I built five scenarios where I know the right answer. Cyberpunk 2077 with path tracing on, where the GPU is simply at its limit. Dota 2 capped by VSync, where the frame rate is flat because it's being held back on purpose. Hades stuttering because OneDrive was syncing on the same drive. Cyberpunk 2077 running out of video memory. Dota 2 without RivaTuner, so there's no frame rate data at all. Each scenario has checks. In the VSync case, the answer has to name VSync as the cap, early. In the no-RivaTuner case, it has to say there's no frame data and how to get it, instead of inventing advice. The answers get written to a file I read in full too, because a check can pass on an answer that's still badly put. The bugs were mostly mine Looking into why answers went wrong, most of the time the AI had done a reasonable job with what it was given. What it was given was wrong. A 30 fps limit that wasn't there. Cyberpunk writes its frame limit as a number plus a separate on or off switch. RigSight read the number and ignored the switch, so a limit that was turned off came through as "frame rate limited to 30". That came from my own real settings file, not the pretend one. Any advice built on that would have been nonsense. VSync that went unread. One game stores VSync with a long label ending in "Off". RigSight didn't recognise it, so the AI was told nothing about VSync at all. Path tracing, filtered out for privacy. This one I liked. Before anything is sent, a filter strips out settings that could contain folder paths, so your user name never leaves the PC. It matched the word "path". Cyberpunk's setting for path tracing has "path" in its name, so the filter threw it away. The AI couldn't mention path tracing because it never knew it was on. All three were fixed in RigSight itself, not in the AI's instructions. Then the instructions The rest were real gaps in how the helper approached games, so its instructions for this kind of question got a new version. Look up a guide for this game, this GPU and this resolution before giving settings. Mention path tracing when it's on, because it's usually the biggest cost. When the 1% lows or stutters are the problem, find their cause before talking about average frame rate. Say what RivaTuner adds when it's missing. Name a VSync cap first when the frame rate is flat. The run with the new version didn't finish. My PC ran low on memory partway through. The Cyberpunk answers that did come back were all good. One Dota answer forgot to name VSync, so I changed that wording, and the whole run still has to go again. What's next Pretend PCs are good at checking known problems. They can't tell me how the helper does with the mess of a real PC. So the next step is the same kind of test on a copy of my real history, with questions whose answers I already know from my own games. The thing I keep relearning with this helper is that it can only be as right as what it's given. A lot of making the AI good turns out to be making RigSight's own readings right.

t: Picking an AI model blind, and not picking my favourite
d: Six AI models answered the same questions about my PC, hidden behind letters A to F. Gemini 3.8 Flash won my vote. Claude Haiku 5.5 got the job.
l: The AI journey
b: Picking the AI model for RigSight AI sounds like a quick decision. Look at a leaderboard, take the top one. But leaderboards test general knowledge and coding. I needed something narrower, a model that reads look-ups about one PC and explains them to a person who just had a game crash. The only way to know was to try it on exactly that. Six models, six letters On 21 October I picked six models from different companies, from very cheap to expensive, and gave them all the same setup. They had the same instructions, the same look-ups into my PC's real records, the same questions. Things like why a game crashed, whether my GPU runs hotter than it used to, where my time went last week. Then I hid the names. Each model became a letter, A to F, and the answers went on one page side by side. I read them and voted for the best answer to each question without knowing who wrote it. If I knew which company made which answer, I'd have had opinions before reading a word. F was clearly my favourite. Its answers were warm, well organised and easy to read. I only looked up who was behind each letter after voting. A was Qwen3.8 Flash B was DeepSeek V4.1 Flash C was GPT-5.6 Luna D was Claude Sonnet 5.5 E was Claude Haiku 5.5 F was Gemini 3.8 Flash Cost per question The price per question varied a lot, because it depends on the model and on how much it reads. The most expensive model in the test, Claude Sonnet 5.5, cost about 7.3 cents for one question. Gemini 3.8 Flash cost about 1.5 cents. Claude Haiku 5.5 cost about 0.4 cents. That matters because the helper looks things up. A good answer can involve several look-ups and a fair amount of reading, so the cost of each question adds up quickly. The most expensive model was out on price alone, whatever its answers were like. Then I tightened the rules Reading dozens of answers side by side showed me patterns I didn't like in all of them, so I wrote stricter rules for how every answer must be put together. Say "likely" for a likely cause, and only call something certain when the records prove it. Check counts before saying them. "Three crashes" has to be three. No describing words the data can't back up. If it says "much hotter", the numbers have to show it. Facts from the web that change over time get a note on where to check them. I also decided the helper speaks as RigSight. It says "we found", never "RigSight found", and when it uses something from the web it blends it into the answer instead of labelling it. Then I ran the test again. Gemini 3.8 Flash, my favourite, followed the new rules only partly, and it got slower. Some answers took 43 seconds. Claude Haiku 5.5, the cheapest of the good ones, followed them closely. Choosing the one that follows the rules So Claude Haiku 5.5 got the job. Not because I liked its writing more. I didn't, at first. But in RigSight, following the rules matters more than the writing. An answer that's a little plainer but never claims more than the records show is worth more to someone with a crashing PC than a beautiful answer that guesses. And 43 seconds is a long time to wait for an answer about your own PC. A bug that looked like the model's fault One more thing from that week. With Haiku, some answers came back completely empty. No error, just nothing. The model thinks before it writes, and that thinking counts toward the length limit for an answer. I had set the limit at a size that's plenty for the answer itself. On harder questions, the thinking used it all up, and the answer was cut off before its first word. Raising the limit well above what an answer needs fixed it. It's a good reminder that when an AI gives a strange result, the first place to look is often the code around it, not the model. The next post is all about that.

t: Three ways to ask, including one that never leaves your PC
d: The helper can run on your own PC, on your own AI account, or through RigSight. Why there are three, and what each one sends.
l: The AI journey
b: When I removed Riggy, the reason was simple. A real AI meant either a big download to run it on your PC, or your PC's records going to a server. In October those still looked like the only two choices. So rather than pick one for everyone, the new helper lets you pick. The first way runs locally on your own PC The first way I built, starting on 20 October, runs the AI on your own PC with Ollama, a free app for running AI models locally. RigSight talks to it on your PC, and nothing leaves the machine. You need no account or key, and nobody else is involved. There's a cost, and I'd rather be clear about it. A model good enough to reason about your PC needs a decent GPU, takes a while to load the first time, and is slower than the big services. RigSight shows what it's doing while you wait, such as which of your records it's reading, with a thinking word in between. Each answer says which model wrote it, so you always know what you're reading. I built this way first on purpose. If the helper only worked by sending your data somewhere, it would have been a step back from everything RigSight said about privacy. The second way uses your own key The second way is for people who already pay for an AI service. Paste your key from the provider you use, pick a model from a list you can search, and RigSight asks that model directly. Only the look-up results the model asks for are sent, the same as always, and only to the provider you chose. For both of these, you can edit the instructions the AI follows. Maybe you want shorter answers, or more detail, or answers in a different tone. Your edits stay on your PC. RigSight's own rules are added after yours, so a change in tone can't switch off the rules about only using your real records and saying when something isn't shared. I tested that by telling it to talk like a pirate. It did, every sentence. And it still used the look-ups, still pointed to the records it read, and still ended with a next step. The third way is RigSight AI The third way is for people who just want it to work, without installing a model or signing up anywhere. Questions go through a small service I run, which passes them to the AI model and streams the answer back. This is the one that needed the most rules, because it's the one where I'm in the middle. It has these rules. The app never contacts it until you've chosen RigSight AI and asked a question. No check-in at start-up. Your IP address is never stored, not even scrambled. There's no usage tracking of what you do in the app. When I wrote this, how it would be paid for was still being worked out. It launched in version 1.0.0 with a free trial and paid plans. Where your look-up results go with each way of asking. In all three, your full history stays on your PC. Before the first question Whichever way you pick, the first question you ask shows a short window first. It says, for that way, what gets sent and where, with a link to the switches. You read it once, and then you ask. Your conversations are kept on your PC, so you can come back to them. You can pin them, rename them, archive them or delete them. Three ways is more to explain than one. But each one exists because a real person would want it, and the one where nothing leaves your PC is the reason I felt alright bringing AI back at all.

t: Putting RigSight into Spanish, all 3,097 lines of it
d: People asked for Spanish. Translating the words was the easy part. Sentences built from English pieces, and a history stored in English, were the hard part.
l: Building RigSight
b: On 19 October people asked for RigSight in Spanish. It was a fair ask. A lot of PC gamers don't use English as their first language, and a monitor full of half-understood warnings isn't much use. I thought it would take a day. It did take a day, but a very long one, and almost none of the time went into the actual translating. A pack, not a bigger installer The first choice was how Spanish should arrive. I didn't want every user downloading every language forever. So English is built in, and other languages are packs. You pick Spanish in Settings, RigSight downloads that one file, and from then on it comes along with each update. I also chose not to follow Windows' display language. Plenty of people run Windows in English and would rather read RigSight in Spanish, or the other way round. It's your pick, in Settings. Finding every word Before anything could be translated, every piece of text in the app had to go through one place that knows about languages. Page titles, buttons, tooltips, notifications, the tray menu, the overlay, chart labels, crash findings, exported spreadsheets. It came to 3,097 texts. Then a check that fails the release if any of them is missing a translation. That one matters more than it sounds. If I reword an English sentence later, its Spanish version no longer matches, and without the check that line would quietly turn back into English for Spanish users. Sentences glued from pieces The real work was sentences. In English it's tempting to build a sentence from parts, like an app's name, then "crashed", then "in", then a cause. That works in English. In Spanish the parts change shape, need an article, or go in a different order. An example of the problem. Glued pieces can't follow another language's grammar. A whole sentence with a gap for the name can. So every sentence like that was rewritten as one whole sentence with gaps for the names and numbers. Sometimes Spanish needed more than one sentence where English had one. One day and many days each got their own, and so did a time and a day. A culprit that needs "el" or "la" did too. Dates got their own care too, so 19 October reads "19 de octubre". Numbers and dates still follow your Windows region, whatever the language. A history that was stored in English The trickiest question was the history. RigSight saves lines like change titles and crash causes when they happen. Months of them were already stored, in English. I could have saved new lines in the language in use. But then switching languages would leave your history half in one and half in the other. So history keeps one fixed form, and every saved line is translated when it's shown. Old lines included. Switch to Spanish today, and your crash from September reads in Spanish too. What happens when the download fails One last rule, because downloads fail. If this version's Spanish pack can't be fetched, RigSight uses the newest earlier pack. A few new words might show in English for a while, and nothing crashes. And a working pack is never replaced by an older one. The translation itself was checked against one glossary, so a word like "crash" or "1% low" means the same thing on every page. Then a fluency pass on the whole app, page by page, because a correct sentence can still sound like a machine wrote it.

t: Bringing AI back, with rules this time
d: Nine days after removing Riggy, I started on a real AI helper. Before writing any of it, I wrote down what it would never be allowed to do.
l: The AI journey
b: Riggy taught me what didn't work. A helper with answers written ahead of time is only filling in a form. If RigSight was going to answer questions, it needed a real AI, one that can read your records and say something it wasn't told to say. On 17 October I started planning one. Here is the idea, in the words I wrote down that day. A helper which understands the system better than the user, to tell them easily what the issue is, or that it lacks the information to say. That last part is the important bit. Three kinds of answer Every answer from the helper is meant to be one of three things. Here's the problem. One plain sentence, then why, then what to do about it. This is normal for your PC. Because a lot of worry is about things that are fine. I can't tell, and here's what I'd need. For example, start RivaTuner before the game and ask again, so there's frame data to look at. The third kind is the one I care about most. An AI that always has an answer will sometimes make one up. I would much rather it said "I don't have enough to go on" and told you how to get it. It explains, you decide The helper never changes anything on your PC by itself. It can tell you what's likely wrong and what to try, and show you the chart or the crash it's talking about. Some answers come with a button, like opening the right Windows settings screen, scanning a drive or closing an app that's stuck. Nothing happens until you press it. A tool that reads your crash history shouldn't be able to uninstall your graphics driver because it thinks that's a good idea. What leaves your PC This was the reason Riggy went. A real AI means either a big download or your data going to a server. So the design starts from the question of what gets sent. The AI model doesn't get your history. It gets a set of look-ups it can ask for, like this crash, temperatures for that day, what changed last week, how this game ran. The app runs each look-up on your PC and sends back only its result. Your Windows user name is never sent. Neither are the names of your own files. There is one place where folder names do go. If you ask what's filling up a drive, the AI gets that drive's biggest folders, so it can tell a Steam library from a Downloads folder. Even then, your own user folder is sent as "your user folder", and the files inside are described only by their kind and size. The model can ask for a look-up. The app answers it on your PC, and only that answer leaves. Every page of RigSight the AI can look at has its own switch in Settings, for Crashes, Temperatures, Games, Storage and the rest. Switch off Storage and no drive or folder is ever sent. If you turn one off and then ask about it, the AI is told it isn't shared, and it tells you which switch to turn on. Under each answer, a short line shows which of your records it looked at, and each one opens the page it came from. Off means gone Two more rules came from watching how other apps handled AI. Turning the helper off hides every Ask and Explain button in the app. They disappear completely. People get rightly annoyed by AI buttons they can't remove. And RigSight doesn't contact the AI service at all until you choose it and ask a question. Opening Settings doesn't count. Starting the app doesn't count. Nothing checks in by itself. Where it shows up You can ask from a small window that floats over any page. But the place I think it'll help most is next to problems RigSight already shows. An opened crash has an "Explain this crash" button, so you get the helper's take on that exact crash, with everything RigSight recorded around it. It's also meant to talk like a friend who knows PCs. Someone who just had a game crash will type "why did this crash?", not a carefully worded question. A casual question gets a casual answer, and numbers only show up when they help. The helper is being tested now. I'm not giving it a date. When it's ready, the privacy page will say exactly what it sends before anyone can use it. The next posts are about how it's being built, covering where the answers come from , picking the model and testing it on PCs that don't exist .

t: Teaching crashes to say how sure they are
d: Every crash now says what most likely caused it and how sure that is. Getting there meant one big feature, and cutting most of the next one.
l: Building RigSight
b: When a game crashes, you want to know why. Windows does keep a record, but it reads like faulting module nvwgf2umx.dll , exception code 0xc0000005. If you know that file belongs to the NVIDIA driver, it's a clue. If you don't, it's noise. For its first three weeks, RigSight's Crashes page did roughly what everyone does. It showed Windows' entry and guessed a culprit from the file name. That's better than nothing. It's also often wrong, and it never told you how much to trust the guess. An answer with a confidence word Version 0.24.0, on 14 October, gave every crash a finding. Each one has a headline, what to try, what points to the cause, what it wasn't, and what's still unknown. And it has one of four words for how sure it is. Confirmed , when Windows' own record says what happened Likely , when the evidence points one way Possibly , when it fits but other causes fit too Not enough to say , when RigSight honestly doesn't know That last one matters as much as the first. A tool that always has an answer is a tool that's sometimes making one up. What a finding is built from A finding looks at more than Windows' crash entry. It reads the rest of what Windows wrote, like versions, how long the app had been running, what a frozen app was waiting on, hardware errors at the next start. Then it adds what only RigSight has, the minutes before the crash. Was the GPU hot? Was memory nearly full? Was anyone even at the PC? Did a driver or Windows update arrive in the week before? The "what it wasn't" list is the part I'm proudest of. "It wasn't overheating, the GPU was at 67°." "Memory wasn't full." "Nothing new was installed." Ruling things out calms people down, and it stops them from replacing parts that were fine. There is one more rule. Everything that talks about crashes reads the same engine. Home, Reports, the notifications and the Crashes page can't disagree, because none of them makes up its own story. The feature I almost over-built The next step on my roadmap was a close-up of the moments around a crash, second by second. My first plan for it was big. A recording mode you could switch on. Recordings you could start, stop and read. A settings card. Labels on every row. I looked at the plan and had a feeling I couldn't explain at first. We are over-complicating this, and nobody will use it. When I thought it through, the reason was clear. People open a crash for an answer. Version 0.24.0 already gave them one. The plan piled expert tools on top that asked people to do work and handed them raw data. So I cut it down to the parts that help without asking anything of you. Every opened crash shows the 10 minutes after it too, even for old crashes. App crashes get a close-up. RigSight keeps the last few minutes in memory and saves them the moment something crashes. Graphics driver resets, the black screen that comes back after a few seconds, became their own kind of problem. Even the confidence word changed. My first name for the top level was "Named by Windows". It was accurate, but it read oddly and nobody could tell what it meant. It became "Confirmed", and hovering it says that Windows' own record says so. That release went out on 15 October, and it was much smaller than the plan. I think it's much better for it.

t: Making RigSight work without admin rights
d: On a standard Windows account RigSight asked for an admin password at every start and recorded nothing without one. Here's how it learned to do what it can, and say what it can't.
l: Building RigSight
b: Some of what RigSight reads is locked away by Windows. The CPU's temperature, the motherboard's fans and voltages, drive health and each app's internet use are only available to programs running with admin rights. So from the start, RigSight's recorder ran as admin. On my PC, and on most gaming PCs, that's fine. You are the admin. But plenty of PCs aren't set up like that. A family PC where the kids have standard accounts. A work laptop. A shared machine where only one person knows the admin password. On those, RigSight behaved badly. At every start it asked for an admin's password. If nobody typed it, it recorded nothing at all. Do what you can without admin rights Version 0.23.0 makes the recorder look at the account it's running in first. It can be an admin, an admin that hasn't been given admin rights yet, or a standard account. On a standard account it now runs without admin rights and never asks for them. Then it records everything Windows does allow. That's more than I expected. CPU load, which Home uses for "CPU busiest" instead of the CPU temperature GPU temperatures and fans Space on every drive The whole PC's internet use, from the network cards' own counters Apps, time on the PC, games and crashes Say what you can't The part I cared about most was the missing readings. The easy thing would have been to store zeros. That would have been a lie that looks like data. A CPU at 0° isn't a cool CPU, it's a reading that never happened, and a chart of zeros would sit in your history forever looking real. So those readings are switched off and labelled as off. A "Standard account" card explains it once, and an "Admin rights" tab in Settings lists what's missing and why. No false zeros are stored, ever. Before A password prompt at every start. Without it, no history at all. Now Starts quietly, records what Windows allows, and names what it can't read. One PC, several people Running on standard accounts raised a question I hadn't thought about. Whose history is it? The answer is simple. Each person's history and settings stay in their own Windows profile, even when an admin's password was used to install it. If two people are signed in at once, each gets their own recorder. For whoever looks after the PC, setup has two new boxes on PCs with more than one account. One installs it for everyone, and the other keeps it updated for everyone. The updater only runs when RigSight starts or when someone presses Update. It never runs on a timer in the background, and it waits while a RigSight window is open. Testing on PCs I don't own I only have one PC, and I'm the admin on it. So I tested this on throwaway Windows machines that only last 50 minutes each. I tried an ordinary admin upgrading from the old version with their history counted before and after, standard accounts, two admins, the updater and uninstalling. Then on my own PC, over the previous version. It's not the most exciting release I've made. But it's the one that let a whole group of people use RigSight at all, and it set a rule I've kept since. When RigSight can't know something, it says so in words, and the history only ever holds readings that really happened.

t: The tests said 15 milliseconds. The app froze.
d: Switching pages felt slow, but every test passed. Made-up history was too tidy to show the problem. Real history showed it at once.
l: Building RigSight
b: RigSight has a lot of tests. By late September there were about 3,160 of them, and before every release a full check builds the app, runs it as a separate test copy on a year of generated history, and measures how fast it starts, how much processor and memory it uses, and how quickly pages switch. Each number has a limit, and the release stops if one goes over. So on 8 October, when switching between pages felt laggy to me, I looked at the test results first. They said a page switch took about 15 milliseconds. That's instant. Everything passed. But the lag was real. I could feel it. Measuring the real thing So I measured the installed app, on my own history, the way I actually use it. After every switch, the window froze for a moment. How long the window froze after coming back to a page. Violet is before the fix in 0.18.1 and cyan is after. Measured on my own history. Every visit to a page rebuilt it from scratch. RigSight read the period again and replaced every row in every list with brand new rows, even when nothing had changed. On the made-up year, the lists were tidy and regular, so rebuilding them cost almost nothing. My real history was messier, with more apps, more icons and more of everything, and rebuilding it showed. The fix, and the bigger fix The fix itself was simple to describe. When you come back to a page, it keeps the rows it already has and only replaces the ones that changed. Network keeps each app's row and just gives it new figures. App icons are read in the background instead of on the window's own time. The bigger fix was to the tests. The full check now runs on a copy of my real history by default, with its own limits. The made-up year still runs too, because it covers cases my PC hasn't had yet. But it isn't the one that decides whether something feels fast. The next day, the same lesson A day later I noticed something else. When I opened RigSight from the tray, the readings and lists took seconds to show up. Measured on the installed version, the first readings arrived 0.35 to 2.7 seconds after the window connected, and the list of running apps 0.5 to 5.2 seconds after. The recorder sends readings every two seconds and the app list every five. A new window just waited for the next turn. Version 0.19.2 sends both the moment a window connects, so they now arrive in about a third of a second. While I was there, I fixed something that bothered me more. Pages that were still waiting for their data said "nothing recorded". That's a lie for a second or two, and you might believe it. Now a box that is waiting shows a small loader instead, and only says "nothing" once it really knows.

t: The driver update that knocked RigSight out
d: An NVIDIA driver update crashed RigSight's recorder ten seconds after the new driver started, and nothing brought it back.
l: Building RigSight
b: On 7 October I updated my NVIDIA driver, like you do. Ten seconds after the new driver started, RigSight's recorder crashed. It had been in the middle of asking the GPU for its temperature through NVIDIA's own library. The old driver was gone, the new one had just arrived, and the call landed on memory that wasn't there any more. That's an access violation, and it took the whole recorder down. The worse part came after. Nothing started it again. RigSight starts with Windows, so it would come back at the next restart, but until then there was simply no recording. I had to start it by hand. Why this one mattered A graphics driver update is about the most normal thing a gamer does. NVIDIA and AMD ship new drivers every few weeks. And a history app has one job, which is to be there for the moment something goes wrong. A recorder that dies during a driver install misses exactly the moments people later ask about, like "my game started crashing after I updated". So the fix in 0.17.1 has two parts. One stops the crash. The other makes sure a crash, if one ever gets through, doesn't become a silent gap. Step back while the driver changes Windows can tell a program when a GPU's driver goes away or arrives. RigSight now listens for that, only for real GPUs, so virtual screens from remote desktop tools don't set it off. When it hears a driver change, it stops reading the GPUs at once. Then it waits until things have been quiet for half a minute and restarts itself cleanly, picking up the new driver from scratch. And if it crashes anyway Windows has a way for a program to say "if I crash, start me again". RigSight's recorder now uses it. If it crashes after running for at least a minute, Windows brings it back, and its log notes that it came back after a crash. I tested both halves with a pretend driver change and with a crash I caused on purpose. In the forced crash, Windows had the recorder running again in 7 seconds. 7 s How long Windows took to bring the recorder back after a crash I caused on purpose, with the new restart in place. Telling you about it, too There was one more thing worth doing. If a game or app crashes while a graphics driver is being installed, that's almost certainly why. So the Crashes page now says so. An app that went down within two minutes of a driver install shows the driver that was being installed at that moment. The same release, from a comment One more thing went into 0.17.1 because of a commenter. Their Windows power plan kept switching from High performance to Balanced on its own, and they couldn't tell when. RigSight already followed Windows settings, so the power plan joined them. It's shown on the Timeline's "This PC now" panel with the date it was set, and every switch is its own Timeline line saying what it was before. The bigger lesson from that week was about how RigSight fails. Crashing is bad. Crashing quietly, and staying down, is much worse. Since then, every time I look at a way the recorder can fail, I ask two questions. Will it come back by itself? And will you be able to see that it was gone?

t: Three ways my temperature chart was lying
d: Peaks that moved every second, a 74° high that never showed on the line, and a gap that looked exactly like a cool PC.
l: Building RigSight
b: The temperature chart is the most looked-at thing in RigSight. It's also the one I thought was done. Then, in the first week of October, I found it was misleading people in three different ways. Peaks that moved every second A user on a laptop wrote that on the one hour view, the peaks seemed to jump around every second. A spike would be in one place, then a bit to the left, then a different height. A chart an hour wide has more readings than it has pixels, so readings get grouped. Mine grouped them by where they landed on the screen. Every second the chart slid along by a little, the groups changed, and a reading that jumped around a lot, as laptop CPU temperatures do, landed in a different group and changed the line's shape. Version 0.16.1 groups readings by the clock instead, with one point for each minute, the same minute every time. The chart still moves along, but a minute that already happened keeps the shape it had. A 74° high that the line never showed The next one was a mismatch between two numbers on the same page. A day's highest GPU temperature was 74°, but the line on the chart topped out at 68°. Both were right. The line showed each minute's average, and inside one minute the GPU had touched 74 for a few seconds. That's confusing if you're looking for the moment it got hot. So from 0.18.0 the chart has a switch for each minute's average, its highest or its lowest. Hovering a minute shows all three. I kept the average as the default because it shows the trend, and the highest is one click away when you're hunting a spike. 74° vs 68° The day's real high, and the highest point on a line of minute averages. Both were correct numbers. A gap that looked like a cool PC The third came from someone on X. They pointed out that a gap in the chart, time when RigSight recorded nothing, looked exactly the same as a PC that had stayed cool. They were right. A gap and a quiet PC looked identical. Since 0.18.0, any stretch with nothing recorded is shaded and labelled "Not recorded". Hovering it gives the times and, when Windows' own log says, the reason. The PC was off, or asleep, or it started up again. What I check now All three charts were drawn from correct numbers. Each one still told people something untrue. So now, when I change a chart, I ask three questions. Does a point keep its shape while the chart moves? Can the highest reading of the period be found on the chart? Can you tell missing time from calm time? The same goes for the pictures on this website. A spiky chart full of gaps looks broken, even when it's honest, so the pictures on the site use a stretch of time where the test PC was on the whole way through.

t: Riggy, the helper I shipped and removed two days later
d: The first try at letting you ask RigSight questions. It was clever, it was careful, and it wasn't really AI. So it went.
l: The AI journey
b: Early on, I wanted RigSight to answer questions as well as draw charts. Questions like "why did my game crash last night?" or "was I gaming more this week than last?". The data was all there. The problem was getting from a question in plain words to the right piece of it. On 5 October I built a first answer to that. On 6 October it shipped as an experiment called Riggy. On 8 October I took it out. What Riggy was Riggy was a small robot face that peeked out of the bottom right corner of the window. I drew it myself, with a chunky screen for a head, big white eyes, a little smile. Hover it and it popped out. Click it and a chat opened. Behind the face there was no chatbot. There was a 23 MB model whose only job was to read your question and decide which of about 17 topics it was about, like crashes, heat, what changed, where your time went, internet, storage, fans and so on. Rules picked out the time, the app and the part you meant. Then code put an answer together from the same reports the pages use. Riggy's insides. The model understood which kind of question it was. It never wrote a word itself. I was careful with it. It never guessed. If it wasn't sure what you meant, it asked back. It could compare two periods, like this week against last week, and it only compared heat like for like. It could follow up on "that", as in "when did that start?". If it misunderstood you, you could tell it what you meant, and it would remember that wording next time. Why it went Using it for a couple of days, the problem was obvious. Without a real AI behind it, it wasn't that useful. Every answer had been written ahead of time, for about 17 kinds of question. Ask something a little outside those and you got a polite "I'm not sure". Ask something inside them and you got an answer that felt like a form being filled in, because it was one. It could learn new ways to ask the same question. It could never learn a new kind of answer. A real AI would have meant one of two things. Either a download of around a gigabyte to run a model on your PC, or your PC's history sent to a server somewhere. At that time, RigSight's promise was that your data never leaves your PC, and I wasn't going to quietly break it for a feature that was "experimental". So the robot, the model, the chat and the settings all went. The installer dropped from 73.9 MB to 54.5 MB. Memory, Timeline and Crashes got plain search boxes instead, where every word you type has to be in the row. There's no model behind them. Saying so out loud I didn't want Riggy to just disappear in an update. The What's new card for 0.18.0 had a plain grey "Removed" card that said why. It wasn't a real AI, its answers were written ahead of time, and a real one would mean a big download or sending your history to the cloud. Removing your own feature two days after shipping it doesn't feel great. But I think it was the right call, and it taught me what a helper in RigSight would need to be. It would have to understand any question, not 17. It would have to work from your real records and show which ones it used. And it would have to say "I can't tell" when it can't. About ten days later, I started on that.

t: Bugs that make no noise
d: Internet use that silently stopped being recorded, an app 'updated' 45 minutes early, and a game 'installed' ten minutes into a 55 GB download.
l: Building RigSight
b: A crash is a gift, in a way. Something stops, you get a report, you know where to look. The bugs that worry me more are the quiet ones, where everything keeps running and the history just isn't true. Nobody gets an error. You only notice if you happen to remember what really happened that day. Here are three of them. Internet use that stopped being recorded RigSight tells you which apps used your internet and how much. To see that per app, it listens to a stream of network events that Windows can send to programs that ask for it. In early October I found that internet use could simply stop being recorded. No error, no warning. The recorder was running, the network was busy, and the stream was delivering nothing. The cause turned out to be my own testing. Test copies of RigSight open their own streams. When a test copy ended badly, its stream was left open with nobody reading it. Once a stream like that fills up, it can stop every other network stream on the PC, including the real RigSight's. Version 0.15.3 watches for exactly this. If the stream delivers nothing while the network cards are clearly busy, the recorder starts it again. It closes streams left behind by test copies. And if neither helps, the Network page says so, instead of showing you a quiet day that wasn't quiet. Discord, updated 45 minutes early The Timeline page lists what changed on your PC, like drivers, Windows updates, and apps installed and updated. One morning it said Discord had updated at 7:19. I had been using the old version until about 8:05. Discord writes its new version number into Windows' list of installed apps as soon as the update is downloaded, while the old version keeps running. RigSight believed the list. Since 0.18.0, an app's update only counts once the new version is actually the one running. 45 min How early the Timeline said Discord had updated, because the app wrote its new version number before it was in use. A game "installed" ten minutes into its download The same thing happened with Steam, bigger. The Timeline said ARC Raiders was installed. At that moment it was ten minutes into a 55 GB download. Steam lists a game as soon as its download starts. Version 0.21.1 waits until the download is done before calling a game installed. What they have in common In each case RigSight trusted a source that was telling the truth about something slightly different. Windows' list said what was downloaded, not what was running. Steam's list said what was started, not what was finished. A network stream said nothing, which looked the same as nothing happening. The fix each time was to check the thing itself. Is the new version the one running? Is the download finished? Is the network busy while the stream says it's quiet? I also changed how I treat silence. In a few places RigSight now tells a gap apart from a quiet moment and says which one it is. A stretch with no readings is shaded as "Not recorded" on charts. A Storage scan shows how far along it is, after a user saw nothing happen and thought the app had crashed. When RigSight doesn't know what happened, it should say so, and never show it as "nothing happened".

t: My PC wasn't losing power in its sleep
d: RigSight said my PC kept losing power while asleep. It didn't. I had misread a number in Windows' own crash record.
l: Building RigSight
b: When Windows goes down without a proper shutdown, it writes an entry to its event log the next time it starts. It's event 41, from a source called Kernel-Power, and if you have ever looked into random restarts you have probably met it. RigSight reads these entries so the Crashes page can show when your PC went down and why. By the start of October, RigSight was telling me my own PC lost power while it was asleep. Again and again. In the 30 days up to 1 October, it counted 22 shutdowns that didn't finish properly and only 7 that did. That's the kind of thing that makes you look at your power supply with suspicion. But I don't switch my PC off at the wall, and the lights in my house hadn't been flickering 22 times a month. A field with a misleading name Event 41 has a field called SleepInProgress . I read it the way the name reads, as "was the PC asleep when it went down?" If the value was anything but zero, RigSight said yes. That's not what it means. The field holds the power state Windows was moving into when things stopped. It's a number, and each number is a different state. What the number in event 41 means. My first reading treated anything above 0 as "asleep". On my PC the number was a 6. Windows was switching off, and the shutdown never quite finished. RigSight saw "not zero" and called it a power loss during sleep. Fast Startup makes it worse. It's on by default in Windows, and it makes "Shut down" work a bit like hibernating, so the PC starts faster next time. That means a normal shutdown with Fast Startup goes through state 5. Any of those that didn't finish would also have looked like sleep. There was a second field I had leaned on, SystemSleepTransitionsToOn . It counts how many times the PC has woken up since it last started. That tells you nothing about what was happening at the moment it went down, so RigSight stopped using it for that. The fix, including the old entries Version 0.14.2 reads the number as a state. A 5 or a 6 now means "the PC didn't finish shutting down", which is what it really means, and true sleep only comes from 2 to 4. Fixing it going forward wasn't enough, because RigSight keeps history. Every wrong label from before would have stayed wrong. So the next scan of Windows' log went back over the stored shutdowns and corrected them too. Being careful with the word "power" That bug made me careful with anything that sounds like a power cut. Two weeks later, when crashes started getting a cause and a confidence word, the rules for power got strict. A shut-off is only a likely power cut when the PC was idle and cool, nobody held the power button and Windows logged nothing else. A shut-off under load is only a possible problem with the mains or the power supply. The time a PC went down comes from the last minute RigSight recorded, not the earlier time Windows sometimes gives. The lesson I took from it is a plain one. A field's name is a hint, not a definition. When a reading tells a dramatic story, like power failing every night, check what the number really holds before believing the story.

t: How light is light? Measuring an app that never closes
d: Someone suggested rewriting RigSight's sensor reading in C++. Measuring first showed where the time really goes, and that I had read the wrong memory number.
l: Building RigSight
b: RigSight's recorder never closes. It starts with Windows and reads your sensors every couple of seconds for as long as the PC is on. If it cost even 1% of your processor, that would be a real tax on a gaming PC, all day, every day. So "how light is it?" is a question I get a lot, and one I ask myself. On 30 September a user made a good suggestion. Write the hardware polling in C++ instead of C#, to make the app lighter. It's a fair instinct. C++ has a reputation for being fast. Before rewriting anything, I wanted to know where the time actually went. Where the time goes I measured the installed recorder with its window closed, for two minutes, on my PC. It used 0.078% of one processor core in its own code and 0.208% inside Windows itself. So about 73% of its time wasn't RigSight's code at all. It was Windows and the drivers, talking to the hardware. Then I timed one full read of every sensor on the PC, the slowest case possible. It took 214 milliseconds of waiting. Almost all of it was the devices themselves taking their time to answer. One full read of every sensor on my PC, by device. The GPU and the spinning hard drive are slow to answer, whatever language asks. The C# part of that read was about 6% of its processor time. And the real recorder never does a full read. It asks only for what it needs, which costs about 6 milliseconds of processor time every two seconds. So a rewrite would have been weeks of work, and it would have meant replacing the sensor library RigSight is built on, for a saving too small to see in Task Manager. I tried the one cheap native option too, compiling the existing code ahead of time. The tooling for the recorder's kind of app doesn't support it. I wrote all of this back to the user, with the numbers. The number I got wrong The same day I made a mistake that is easy to make on Windows. I looked at the recorder's "private bytes", saw about 110 MB, and told the user its memory was high and growing. It wasn't. Private bytes counts memory the program has reserved, including memory it has never touched. The number Task Manager shows, and the one that actually takes RAM from your games, is the private working set. After five and a half hours, that was 21.8 MB. I corrected myself the same day. I keep that one as a reminder. Measuring is only useful if you measure the right thing, and with memory on Windows there are at least four "right-looking" numbers to choose from. Lighter where it counts Not every idea that makes RigSight faster is worth its cost either. Later, in 0.19.2, I tried sending readings to the open window every second instead of every two. With the window open, the recorder went from 0.13% to 0.22% of the PC. Smoother numbers weren't worth that, so I left it at two seconds. Today the site says about 0.02% of the PC on my test machine, a Ryzen 7 5700X3D, with the window closed, measured in Task Manager. It's a small number, and I check it before every release. If it ever grows, I want to know before you do.

t: The day RigSight told me my healthy fan was clogged
d: A warning that compared a resting PC with a gaming one, and the rule it left behind. Compare like with like, or say nothing.
l: Building RigSight
b: A big part of RigSight is the short lines it writes about your PC. "You gamed 25 minutes less than your usual Saturday." "Your GPU was hotter than usual in this game." I call them insights, and they are the reason the app exists. Anyone can draw a chart. Telling you which part of the chart matters is harder. On 29 September one of them told me this. Your GPU fan runs 1,473 rpm faster than usual at the same temperature. Your cooler may be clogging. That's a scary sentence. It's the kind that makes you open the case and start blowing dust out. My fan was fine. What it had actually compared Most modern GPUs stop their fans when the card is cool. So a big share of "usual" fan minutes were idle minutes at 0 rpm. The insight lined those up with minutes from a game, where the fans were spinning normally, and called the difference unusual. On top of that, the fan readings it used were stale. Every number in the sentence was real. The comparison was nonsense. What it compared Fan minutes at rest, mostly stopped, against fan minutes in a game. What it compares now The same game, at steady load, at the same GPU power, with the room's temperature taken out. Like for like, or nothing I could have patched that one insight. Instead I went through all of them and asked one question. Is this comparing two things that should behave the same? Heat is now only compared at what I call steady load. That means the same app, with the GPU at 80% or more, after its first 10 minutes so the cooler has warmed up. The room is taken out by looking at the PC's resting temperatures on both days. A summer evening and a winter morning are not the same test. For "your GPU runs hotter than it used to", the bar is high. The difference has to be at least 5 degrees, at least 3 degrees more than the change at rest, at the same GPU power within 15%, with an hour of steady play behind it. A lot of insights didn't survive the question, so these went. Week against week temperature comparisons Temperature drift at idle How fast the PC cooled down after a game CPU throttling Fan speed comparisons Advice to put the PC to sleep sooner Some of those sounded clever. None of them were fair comparisons. A fake PC to keep it honest I didn't want to find out about the next bad insight from my own PC. So I built a pretend one. It's a small simulation that plays out months of a PC's life. The room warms and cools through the day and the seasons. A cooler warms up, dust builds up with use, fans stop at rest or wear out, and a GPU throttles. The rule for it is strict. A healthy pretend PC, run for 45 days, 8 weeks or 3 months, must produce zero warnings. And each fault I add, a worn fan or a dusty cooler, has to be found only once it actually happens, never before. Where it went next Three weeks later, version 0.28.0 took the same idea further and called it "Normal for this PC". Each game's temperatures are set against that same game on the same PC over the two months before, at steady load and the same GPU power. Fans that change speed after a restart are read as a BIOS change and start a fresh "usual" instead of raising an alarm. I think about that fan warning a lot. A missing warning costs you nothing today. A wrong one costs you an evening with a can of air, and the next time RigSight says something, you trust it a little less.

t: Getting numbers inside a fullscreen game
d: Why a normal window can't draw over some games, how RivaTuner gets around it, and the see-through panel that turned solid black.
l: Building RigSight
b: A game overlay sounds like the easy part of a PC monitor. Put a small box in the corner, show the temperature and the frame rate, done. The first version, 0.4.0, did exactly that. It was its own see-through window that a shortcut turned on and off. It worked in windowed games and in borderless ones. Then I opened a game in exclusive fullscreen and the overlay was gone. Why the window disappears In exclusive fullscreen, the game takes over the screen. Windows stops putting other windows on top of it, so my overlay window was still there, just not drawn. No setting on my side could change that. The tool that gets around this is RivaTuner Statistics Server. It is what MSI Afterburner uses for its overlay. It hooks into the game's own drawing and adds text to each frame. Other apps can hand it text to show. So from 0.4.1, when a game runs in exclusive fullscreen, RigSight passes its overlay to RivaTuner instead of drawing its own. RivaTuner is optional. Setup offers to install it, and without it you still get everything else. It only adds the frame rate and the overlay inside those games. Two overlays that should look like one Now there were two overlays. One was mine, drawn by RigSight. The other was RivaTuner's, drawn from text and a small set of formatting codes. I wanted nobody to be able to tell which one they were looking at. Same font, same rounded panel, grey units, the same corner. RivaTuner's formatting is limited, so a few things needed tricks. Text near the screen edge got cut off, so it needed padding inside its panel. Only one font works per block of text, so labels can't be bold. Right and left alignment use the same code with a minus sign. None of this is hard once you know it. You just find out one by one. The panel that turned black On 27 September I made RigSight use RivaTuner in more games, any game it was already running in, not only exclusive fullscreen ones. Soon after, the overlay in those games had a solid black panel behind the numbers. The setting said the background should be fully see-through. The cause was a colour code. RivaTuner takes colours with a see-through value in front. A value of 00, fully see-through, is read as "no see-through value given", which RivaTuner treats as solid. So the more see-through you asked for, the more solid you got, right at the end of the slider. The bug had been there since 0.4.4, four days earlier. Hardly anyone saw it, because hardly any games used that path. The moment I sent more games down it, everyone using a clear background saw a black box. The rule that came out of it Changing when an old piece of code runs puts its old bugs in front of everyone. Since then, any change to the overlay gets checked side by side before it ships. I put RigSight's own overlay next to RivaTuner's for every setting, at every size, with and without a background, in colour and in grey. It's a sheet of pictures I look over. It takes a few minutes, and it would have caught this one.

t: Day one, and 25 versions before midnight
d: The first public day of RigSight, what it set out to do, and the first mistake it shipped, which counted the page file as RAM.
l: Building RigSight
b: Every PC monitor I had used works the same way. You open it, it shows what your PC is doing right now, and when you close it, all of that is gone. If your GPU hit 85 degrees at 2 AM in the middle of a game, you will never know, unless the window happened to be open and you happened to be looking. That was the whole idea behind RigSight. Record the temperatures, the apps, the crashes, all day, and keep them. Then let me look back at any day the way I would look at a bank statement. I built RigSight for more than one reason. The first was HWiNFO. It's a great tool and it shows almost every sensor in a PC, but it wasn't giving me the history I wanted. I could see what my PC was doing right now. I couldn't easily see what it did yesterday, or last week, or how this month compared with the one before. The second reason is simply me. I have always loved looking back at time. What I did, how much of it, when. Hours in a game, how late the PC stayed on, which week was the busiest. A PC already knows all of that. It just never writes it down. Two programs, on purpose The first decision shaped everything after it. RigSight is two programs. One is a small recorder that starts with Windows and writes a reading every couple of seconds. The other is the window you open to look at your history. The window can close whenever you like. The recorder keeps going. This split is why RigSight can remember anything at all. It also set the bar for the next month. The recorder has to be so light that nobody ever thinks about it. A very long day The project had lived under another name, ThermoDeck, before 23 September. That day it became RigSight and went public. It also went through 25 versions before midnight. Here is some of what went out that day. Home got its own tiles for the day's CPU and GPU peaks. Peaks started saying what you were doing at that minute, like "while playing Counter-Strike 2". Custom pages built from tiles you drag around, which later became Dashboards. A game overlay that a shortcut turns on and off, and then the same overlay inside fullscreen games. FPS in the overlay, today's highs and lows, 24 hours of history and drive health. That second item is the one I still like most. A number like "GPU 79°" is trivia. "GPU 79° while playing a game for three hours" is something you can do something about. The first thing I got wrong Moving that fast has a cost, and it showed up within hours. The memory reading was wrong. Windows reports a few different numbers for memory. The one I picked first included the page file, the space on your drive that Windows uses when RAM runs out. So RigSight was showing RAM plus a chunk of disk and calling it RAM, a number that had little to do with the memory sticks in the PC. The fix was one line that reads physical memory only. Finding it took longer, because the number looked plausible most of the time. That turned into a habit I kept for the rest of the month. When a reading looks fine, check it against something you trust anyway. For memory, that is Task Manager. What I'd tell myself on day one Shipping 25 versions in a day felt like progress, and a lot of it was. But the following weeks were mostly about making the numbers right, not adding more of them. A monitor that keeps history has a special problem. If a reading is wrong, it is wrong in your history forever, and you might make decisions from it weeks later. That idea comes up again and again in the posts after this one.
